en: Preface to the *Record of Manifested Responses from the Lotus Sūtra*.
The teachings of Western India reach heights that are utterly inconceivable; they cannot be fully extolled even throughout kalpas.
As for the manifestation of their supernatural powers to subdue demons and rescue those in suffering—though these exceed human capacity—they are but secondary matters.
Nevertheless, the reason its teaching has flourished so extensively in the world is largely dependent upon this [translation].
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has been translated three times; however, that translated by Kumārajīva is recited throughout the world.
Its merits and efficacious responses are clearly manifest, as recorded in various biographies and accounts. Indeed, this sutra is truly the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
The *Zang* (Treasury) cannot be understood through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination; thus, its spiritual wonders are such as these.

The local monk Zongxiao recited and practiced it morning and evening, and transcribed it by drawing blood from his own body. Furthermore, he compiled over two hundred accounts from ancient and modern records and documents, resulting in a massive volume that is entirely supported by authoritative sources.
He intends to have it carved into printing blocks for circulation in the world, thereby aiding its dissemination.

I visited Tong’s residence one day; he lived in a state of serene detachment. When I spoke with him, I found his mastery of the various Buddhist teachings (jiao-cheng) to be profound and comprehensive.
I asked why he did not emerge to lead a community of disciples. He replied, "It is not something I dare presume. Thereupon, he presented this book and requested that I write a preface for it.
I said:

The Yellow-Faced Old Man originally had no desire to speak. That which is seen in the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*) and that which is秘 (hidden) within the Dragon Palace and the Ocean Treasury are boundless and inexhaustible;
in truth, he never spoke them at all. How much less could this sutra—which appears as a fragmentary remnant among other matters—be his word?
Since you have already compiled it, why should I further provide a preface? Please do not press me; I shall write this down in a casual manner.

He bestowed [the teachings] upon him and said to him: "If you wish to fully comprehend this before traveling to various regions, then one day, upon ascending to the Precious Abode and awakening to your original nature, you will even forget the trap and the snare—how much more so this [teaching]? Xiao replied, "Yes."

*The Record of Manifested Responses to the Lotus Sūtra*, Volume One (Including Preface).
Compiled by the śramaṇa Zongxiao of Shimizhi in Siming.
In the past, the Chan Master Yongming Zhijue, by means of his great eloquence, composed five rhymed prose pieces (fu), namely: *The Resonance and Communication of the Avataṃsaka*.

The Vajra-attestation, the auspicious portents of the Lotus Sūtra, the manifestation of Avalokiteśvara’s divine power, and the spirit’s abiding in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing—these embellish the sacred teachings and stir the faculties of all sentient beings;

thus, they may be said to have rendered great service to the Semblance Dharma Age. Nevertheless, as for the composition of this prose-poem (*fu*), it is specifically intended for the purpose of singing and praising;
regarding the full details of these events from beginning to end, nothing but a formal biographical record (*zhuanji*) can suffice.
It is widely known that for the *Avataṃsaka* there is the *Ganying zhuan* (Records of Responses); for the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Yingyan lu* (Records of Miraculous Verifications);

for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Lingshui ji* (Collection of Auspicious Omens); for Avalokiteśvara, the *Ganying ji* (Collection of Responses); and for the Pure Land, the *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Those Reborn).

One who observes these closely and reads them extensively will know that the miraculous verifications of the Buddha-dharma are not merely numerous, but truly inexhaustible. Now, regarding this single collection of auspicious omens in the world...
There are two versions. One is titled simply *Lingshui* (Numinous Auspiciousness), and the other is the *Xu lingshui ji* (Continued Collection of Numinous Auspiciousness).
Regarding the version titled simply *Lingshui*, it lists sixty items internally but does not record the person who compiled them; it only contains a preface written by Yang Xi during the Jiayu era.

This original edition existed previously and has recently been re-engraved for publication; however, it does not specify the sources from which the material was drawn, making no distinction between the accounts of monastics and laypeople.

Furthermore, the biographical records of the various patriarchs are incomplete. Such negligence and deficiency hardly constitute a standard model, and thus this *Continued Collection of Spiritual Omens* has been compiled.

Subsequently, during the Daguang era, the Dharma Master Yuǎnyǐng of Wǔxīng renovated the old and added to the new, organizing it into ten sections beginning with "Universal Virtue’s Testimony" and ending with "Fragrant Light’s Auspicious Manifestation.
This version was somewhat superior and largely rectified the errors of the preceding edition.
However, before long, the printing blocks were lost for a long time, and many who sought them were unable to see this version. I have reflected upon this in private...

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the ultimate scripture; it is truly the fundamental source from which all Buddhas descend to manifest in the world, and the profound origin through which all sentient beings attain the Way.
It is that which the Great Beings, who are nearly equal to the Sages, urge others to undertake, and that which the foremost devas protect and uphold.

Today, whether one has left the household life or remains at home, there are none who do not offer their sincere devotion to its recitation and none who do not apply their utmost effort to its cultivation. Should the divine efficacy and magnificent traces of this work not be realized...
Within the archives and records, the words and deeds of former sages would otherwise not be heard in the world; how then could they serve as a basis for exhortation and faith?

Zongxiao, though unworthily invested with the monastic robes, has long cherished the aspiration to hear and uphold the Dharma. He deeply lamented that the previous compilations were incomplete and that the subsequent supplements were likewise deficient.
Thereupon, he conducted a thorough investigation of the Tripitaka, the *Monastic Biographies of the Three Reigns*, and both Buddhist and secular statutes.
Inclusion is made of both the hidden and the manifest, with both new and old accounts listed side by side. In total, there are two hundred and thirty-nine entries.
First, the ancient sages are presented as the preface; next, they are categorized according to four examples: eminent monks, eminent nuns, laymen of faith, and laywomen of faith.

These are divided into two volumes and titled the *Fahua Xianyingshu* (Record of Manifested Responses to the Lotus Sūtra). This is modeled after the *Xianshi* (Manifestations of the Present Age) found in the Tiantai school.
The superior signs manifested through body and speech are what is meant by the "manifestation of the capacity" and the "manifestation of the response.

Those included in this record have for the most part concentrated their spirits on the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and applied themselves deeply to the True Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*). Their firm resolve was sufficient to suppress pines and bamboos; their refined sincerity was sufficient to penetrate metal and stone.
Thus, the gravity of these responses was like the arrival of the ceremonial phoenix at the Xiao Emperor’s summons. For this reason, they are bequeathed to posterity.
Come! If one person understands this, thousands and tens of thousands will be encouraged. Let none fail to realize that their mortal dwelling is destined for incineration.
When the high plateau erupts in a torrential deluge, one must immediately board a lofty, vast, and great vehicle to proceed directly toward the most profound realm; this is my aspiration.

As for those who are carried [by this vehicle], there may be some who possess the causal conditions but lack the corresponding response; this, moreover, manifests how the latent capacity meets with the hidden response. Behold!
[This] fully clarifies [the matter]. On an auspicious day at the beginning of the second month of the *wǔwǔ* year of the Qìngyuán era, Zōngxiǎo respectfully composed this preface.
(The seven matters concerning the ancient sages are all found in the original scripture.
The Many Treasures Stūpa emerged from the earth to hear the Dharma.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna. When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this great vow:

"If, after I have attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa, there should be places in the lands of the ten directions where the Lotus Sūtra is being preached, may my stupa emerge before them for the sake of hearing this sūtra, acting as a witness. Now, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna...
Stūpa. Because they had heard the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they surged forth from the earth and praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
The Buddha Prabhūtaratna had made this vow: "Should anyone wish to show my body to the fourfold assembly, they must first assemble all the Buddhas who are the emanations of that Buddha.

Once they have assembled, open the stūpa. Prabhūtaratna then shared his seat, and Śākyamuni sat upon it together with him. Then he spoke these words of the Dharma: "O Holy Lord, World-Honored One, although..."
Though he entered parinirvāṇa long ago and now resides within a jeweled stūpa, he still comes for the sake of the Dharma. Why, then, do you all not strive diligently for the sake of the Dharma?
Śākyamuni, while seeking this sūtra as a king, never grew weary;
the Buddha told the fourfold assembly: "Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* without ever falling into indolence."
Throughout many kalpas, he constantly served as a king, making vows to seek unexcelled bodhi with a mind that never regressed.
For the sake of the Dharma, he relinquished his royal throne and entrusted it to the crown prince; he then beat the drum to proclaim a decree throughout the four quarters, seeking the Dharma.
"Whoever can explain the Mahāyāna for me, I shall serve and attend upon them for the rest of my life.
At that time, there was a seer named Asita who came and said to the king, "I possess the Mahāyāna, called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim it for you.
Upon hearing the seer’s words, the king rejoiced and leaped for joy; he immediately followed the seer, providing him with all necessities, and gathered [herbs].
He drew water, gathered firewood, and prepared food; even using his own body as a bed and seat, he never grew weary in body or mind.
Thus he served him for a thousand years, diligently attending to him for the sake of the Dharma so that he lacked nothing.
At that time, the king was Śākyamuni; the rishi at that time was the present Devadatta. Because of Devadatta...
Because of the spiritual friend Dharmodgata, I have been enabled to fulfill the six pāramitās, attain equal and perfect enlightenment, and extensively deliver sentient beings;
thus, the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging has propagated the Lotus Sūtra.
In the distant past, during the period of the Semblance Dharma of the first Tathāgata, Vipaśyin-rāja (King of Majestic Sound), there were arrogant bhikṣus who possessed great power.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Sadāparibhūta (Never-Disparaging).
Whenever this bhikṣu saw the fourfold assembly, he would prostrate to them all, praise them, and say: "I deeply revere you; I do not dare to treat you with contempt."
"You all practice the bodhisattva path and shall attain Buddhahood. Yet this bhikṣu does not devote himself exclusively to reading and reciting the sūtras, but only practices prostrations.
Among the fourfold assembly, there are those who give rise to thoughts of anger and impurity, speaking with harsh words and reviling him, saying:
'This is an ignorant bhikṣu; from where has he come? We have no need for such false teachings.'"
[Commentary: The multitude sometimes struck and pelted him with sticks, wood, tiles, and stones.
He fled and stayed at a distance, yet he continued to cry out in a loud voice: "I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas.
Because he constantly spoke these words, he was called "Never-Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta). When this bhikṣu was about to pass away, in the midst of the void...
Having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* previously preached by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna (King of Majestic Sound), he was able to receive and uphold it in its entirety.

He immediately attained the purity of the six sense faculties and extensively expounded this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for others. At that time, the one named "Not-Disdainful" (Adīnaprajña) was none other than Śākyamuni.
Had I not received and upheld this sutra in my past lives and not expounded it for others, I would not have been able to so swiftly attain Bodhi. Thus says the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
A questioner asked: "Why was it that when Śākyamuni appeared in the world, he hesitated and did not speak, whereas Viśeṣacintin, upon a single glance, spoke without hesitation?

The answer is: "If one already possesses goodness, Śākyamuni protects them by means of the small; if one does not yet possess goodness, Viśeṣacintin treats them with the great and forcefully administers the bitter medicine.
Nanping Qingbian Yunqi composed a verse: "A precious sword, not yet drawn, is hidden within its jade scabbard."
The casket: the cold radiance of the seven stars already flickers within. I earnestly tell those nearby: "Within lies the Dragon Spring;
do not treat it with contempt.
With joy, I behold this one who offers his own body as an offering to the wondrous sutra.

In the past, the Buddha Sun Moon Pure Brightness (*Sūryacandraprabhā-vimala*) preached the Lotus Sūtra for the Bodhisattva Delighting All Sentient Beings to See (*Sarvasattvapriyadarśana*), along with a multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
This bodhisattva delighted in accumulating ascetic practices and sought Buddhahood with single-minded devotion.
After twelve thousand years had passed, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana*). Having attained this samādhi, he immediately formed this thought:
He said, "That I have attained these samādhis is entirely due to the power of hearing the Lotus Sūtra. I shall now make offerings to the Buddha and the Lotus Sūtra.
Although I could make offerings through supernatural powers, it would not be as good as making offerings with my own body.
Thereupon, he manifested his own body before the Buddha, and its radiance shone throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty billion Ganges Rivers. Within them...
The Buddhas simultaneously praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent! This is true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata.
His body burned with fire for twelve hundred years. After his life ended, he was reborn in the land of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, in the house of King Viśuddhaśrī.
He spoke to his father, saying, "I have already attained liberation through my previous offerings to the Buddha."

Having heard the *Sarvasattva-bhāṣita-dhāraṇī* and furthermore this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, even after that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, Priyadarśana offered worship before eighty-four thousand stūpas containing his relics by setting his arm—adorned with the hundred blessings—on fire for seventy-two thousand years.
The commentary on the text explains: "Priyadarśana suddenly sacrificed his own body."
He further burned both his arms, regarding his life as light and the Dharma as weighty; though his life was extinguished, the Way remained.

From afar, Miaoyin came to hear the Lotus Sutra, as Śākyamuni Buddha emitted light from the uṣṇīṣa on his crown, which shone everywhere throughout the east across one hundred and eight myriads of koṭis of nayutas of worlds.
Beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a buddha-land called Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom.
In that land, there is a bodhisattva named Wondrous Sound who has long since planted the roots of all virtues.
This bodhisattva wishes to depart from the Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom Buddha’s land with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to come here to this Sahā world.
They wish to make offerings to me and also desire to make offerings while listening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from his own land and set out together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas. Then, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed Gadgadasvara, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You are able to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
Therefore, I have come here.
In the past, there were four bhikṣus who cultivated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
These four bhikṣus of former times conceived a most profound and earnest reverence for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [treating] its secret teachings as the nectar of immortality.

They had not yet received [any support]. Consequently, they formed a bond in the mountain forests, vowing together to pursue the Buddha’s wisdom. As they dwelt in seclusion for many days, their clothing and provisions were completely exhausted.
With a single meal for ten thousand miles, how can one even speak of their aspirations toward the clouds and the heavens?
One of them said: "We four are so impoverished that we cannot even preserve our own bodies; where, then, should the Dharma be entrusted? You three should offer your lives to the Way, while I alone—"

They should provide whatever is required. From then on, he shook his mendicant’s staff at every gate and threshold to seek alms; though the seasons shifted between cold and heat, he remained content and never showed resentment.
Consequently, the three men’s work was perfected and their task accomplished. The benefit to the world shall endure for immeasurable lifetimes.

As for one of them, he frequently traversed the human realm and repeatedly encountered sensory distractions. Being like an unbaked vessel that has not yet been fired, he was difficult to protect and maintain. By chance—
Seeing the king’s comings and goings, with his carriages and horses creating a clamorous throng, they gave rise to thoughts and stirred their minds, coveting that splendor.

Through the cultivation of merit, they received retribution according to their thoughts; they constantly became kings among humans and in the heavens. Although such blessings were beyond measure, they were nonetheless finite.
Once the three men had attained the fruit of the Way, they gathered and deliberated, saying: "We have escaped the cage of worldly existence; this merit is due to this man. As for him—
They are addicted to karmic retribution and increase their conditioned existence; once they die from this state, they shall sink into a pit of fire. It is fortunate that they have not yet fallen;

it is precisely now that you should establish your transformative teachings for them. One person said: "This king is attached to desire and furthermore holds wrong views; unless there is the hook of affection, there is no way to pull him out.
Another said: "One may become a beautiful wife, and two may become intelligent sons. The words of a son’s wife will surely [be effective]."

In accordance with what was appropriate, he established a transformative teaching so that they attained the fruit of reforming their heterodoxy. At that time, the king was none other than King Wondrous Adornment;
he is now the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue. His wife was Lady Pure Virtue; she is now the Bodhisattva Radiant Adorned Mark.
Their two sons from former times were Pure Treasury and Pure Eye; they are now the two Bodhisattvas Medicine King and Superior Medicine. Thus it was said.

This is the prior cause for the Four Noble Ones; therefore, this chapter is titled "The Fundamental Matter" (*nidāna*). For a detailed exposition according to the *Wenju* (Words and Phrases) of the *Lotus Sūtra*, see that work.
Nanping’s verse says: "In years past we gathered at the secluded stream; Three steps toward the blue clouds, one fell into the mud.
With slight skill applied, we gladly suffered the breaking of our horns; Now the Great Master claps his hands as we ascend the celestial ladder."
The Universal Worthy Bodhisattva Encourages the Propagation and Circulation:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra came from the eastern direction and addressed the Buddha, saying, "In the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja,
I heard from afar that in this Sahā world, the Lotus Sūtra was being preached together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas."
Please come and listen. We pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us: how can a person, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*?
The Buddha told Samantabhadra: "If a person accomplishes four dharmas, they shall obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
First, they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Second, they plant the roots of all virtues."
Third, entering the stage of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Fourth, giving rise to the mind that seeks to rescue all sentient beings.
By thus accomplishing these four dharmas, one will certainly obtain this sutra. Samantabhadra addressed the Buddha, saying: "In the latter five hundred years, during the age of turbidity and evil..."
"Whoever upholds this sutra, I shall protect and guard them, removing all their misfortunes and afflictions.

Whether that person is walking or standing while reading and reciting this sutra, I will at that time manifest my own form, riding upon a six-tusked white elephant together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas, to provide offerings and protection.
This is also for the sake of making offerings to the Lotus Sutra. If that person, regarding the Lotus Sutra..."

"If there be a single phrase or a single verse of this sutra that has been lost or forgotten, I shall teach it. The commentary on the text states: The Buddha takes four dharmas as a crown to encompass this entire sutra.
This is the re-enactment of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the renewed proclamation of the Buddha’s wisdom. That he has come from afar to exhort and inspire—such is its meaning.
The eulogy by Nanping says: "Samantabhadra seeks out the sound and comes for this very purpose; the Great Spirit has just opened [the way], severing all subtle obstructions."
Dust. For what reason does the Elephant King frequently shift his steps? It is because he loves the fragrant *pundarīka* flowers covering the moss on the courtyard steps.
[High Monks: (a total of one hundred and seventy-three)] Mahāla Bhikṣus from the Kingdom of India.
Formerly, in the kingdom of India, there was an araṇyaka bhikṣu named Mahāla. He had studied the Mahāyāna extensively, and his virtuous conduct was widely renowned.
The king possessed correct faith; once, he spread out his hair to cover the mud so that the bhikṣu might walk upon it.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu came and said to the king, "This man has not read many scriptures; why do you offer him such great veneration? The king replied, "Once, when I..."
One night at midnight, wishing to see this bhikṣu, I went to his location. I saw him in a cave reciting the Lotus Sūtra.
A person of golden radiance was riding a white elephant, and the king joined his palms in worship.
Just as I approached, that figure vanished. I asked the Venerable One, "Is it because I have come that the person of golden radiance has disappeared?"
The bhikṣu said, "This is Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Samantabhadra himself declared, "If there is anyone who recites the Lotus Sūtra, I shall come riding upon a white elephant to instruct them.
Since I have read this sūtra, Samantabhadra has come of his own accord.
Samantabhadra is none other than the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra within the Lotus Sūtra. Having heard this, I prostrated at his feet and withdrew. Therefore...
I now constantly offer worship to the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa, the Dharma Master who protected the Tripiṭaka from Dunhuang.

He was a man from the country of Yuezhi. At the age of eight, he left the secular world. All... [of his deeds]... (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra). (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the extant portion.)

Upon seeing a scripture, he could recite it from memory; he recorded ten thousand words daily. He traveled west to various countries, mastering thirty-six types of languages, scripts, glossaries, and phonologies.
Having resided for a long time in Dunhuang, he was popularly known as the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva.

During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Western Jin dynasty, he brought Sanskrit manuscripts to Luoyang. Subsequently, he extensively studied the Five Classics and the historical records. By the Yongkang era, at...
At a great monastery outside the Blue Gate (Qingmen) in Chang’an, he translated one work in ten fascicles, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and subsequently expounded it for the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, he translated a total of one hundred and fifty-four other scriptures, all of which were promulgated by imperial decree.

At that time, he was living in seclusion in the deep mountains. There was a clear spring there from which he drew water for his ablutions and daily needs. One day, a woodcutter defiled the area, and suddenly—
The spring went dry. Dharmarakṣa sighed and said, "Because people lack virtue, this clear spring has ceased its flow.

Now that what is required is lacking, I must depart. Having finished speaking, the clear spring surged forth once more. Zhi Dun praised him, saying: "Master Dharmarakṣa realized the state of quiescence; his moral cultivation was profound and beautiful.
As he chanted softly in the deep valley, the dried-up spring gurgled with water. How sublime was Master Dharmarakṣa! Heaven-born and magnificently noble, he washed his feet in the flowing stream."
Sha. *Qingba Xuanzhi* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty).
Dharma Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Three Piṭaka Masters.

"Jiumoluoshi" (Kumārajīva) is translated as "Child Longevity" (Tongshou) in the Qin language. He was a native of Kucha. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and recited [scriptures] daily.
He composed a thousand verses. His mother once took him to the country of Yuezhi, where he met an arhat who said:

"This śrāmaṇera, when he reaches the age of thirty-five, if he does not break the precepts, shall greatly propagate the Buddha-dharma and deliver countless people. If his precepts are not complete, he will merely be a Dharma Master of talent and brilliance.
His mother took these words to heart. One day, she said to him: "The profound teachings of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) should be [propagated] on a grand scale..."

"Revealing the True Dharma is solely due to your power; it simply brings no benefit to your own person. Kumārajīva replied, "The Way of a Great Being is to benefit others even at the cost of one's life.
If the Great Dharma can be spread so that it may cleanse the ignorant masses, I would have no regrets even if my body were cast into a cauldron of boiling oil.
At that time, Fu Jian held sway over Guanzhong. The Grand Astrologer reported, saying, "A star of virtue has appeared in the region of the foreign lands."
"Wilderness. There shall be a man of great wisdom who enters to assist the Central Kingdom. Yao Jian said, "I have heard that there is one named Kumārajīva in the Western Regions;
could it not be he? He immediately dispatched Lü Guang to lead troops to attack Kucha. Having captured Kumārajīva, Lü Guang returned to Liangzhou.
Hearing that Fu Jian had been killed by Yao Chang, he took up residence outside the Passes and usurped the title of Later Liang. Upon Yao Chang’s death, his son Yao Xing succeeded to the throne.
Suddenly, twin-stemmed trees grew within the ancestral temple courtyard, and the chives in the Xiaoyao Garden transformed into calamus; these were taken as auspicious omens.
He subsequently conquered Lü Lóng and welcomed Kumārajīva to Cháng'ān, where he was honored with the rites due to a National Teacher (Guoshī).
Emperor Xìng invited various *śramaṇas* to the Xiāoyáo Garden to listen to Kumārajīva’s expositions. Kumārajīva’s eloquence and penetration were renowned throughout China and the Hu regions.

Observing that the existing Chinese translations diverged from the Indic originals (*húběn*), in the eighth year of the Hóngshǐ era, at Cǎotáng Monastery, he compared the old versions with [the new ones] alongside over eight hundred monks, including Sēngqiè.
After verifying the texts, he translated this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in one volume consisting of seven fascicles.
Daosheng remarked, "The Dharma Master’s intelligence and transcendent realization are peerless in the world; how could he be left without heirs? He then coerced him with ten courtesans.
From that time on, pure practitioners were ashamed even to hear of such matters. Whenever the Master reached the point of lecturing on this passage, he would invariably say: "It is like foul mud..."
A lotus flower grew there; he simply gathered the lotuses and did not look at the foul mud. Later, he suddenly fell ill and addressed the assembly, saying:

"We have met because of the Dharma, yet we have truly not exhausted our hearts. Now that the conditions for our association have ended, may the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other scriptures I have translated be fortunately circulated together.
If what I have translated is without error, I pray that after my body is cremated, my tongue will not be scorched or decayed. Having finished speaking, he passed away. As for...
Upon his cremation, his tongue remained unburnt by the fire. This is clearly recorded in the *Biographies of the Monks of the Liang Dynasty* (*Liáng Sēng Zhuàn*) and the *Book of Jin* (*Jìn Shū*).

In the *Nánshān Gǎntōng Zhuàn*, the Heavenly Being Wei (Weitian) said: "Master Kumārajīva was brilliant and possessed a profound understanding of the Mahāyāna. From the time of the seven Buddhas onward, he has transmitted and translated [the teachings], having received the entrusted legacy of the Dharma King.
As for the common claim that he violated the precepts, there is no need to discuss it; Kumārajīva’s rank was among the Three Sages (*sān xián*). It was not...
Yōuyou (the "Distant One") refers to Dharma Master Ruì of Cháng'ān, whose secular name was Huìruì.
A native of Jì Prefecture, he maintained a lofty and austere integrity. Having traveled abroad to study, he reached the borders of South India.

He was thoroughly versed in the diverse regions and their various scriptures. When Yao Xing, the ruler of the Qin, summoned him for an audience, he was immediately greatly impressed by his refined demeanor and eloquence, declaring him to be a preeminent leader among the four seas.
Previously, when Dharmarakṣa translated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the chapter on "Receiving Predictions," it said:
"The heavens see humans; humans see the heavens. However, when Kumārajīva translated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, at this same point, he stated: "This phrase [is consistent with] the West..."

The meaning of the term *yu* (domain) is the same; it merely expresses that which transcends the substantial. Daorong said, "Is this not the meeting of humans and devas, where both are able to see one another?
Kumārajīva replied joyfully, "Indeed it is. Such was the height of his comprehension and realization. As soon as the translation was completed, he commanded Daorong to lecture upon it.

Daorong then categorized and deliberated upon its profound mysteries, opening them into nine tracks. The first is the "Track of the Mutual Resonance between the Ordinary and the Sage," which corresponds to the Introductory Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*).
Second, the track of entering the teachings to return to the truth, for those of superior faculties. Third, the track of manifesting the latent potential of beings, for those of middling faculties.

Fourth, the track of relating the present to the past, for those of middling faculties who attain understanding through this. Fifth, the track of manifesting causes to advance toward awakening, for those of inferior faculties.
Sixth is the track of praising the journey, which corresponds to the "Chapter on the Dharma Master. Seventh is the track of the non-arising of the original and the manifested;
with the indestructibility of Prabhūtaratna as the original and the non-birth of Śākyamuni as the manifested, though the original and the manifested differ, they are one in their inconceivability.

Eighth is the track of citing causes to verify the fruit, which corresponds to the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" and the "Chapter on the Lifespan. Ninth is the track of extolling the far-reaching salvation, which begins with the "Chapter on Rejoicing."

After he had departed, the scripture was circulated. Zhiyi also composed a preface to the scripture, which is found in the Tripitaka editions. Furthermore, the scripture contains twenty-eight chapters on its origins;

Master Jingxi remarked that it possesses great structural coherence. The Master constantly dedicated his merits from propagating and praising the Dharma for the benefit of others, vowing to be reborn in the Western Paradise.
On the day of his passing, he bathed, changed his robes, burned incense, and performed prostrations. He then sat facing west with palms joined.

At the time of his death, five-colored fragrant clouds were seen emerging from his chamber. The world refers to the four sages born in the school of Kumārajīva as Sengzhao, Daorong, Tanyue, and Daoyi;
the Master was one of them (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* of the Liang Dynasty, cited in the eighth fascicle of the *Fahua Wenju*).

The Dharma Master Huqiu Sheng, whose personal name was Daosheng, took Zhu as his family name following his teacher’s surname. When he reached the age of study, his speech and demeanor were fresh and refined; all people stood in awe and submission before him.
He always held that the essential path to entering the Way is rooted in wisdom and understanding; therefore, he delved into and revered the various sutras without shrinking from toil or hardship.

He subsequently traveled to Guanzhong to receive instruction from Kumārajīva. His eloquence and inquiry were so transcendent that everyone praised him as having attained divine insight (*śrutavimukti*).

Later, he withdrew to Tiger Hill Monastery (*Hǔqū Sī*), where a stone lecture platform remains to this day. At one time, while residing at Bantang, he was reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*).
Suddenly, a pheasant would regularly come to listen. One day it did not appear, and the Master missed it. It entered his dream at night and said: "Because of me..."
Having listened to the sutras, he subsequently attained a transformed rebirth; he is now the son of a certain family and will return to serve [the Master] after several years have passed.
When the Master inquired about this, it was indeed so. Not long after he had left the household life, the youth passed away at the age of seven.
He was buried in a grove, where one night a light suddenly emanated, its radiance illuminating the ponds and marshes. The villagers found this extraordinary and opened the grave to look. It was—
He obtained a single tongue that grew into a blue lotus flower; because of this, a stupa was erected, which later was expanded into a monastery—this is the present-day Bantang Temple.

The Master once proposed the view that "goodness does not receive retribution" and that one attains Buddhahood through sudden enlightenment; however, those who adhered to the literal texts and traditional learning regarded these as heterodox teachings.
The Master made a vow before the assembly, saying: "If what I have established does not contradict the scriptures, then at the time of my passing..."

He sat upon the lion throne. Later, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was translated, its contents accorded perfectly with what he had taught. The Master then ascended the seat and expounded the Dharma; his listeners were enlightened and filled with joy.
As the dharma assembly was nearing its conclusion, his fly-whisk suddenly fell to the ground with a flutter. Sitting upright with a composed countenance, he passed away.
He appeared as if he had entered meditative absorption. People of the time said, "Shengrui has manifested his innate truth. Thus we know that those who excel and stand out are precisely such as this.
(The traces of Bantang Temple are found in the *Xu Lingrui Ji*; the rest is from the *Liang Gaoseng Zhuan*.)
The Great Dhyāna Master Sengzhao of Mount Nanyue, whose name was Huisi, was born into the Li clan of Wujin. In his youth, he dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to leave the household life;
he subsequently entered the Way. He resolved to take only one meal per day and never accepted separate offerings. For ten years he specialized in reciting the Lotus Sūtra, and for seven years...

He constantly practiced the Vaipulya sutras and sat in meditation for ninety days, cultivating the Samādhi of One Practice. Through the power of this diligent effort, he clearly perceived the traces of his practice throughout three lifetimes.
He subsequently traveled to the Chan Master Huiwen of Northern Qi to inquire about and receive instruction in the methods of Chan.
During the long summer retreat, he concentrated his mind; when the summer concluded and the *varṣā* ceremony was performed, he lamented that he had attained no realization.
As he leaned back against a wall, before his body even reached it, he suddenly and expansively awakened to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* as well as other Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna dharma-gates.

Later, while residing at Mount Dasu in Guangzhou, laypeople and monastics offered him gifts of gold to commission the transcription of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras in golden characters. When the assembly requested him to lecture on these two sutras, he immediately...
They discussed these matters together, all of which were profound and subtle. Next, they went to Mount Nanyue and saw that the forests and springs were lofty and pure;
he then said, "This is the site of an ancient temple. Following his words, they dug there and indeed discovered the foundations of a hall and various vessels.

They then went to the base of a cliff, where he said, "In my previous life, I sat in meditation here until a bandit severed my head. From that, my life ended and this present existence began. All of them [believed him].
He searched for it and found a withered skull. The Master took it and wore it upon his head, subsequently erecting a stupa to repay the kindness of his past life.

Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty issued an edict for him to reside at Qixuan Temple; both monastics and laypeople looked up to him with reverence. Once, when he went to Waguan Temple, he was not wet by the rain, nor did his feet become soiled by the mud.
At times he manifested himself in various sizes, and at other times he would suddenly vanish from sight. The water in his jar was always full, as if he were a celestial youth.

He served as an attendant. When someone asked about his spiritual rank, he replied, "I am merely at the stage of the Ten Faiths. On the day of his passing, he gathered his disciples and preached the Dharma;

those who heard it were struck with awe and trepidation. He then declared, "If there are ten people who do not begrudge their own lives and constantly practice the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Pratyutpanna* Samādhis, I shall provide for them all my life.
If no such persons exist, I shall depart immediately. To carry out such ascetic practices is indeed difficult.
No one offered a reply. Thereupon, he withdrew his thoughts and proclaimed, "The assembly of sages comes to welcome me.
He passed away peacefully, causing a rare fragrance to fill the room, which was heard by all far and near. He was sixty-four years old; this was the ninth year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty.

Since the arrival of the Buddha-dharma, many have emphasized various doctrinal gateways, yet only this Master propagated both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) together. His words reached far and wide throughout the North and South.

There was no one in the Chan school who did not follow and uphold his teachings. He once received the crown of his head being rubbed by Samantabhadra, causing a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) to emerge;
those who saw this found it most extraordinary. Practicing great compassion, he observed the Bodhisattva precepts, wearing only coarse cloth and hemp rags rather than leather or silk.
Enduring wind and frost, all that he composed was dictated orally and set down in writing. As many generations passed, these various writings were scattered and lost.

[The text] survives. Only the meaning of the *Anraku-gyō* (Peaceful Practices) from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Ganshomon* (Text on Making Vows) circulate in the world (*Tang Xu gaoseng zhuan*).

Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, National Preceptor of both the Chen and Sui dynasties, named Zhiyi, was descended from the Yingchuan region. His ancestors resided for generations in Huāróng County, Jīngzhōu. As for the Master himself—
He was the middle son of Chen Qizu, a Palace Attendant. His mother was Lady Xu. One night she dreamed that fragrant clouds entwined around her breast, and consequently she became pregnant.

Upon his birth, a divine light manifested in the room. Like Shun with his double pupils and Yao with his eight-colored eyebrows, [he possessed auspicious marks]. At the age of seven, he went to a monastery;
when a monk orally transmitted the *Bannihuanpin* (Universal Gate Chapter) to him, he mastered it entirely upon a single recitation. At fifteen, before a statue in Changsha, he made a vow.
He vowed, "I wish to become a śramaṇa and shoulder the burden of the True Dharma. At eighteen, he left home at Guoyuan Temple in Xiangzhou; at twenty, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He immediately went to Mount Daxian to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, and the *Universal Worthy Visualization*.

After twenty days had passed, he had completed all three texts. With his mouth reciting the golden words and his hands correcting the scriptures and images, his mind and spirit became clear and sharp. Furthermore—

Delighting in the joy of dhyāna, he proceeded next to Mount Dasu to pay homage to Master Zhiyi. Upon seeing him, Zhiyi sighed and said, "In days of yore at Vulture Peak, we heard the Lotus Sūtra together.
Pursued by our past affinities, you have come here once more. He then bestowed upon him the Four Practices of Peaceful Joy from the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-caryā-prasthāna*.
Day and night, he applied himself with diligent effort, training his mind according to the teachings. After two weeks had passed, he was reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*.

When the sutra reaches the passage on the Bodhisattva Medicine King’s relinquishing of his body, all Buddhas praise him in unison, saying: "This is true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata.

Upon reaching this point, his mind was suspended in anguish, yet he suddenly entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*). He clearly illuminated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as if the brilliant light of the sun descended upon a secluded valley.
He attained realization of the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), like a pure breeze wandering through the great void. He inscribed these words of reflection: "It is not you."
I have not yet realized it; were it not for me, who else would know? That state of meditative concentration you have entered is the preliminary skillful means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

That which you have awakened to and maintained is the *Prathama-āvartā-dhāraṇī*. Even if there were thousands of groups and tens of thousands of masses of Dharma masters skilled in words and letters, they could never exhaust your eloquence.
I have long admired Mount Nanyue, yet I regretted having no one to whom I might entrust the Dharma. You may now transmit the lamp and transform others.

He admonished his disciples, saying, "Do not become those who are the last to sever the seeds of the Buddha. Following his teacher’s strict instructions, he then took up his mendicant's staff and traveled to Jinling, where he resided at Waguan Temple.
There, he was the first to expound upon the *Mysterious Meaning of the Lotus Sutra* (*Fahua xuanyi*). He propagated this teaching for a total of eight years.

Subsequently, as the number of his followers increased while those who attained the Way remained few, he withdrew from the world to preserve the profound mystery, retiring to Mount Tiantai. Initially, he rested in seclusion at Yindi.
At that time, he practiced walking meditation on the southeastern peak, or resided in his quarters reciting the Lotus Sūtra and entering samādhi.
Various māras and malevolent spirits vied with one another to come and harass him; yet while in meditative concentration, the Master remained unaware of these supernatural disturbances.

Once, while lecturing and reciting the Lotus Sūtra, he was moved by the appearance of Samantabhadra riding a white elephant, leading the way before him. When he preached the Dharma, it occurred during the five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching].
The eightfold classification of the teachings exhaustively interprets the entire corpus of the Buddha’s scriptures without exception; indeed, the Tiantai teaching system originated with this Master.
Following his summons, he traveled to Jinling, where he lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* in the Daji Palace and expounded the *Ratnaketuparivarta-sūtra* (Renwang jing) at Guangzhai Temple.
The Chen ruler presented him with the Three Rituals to demonstrate his reverence. When the Sui dynasty annexed the Chen, he retired to Mount Lu.

During the Kaihuang era, when Emperor Yang was still a prince in the frontier regions, he invited him to serve as his Bodhisattva Precept Master and bestowed upon him the title "Zhizhe" (Wise One). Later, he returned to reside at Mount Tiantai.
One night, he suddenly dreamed that a great wind blew down a jeweled pagoda. At that time, imperial edicts repeatedly summoned him, and he arrived at Shishi.
In front of the city image, he suddenly claimed to be ill. He then summoned his disciples and commanded them to chant the *Lotus Sūtra*, while he himself offered this self-praise:

"The Dharma-gate is my father and mother; from it wisdom and understanding are born. Its fundamental and manifested aspects are vast and great, subtle and wondrous beyond measure. Now I shall set down my chisel and sever my strings."

It was on this very day. He further said, "I shall no longer lead the assembly; I must purify my six sense faculties. For the sake of others, I have sacrificed myself and shall recede to the level of the five grades.
My teachers and friends, Avalokiteśvara is coming to welcome me. Having spoken these words, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. This was at the hour of Wei (2–4 p.m.
on the twenty-fourth day of the second month of winter in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, the Ding-si year. He was sixty years of age and had completed forty summer retreats.
An imperial edict enshrined his spirit stupa on the southwest peak of Fulong. Every year, an envoy was dispatched to open the stupa to present offerings.
When it was opened for the last time, the entire body was no longer to be seen. The King of Wuyue, Qian, once posthumously conferred upon him the titles of Dharmakāśa and Ratnabodhi.

From the Master’s passing until this year, exactly six hundred and two years have elapsed. The Master propagated the teachings of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Consciousness-Only) and did not maintain [any personal possessions].
Regarding his commentaries (*zhangshu*), he exclusively unleashed the eloquence of a cascading river.

Beyond lecturing on various sutras, he expounded the profound passages of the *Lotus Sūtra* to open up wondrous understanding, followed by the exposition of *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) to establish correct practice based upon that understanding. Thus, Jingxi said: "Without the *Profound Meaning* (*Xuanyi*), there would be nothing to guide;

without the *Textual Commentary* (*Wenju*), there would be nothing to sustain; without the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, there would be nothing to penetrate; and without this 'One House' (*Yijia*), there would be no way to advance. This—
Is this not what was meant? How magnificent! The scriptures for saving the world and clarifying the Way are found in the three treatises of the Tiantai school.
The Master’s transformative guidance extended across more than sixty prefectures; his Way has become increasingly luminous over the long course of time.
All of these historical accounts are detailed in the *Biographies* and the *Records of the Twelve Monasteries of the Tiantai School*.
The Vinaya Master Daoxuan of Nanshan Chengzhao was a native of Dantu.
His father was Qian Shen, an Assistant Director of the Ministry of Personnel. When his mother was pregnant with him, she dreamed that a lunar disc pierced her womb;
subsequently, she again dreamed of a foreign monk who said to her, "That which you carry is the Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang Dynasty."
Master [Dao]you was none other than Senghu of Yinyue Temple on Mount Shanxi during the Southern Qi dynasty. He was destined for renunciation and would greatly propagate the Buddha-dharma.

When he reached the age of fifteen, his mother recalled her dream and permitted him to leave secular life. As for his studies, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and other scriptures until he mastered them all.
At sixteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination, specializing in the study of the Vinaya. In the end, he brought this [tradition] to a revival.
Daoshan was a worthy successor to Upāli. His teacher’s three robes were all made of ramie; he ate only beans as his sole meal.
Although fleas and lice swarmed over him, his body remained like wood or earth. Wherever he stayed, he invariably moved the spirits to offer flowers and fruits as celestial delicacies.

At times, when he stumbled on the front steps, Nanda would come to support and protect him; at other times, when he constructed a jeweled altar, divine monks would appear to pay homage and offer praise. From the Qianfeng era onwards...
Thereafter, devas and humans came in continuous succession to engage the Master in discussions on matters such as the Vinaya-piṭaka and its commentaries.

Consequently, the commentaries and sub-commentaries composed by the Master captured the original intent of the Buddha, for he was one who had attained communion with the divine. The world and future generations took him as their model;
his Way prevented wrongdoing and halted evil, and thus it is known as the Nanshan Teaching. The Master placed the "Preface to the Propagation of the Lotus Sūtra" at the beginning [of his works].

The intent of this scripture’s opening is vast and profound, and its phrasing is sublime and exquisite. It remains unaltered through the reigns of a hundred sovereigns and has been propagated throughout the ages for a thousand autumns.
Its exposition of the original vow states: "May I soon purify the six sense organs to look up to the auspicious assembly of the Compassionate Honored One;
may I swiftly perfect the four virtues to follow the mysterious path to the Land of Bliss" (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).
The Dharma Master of Ci'en Monastery in Jingzhao was named Kuiji.
He was the nephew of Wei Chi Jingde of the Tang dynasty. His father was Zong, General of the Imperial Guard; his mother was Lady Pei.
She conceived him after dreaming that she had swallowed the moon. When he was only six years old, his intelligence surpassed that of others, and he already composed treatises on the art of war.

It consisted of several thousand words. At that time, the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang, who had traveled westward, obtained a young boy who was exceptionally skilled at memorization and questioning. Consequently, he brought him to pay his respects to [Master] Zong.

Zong called for Ji to prostrate. Xuanzang then had the boy recite the book he had composed; as Xuanzang counted the eyes of the boy, he memorized the text, and by the time the recitation was finished, it was complete.
Xuanzang deceived him, saying, "This is merely an ancient book. Kuiji did not yet believe him, so Xuanzang had a young boy recite it from memory;

not a single word was omitted. Kuiji, enraged that he had plagiarized the work, intended to kill him. Xuanzang then begged for permission to enter the monastic order. Kuiji said, "I will grant you this if you agree to three conditions."

Upon seeing the evening meal containing meat and strong flavors, he immediately sought ordination, saying, "If not, I would rather submit to the sword and die. Xuanzang, admiring his brilliance and clarity, feigned consent.
He entered the monastic path and resided at the Great Ci'en Monastery, where he became proficient in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings;
upon reading any treatise or commentary once, he could recite it without error. Previously, Master Xuanzang had received the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* from the master Śīlabhadra in the Western Regions.

The fundamental tenets of Yogācāra had not been continued by anyone until the Master alone received and inherited them. Whether as a founder of a school or as an exegete, he composed a hundred treatises, earning him the title "Master of the Hundred Treatises.
The Master traveled everywhere to convert disciples, and those who benefited from his teachings were numerous. He journeyed eastward to Boling.
Being requested to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he subsequently composed the *Fahua xuanzan dashu* (Great Commentary on the Profound Praise of the Lotus Sutra) in ten fascicles.

In the preface to its title, he wrote: "It grasps the ultimate proclamation of the grand framework and proclaims the comprehensive name of this single division. Its 'Dharma' contains the principles of preservation; it binds together all auspiciousness to manifest its 'Wondrous.

Its 'Lotus' combines exquisite blooming; it synthesizes all beauties to reveal the 'Lian' (Lotus). Thus, establishing the discourse and founding the school, he expounds and propagates [the teaching]."

Regarding the *Āraṇyaka*: the masters of the Northern School frequently lectured upon and mastered it (the details of the Master’s conduct are found in the *Great Song Biographies of Eminent Monks*; matters concerning his renunciation of the household life appear in the *Chronicles of the Śākya Clan*).

National Teacher Qingliang of Wutai, Shi Chengguan, was surnamed Xiahou and was a native of Shanyin. He left the household life at Yingtian Temple and recited the Lotus Sūtra fourteen times before receiving full ordination.
Initially, he studied the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Nanshan school; subsequently, he transmitted the Three Treatises (Sanlun) in Jinling.
He traveled again to India to study the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Later, he resided in Suzhou, where he received the Tiantai system of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* from Chan Master Jingxi.

He listened to lectures on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and other scriptures. Furthermore, he visited Niu-tou Zhong and Jing-shan Qin, thereby acquiring the Chan methods of both the Northern and Southern schools.
The Master was profoundly learned and deeply investigated the teachings; his insight and capacity were vast and far-reaching. He authored works such as the *Huayan-zhenyuan* [commentary].
Commentary: His creation of statues and transcription of sutras are too numerous to mention in full. He once made ten great vows that he practiced throughout his life:
First, to possess only the three robes and one alms bowl, never storing any surplus; Second, to cast aside worldly fame and profit as if they were discarded refuse;

Third, never to look upon women with the eyes; Fourth, never to let one’s shadow fall upon the houses of the laity; Fifth, to constantly recite the Lotus Sutra; Sixth, to constantly read the Great [Nirvana Sutra]...

He practiced the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra*. Seventh, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* for seven years. Eighth, throughout his life, he did not lie down day or night. Ninth, he was never confused by the masses and did not boast of his own virtues.
Tenth, his great compassion never regressed. Throughout his life, the Master served nine successive reigns as the preceptor to seven emperors.

Emperor Xianzong once summoned him to lecture on the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which so delighted the Emperor’s mind that he issued an imperial decree for the relevant authorities to cast a seal for him and promoted him to State Preceptor (*Guoshi*), overseeing the entire order.

He was the preeminent leader among the monastic community under heaven. He lived to the age of one hundred and two; his height was nine chi and two cun. His eyes emitted light at night, and by day he did not blink.
His voice could sustain two tones simultaneously, and its resonance was like a bell. A Buddhist monk from India declared him to be the reincarnation of Mañjuśrī.

Upon cremation, his tongue was as red as a lotus flower, and the *śarīra* relics were lustrous and smooth. Prime Minister Pei Xiu, acting on imperial decree, composed the inscription for his stele. (His life history...)
(See the *Shishi bianian lu* for the nine dynasties; the remainder is from the *Dazhong xiangfu Sengzhuan*).

The Koryo Master Gwang, the śramaṇa Xuan-guang, was a native of Xiong Prefecture in Haidong. From his youth, he grew weary of the mundane dust and devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Upon reaching adulthood, he...
Crossing the vast ocean, he sought the Chan teachings of the Central Kingdom. Thereupon, he traveled to the capital to observe its splendors and went to Mount Heng to visit Master Sida.
Sida examined his spiritual capacity (*indriya*) and bestowed upon him the "Four Practices of Peaceful Joy. Like a divine awl, Guangli’s penetration was such that nothing solid could resist it;
he received and practiced these instructions until he suddenly realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Sida certified this realization, saying: "That which you have realized..."
"This is true and not false. You shall return to your native land, employ skillful means (*upāya*), and propagate my teaching. Having received this, he prostrated himself in light and took his leave.
He immediately returned south of the Yangtze River and boarded a boat for the great ocean. There, he happened to see a multicolored cloud approaching with elegant oars and crimson banners.
A voice from the sky proclaimed: "The Celestial Emperor summons the Chan Master Xuan-guang of海东 (Haedong) to his palace of honor to discourse on intimacy."

At the Gate of Realizing the Dharma, Fotudeng bowed his hands in deference and withdrew. He saw only a man in green robes leading the way as they entered the palace city, which was unlike any human government office;
it was inhabited entirely by fish-scaled and shell-clad spirits. Once they had ascended the jeweled hall and subsequently climbed the high dais, they conversed as if in dialogue for seven days.
When the business was concluded, the King personally escorted him to the parting. Fotudeng boarded the boat once more, and the boatmen said they were drifting away.
Yang did not advance for half a day. Guang subsequently reached Mount Wengshan in Xiongzhou and built a thatched hut, which eventually became a Buddhist monastery.
Among those who ascended the hall, one person realized the Fire-Light Samādhi and another realized the Water-Light Samādhi.
The rest were like flocks of birds settling upon Mount Sumeru; they all became one color as he manifested his passing into extinction, leaving no one to know where he had gone. — Nanyue.
The Ancestral Hall lists twenty-eight patriarchs; Guang was one among them (*Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).

Chan Master Cheng of Jingzhou, whose monastic name was Huicheng, was the son of the Duans of Liyang. He became a monk at Zhizhu Temple and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He had produced over ten volumes [of commentaries]. Later, while traveling to seek the Way in various regions, he arrived at Mount Lu and met with the Chan Master Tiantai Zhiyi.

Upon hearing that the Great Master Nanyue Huisi was still living, he went to visit him. Once they met, he looked up to him with great admiration and wished to study the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Huisi said, "The merit of your life's work on commentaries and treatises does not even equal the heat of my hand when you try to warm it by it; you have wasted your efforts in vain."
How lamentable! Cheng immediately resolved with indignation to burn his memorials and petitions. From night until dawn, he sat in meditation with eyes open for fifteen years.
Sengsi further directed him to enter the Lotus Samādhi and Bhadrapāla practice hall to eliminate hindrances for three years, and subsequently instructed him in the True Dharma;
thereupon, he realized the *sarvasattvabhāṣā-vijñapti-samādhi*. Compared to closing one's eyes to enter contemplation, upon opening them—
The difference between them was as vast as that between heaven and earth. Sengsi remarked, "Zhiyi first attained samādhi and later realized dhāraṇī;

Hui Cheng has reached this same level. These two disciples are equal in both understanding and practice. Cheng then traveled to Zhiyang in Jingzhou to establish a monastery; through the reach of his virtue and wisdom, it was completed in no time.

Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty summoned him repeatedly before he finally arrived. After bestowing the precepts upon the Emperor, he returned. At that time, he was about to manifest supernatural transformations.
He was then lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* when, suddenly, Zhiyi arrived from Yuquan Temple. Their meeting was as if preordained by the unseen;
they discussed profound principles for a long while before [Zhiyi] passed away (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Chan Master Chao of Zhongnan was named Huichao.

He was born into the Shen family of Danyang. By nature he was gentle and dignified. From childhood he followed the Buddhist teachings, specializing in the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Hearing from afar that Chan Master Sida of Guangzhou possessed both clarity in meditative concentration and wisdom, and was likewise proficient in the Vinaya, he [together with Zhi... went to him.

With a humble mind and a purified self, he adjusted his robes and requested instruction. He thought to himself, "He has reached the divine treasury of transcendence; he is one who has attained the stages of patience.

Later, while traveling to Mount Heng, he again followed the same path as Zhiyi, reciting the sutras together for years. Subsequently, he lived in seclusion at Mount Zhongnan for eight years, where his practice of the Way flourished and his mastery of the three types of wisdom doubled.
When the Daye era began and the mandate was received, an imperial edict was issued inviting him into the inner palace. The Great Tang...
At the beginning, Master Rongzhong resided in the capital. From the moment he entered the Way, he recited the Lotus Sūtra for over fifty years, more than ten thousand times.

When his illness reached its end and he was about to pass away, he summoned the assembly and said: "Coming and going is my constant state. I do not rejoice in long life, nor do I grieve at death at nightfall.
The emptiness of the primary truth and the pure observation of wisdom are my staff. Having spoken these words, he passed away.

He passed away heading west. His final instructions were that his body be left exposed among the pines and rocks to be offered to birds and beasts. His disciples followed these teachings and kept the body for over a month;
its complexion remained as if alive. Afterwards, they constructed a stupa to inter it (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).

The Dharma Master Guan of India, Shi Zhen-guan, was surnamed Fan and was a native of Qiantang. His mother sought a son by reciting the *Bhaiṣajyaguru* and *Avalokiteśvara* sutras, and thus obtained the Master.

The Master possessed integrity from his youth. His tongue was marked with purple veins, and his hands displayed extraordinary signs. He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, completing one fascicle every day.

Having studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under a teacher, he surpassed all previous standards. Suddenly, he dreamed of a person who said to him, "You possess great roots; why do you cling to the Lesser Vehicle?
The Master then proceeded to study Mahāyāna, resolving doubts and clarifying difficult points as he plunged into the profound gateway. At that time, a popular saying went:
In Qiandang there was Zhi Guan, who at that time was among the foremost monks in half the world. His seniority in the monastic order was equal to that of Zhizhe, and they were brothers in the Dharma.
Their lofty discussions on quiescent illumination were as harmonious as metal and stone. Later, he established Nantianzhu Temple on Mount Lingyin and resided there.
He constantly lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* as his essential practice, upholding, reciting, and personally transcribing it to propagate it. Five...
The Dharma Master Zong was present there. Whenever he washed his hands, the residual droplets did not moisten the ground, and everyone marveled at this.

One day, the deity of Gaotingshan requested that he lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Moved by this, the deity relinquished the shrine to become a monastery. Later, Sima Li Zishen invited him to lecture on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
When they reached the chapter on "Manifesting Illness," he dreamed of three men holding banners who told him: "The Śuddhāvāsa devas have sent us."
Upon his arrival, [Zhiyi] immediately lay ill. He dreamed that he was in the same carriage as Zhizhe, escorting the Buddha back to the mountain.
Upon waking, he sighed and said: "Formerly, I believed my sixty-two years would be my end; through the power of lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra*, my life was extended by another decade.

Now, at seventy-four, this further sign has appeared. My allotted span of life is now complete. He then opened his hands and feet and said: "Those who wish to transcend birth and death must maintain the precepts and cultivate [the path]."
Diligently train in concentration and wisdom, and propagate the True Dharma; do not let your time pass in vain. At that moment, the sound of celestial music was heard from the air.
By midnight, he sat cross-legged and entered a state of stillness. This Master was the founding patriarch of Ling Shan Temple in Southern India; his conduct and deeds were miraculous.
Formerly, Chan Master Zhangan Zhi handed down a separate biography to record his virtues, but it has not survived due to the passage of time. Now...
He is mentioned only in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks). His stupa still exists, and the repentance master Ciyun Shi once renovated it;
this is recorded in detail in the *Lingyuan ji*. A brief excerpt states: "The Master’s will was set upon the Buddha-vehicle, and his realization of the Way reached its ultimate limit.
In leaving the world, he did not comply with the influence of emperors, princes, dukes, or lords; in remaining in the world, he did not seek fame for his extensive arts or eloquence."
In chaos, he remained exalted above the world; how remote and sublime, beyond all comparison! Now the earth has opened of its own accord, leaving behind not a single object.
Yet it remains unknown whether he has preserved his body to join the assembly of Prabhūtaratna for the certification of the sutra, or whether he has manifested his passing at Mount Foshouling.
I have respectfully composed six stanzas of verse to perpetually honor this memorial marker. [The Master was summoned three times by the Sui Emperor, yet the kings and nobles never bowed before him.]

Lao. The two Aśokas of the Qin King both declined their appointments, citing illness (the others are as in the collected poems). This is the body of one who has left the household life; the white bones have already become dust, yet the pure wind still chills those who encounter it.

When the tomb mounds crumble, they are repaired; when the temples fall into ruin, they are rebuilt anew. Only the ground that remains unsullied—no one follows in its wake. (The remaining poems are as in the collection.)
The Chan Master Zhang’an Zongchi, whose name was Guanding and whose posthumous title was bestowed by the King of Wuyue, was born into the Wu clan of Zhang’an.

From his earliest childhood, at the age of three, he was already able to recite the names of the Triple Gem alongside his mother; everyone was struck with wonder at this, and thus he was given the name [Zong]chi.
His courtesy name was Fafan. Upon entering the Way, he was able to memorize ten thousand words daily. He devoted himself equally to the profound mysteries of Buddhism and Confucianism.

Having received the teachings of Tian-tai on samādhi and prajñā, he succeeded to the ancestral lineage and maintained the family tradition. Whenever the Master of Wisdom (Zhi-zhe) preached the Dharma, the Master recorded it all in writing to form a textual record.

In his later years, he resided at Chengxin Monastery, where he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* for a long time. His transformative influence spread among the bustling laity, and his spiritual efficacy was boundless.
At that time, there was a villager from Falong Village, thirty *li* from the mountain, who fell gravely ill and was nearing death. His son rushed to him to seek salvation;
the Master recited the *Lotus Sūtra* for him and burned sandalwood incense. The patient smelled the fragrance from afar and was immediately healed. (From the *Leʼan Nan*)

A mountain ridge was called Anzhou (Peaceful Isle). With its emerald trees and clear streams, it was inaccessible by human path. The Master went there to observe it and remained for some time, unwilling to depart.
He then made a vow, saying, "If this land is made level and smooth, I shall come here to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
Before even ten days had passed, white sand surged forth everywhere until the ground was as level as a jade mirror. The Master fulfilled his prior resolve and went there to preach. Furthermore—
Once, while lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Shejing Temple, he encountered a raid by sea pirates. The Master struck the bell and proceeded with his lecture.
When the pirates entered, they saw banners and standards shining like the sun, and the men holding bows and halberds all appeared over ten feet tall; consequently, they retreated and dispersed.
In the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, the Master manifested illness at Guoqing Temple. He declined medical treatment, yet a wondrous fragrance filled his chamber as he addressed his younger brother.
The Master said, "The *Maitreya Sūtra* states that on the day the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, incense smoke will rise like clouds. You must burn much incense; I am about to depart.
Having spoken these words, he passed away. At that time, there was the Chan Master Zhixi, who entered parinirvāṇa in the first year of the Zhenguan era.
As he was departing, he announced: "I have been born in Tuṣita Heaven. I saw the Dazhi (Zhiyi) sitting upon a jeweled throne, with people lined up in rows, of whom there was only one [who remained]."
He sat alone in solitude. A deity said, "Six years hence, the Chan Master Guanding shall ascend this seat to preach the Dharma. He burned incense to verify this intention;
it was indeed the descent of Maitreya. Calculating the years and deliberating the timing, he examined [the signs] and found the words were not false (from *Gushan Xianju Bian*).
Chan Master Zao of Tiantai, the śramaṇa Zhizao, was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Qingyi. At the age of seventeen, he lost both his parents and fell gravely ill.
Realizing that his life was at an end, he suddenly saw the moon one night and immediately called upon the Bodhisattva Candraprabha; consequently, he recovered.
Deeply perceiving that the Triple Gem was his sole reliance, he went to Anjing Temple to renounce the world. His resolve was lofty and far-reaching, and his words and deeds were both sincere.
Hearing from afar that Zhiyi’s realization surpassed all others, he traveled to Mount Tai to submit himself to him and receive the Way. Zhiyi observed him...

Regarding his spiritual capacity, he was sent to practice the Lotus Samādhi. When he had cultivated it for two weeks, during seated meditation in the early night, he saw a nine-headed dragon emerge from the earth and ascend into the void.

The next day, he informed his teacher, who said, "This signifies that sentient beings of the nine realms, upon hearing the Lotus Sūtra, will in a future age shatter ignorance and enter the emptiness of the Dharma-nature."
[The Master] heard it. Furthermore, while once at Baolin Monastery, he had made a formal vow to practice the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

When he began his practice at the first watch of the night, it was as if someone were coming to rattle the door panels. The Master questioned them, and they replied, "I am the lamp that has come. This occurred several times, and the answers and questions remained as before.
There was a Zen Master Huicheng in the monastery who, upon hearing of this matter, remarked: "That hall has always been..."
There was a great malevolent spirit that, upon hearing this sound, thought, "This must surely come to harm me. At dawn, he knocked on the door to inquire after him;

seeing that he was still there, he was greatly relieved. He then went to report this to Prince Yongyang. The Prince immediately dispatched several dozen soldiers and officials armed with staves to guard him.
The Master said, "Life is determined by karma; how can it be protected by such guards? He thanked them and departed. This happened a second time.
At night, a ghost immediately entered and struck at things everywhere; for twenty-one days it constantly caused such disturbances. The Master remained composed and fearless.
When the ritual was nearly completed, he saw a youth dressed in blue robes who praised him, saying, "Excellent! Having spoken, he vanished.

The Master’s virtuous conduct was complete in both principle and practice; he served as an assistant to Zhiyi. He appeared at court before the Son of Heaven on nine occasions, maintaining excellence from beginning to end.
He passed away at the age of eighty-three (*Xu Gaoseng zhuan*).
Master Lushan Zhi was the son of the Gu clan of Kuaiji. Having left home to enter the monastic life while still a youth, he served as a disciple to Tiantai Zhizhe.

Zhizhe, seeing that his physical presence and spirit were refined and detached, and that he stood loftily beyond worldly things, gave him the name Dazhi. He recited the Lotus Sūtra, remaining serene and tranquil in solitude.
His voice was clear and melodious; those who heard it forgot their fatigue. Later, on Mount Lu at Gāndhamādana Peak, he practiced the dhūta austerities.

At times, he threw himself before fierce beasts, yet they all retreated. When his grain supply was exhausted, he sustained his life solely on cakes and fruit for seven years, never ceasing his meditation and recitation.
He passed away at Shifu Lin Temple during the Daye era, when the monastic community was suppressed.
In Buddhism, lamenting that the Great Dharma was in decline, he donned mourning clothes within the Buddha hall and wailed for three days and nights.

He vowed to sacrifice his physical form to propagate the orthodox teaching. He immediately went to the Eastern Capital and submitted a memorial, saying: "I pray that Your Majesty will cause the Triple Gem to flourish.
This humble monk shall burn one of my arms on Mount Song to repay the kindness of the state. The Emperor granted his request. Thereupon—
A great vegetarian feast was prepared, and the seven classes of followers gathered together. The Master abstained from food for three days, then ascended into a large wooden structure.
He wrapped his arms in cloth and doused them with wax; he set them ablaze like torches, and the light illuminated the cliffs and grottoes, shining with brilliant clarity.

Seeing his ascetic practice, the assembly felt its pain penetrating to the very marrow of their bones, yet his countenance and form remained unchanged. Sometimes he recited the scriptures, sometimes he praised the virtues of the Buddha, or [acted as]...

The assembly preached the Dharma, the sound of their voices never ceasing. Once the cremation was complete, he descended from the platform, sat in the full lotus posture, entered meditative concentration, and passed away after seven days.
The Master left behind more than seventy sheets of his *yuanwen* (vow-texts), his intention being to serve as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to all sentient beings.
Those who saw them were moved to the core of their hearts; there was no one who did not shed tears (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*).

Chan Master Yue of Jingzhou, whose monastic name was Daoyue, was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Jingzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of twelve at Yuquan Temple. His capacity and insight were profound and far-reaching;

he lived in poverty with austere discipline. Throughout his life, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* as his primary spiritual practice. Yuquan Temple was originally founded by Zhiyi. It had not yet... [text fragment ends]

He possessed a set of bells and chimes. The Master obtained a piece of strange stone from a spring source and suspended it. Whenever he finished reciting a scroll of scripture, he would strike it once;

its resonance was clear and penetrating, and those who heard it were struck with solemn reverence. Those from the realm of the unseen frequently experienced auspicious responses, yet he knew them and did not speak of them.

Once, he suffered from a severe abdominal swelling so urgent it was like being beaten by a drum. One night, while he was reciting the scriptures, the water suddenly began to flow out, and his great edema subsided.
