It was instantly digested. At that time, Zhu Can was raiding and plundering; only Huiyue remained to guard the monastery. The rebels ordered him to lead them as a guide. The Master said, "A monk is not a guide for others.
This illusory physical form may be left to the mercy of the white blades. The rebels respected him and showed him clemency.
Later, Prince Han Yang invited him to serve as his preceptor and presented him with garments of dyed silk. Huiyue would not accept them. The Prince asked, "Why do you not wear these silks?"
Yes. Yue said, "Silk garments involve the taking of life, which contradicts the reputation for patience; cloth robes are simple and frugal, manifesting the mark of compassion.
The King said, "Zhongyou felt no shame when his Master praised him; it is certainly the same with the śramaṇa’s compassion and patience" (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).

The Chan Master Sengzhiyue of Tiantai was born into the Zheng family of Nanyang. From his youth, he possessed the aspiration to transcend the mundane world. When his father sought a marriage alliance for him, he skillfully found means to evade it.
At that time, the Prince of Yueyang governed Jingzhou; recognizing the master’s exceptional character, he subsequently performed the tonsure for him. Later...

Traveling from place to place in search of the Way, he arrived at Jinling, where he encountered Zhiyi as he was expounding the teachings. He purified himself to request instruction and attained a profound mastery of the essentials of Chan.
Furthermore, he maintained the precepts with meticulous care and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* more than ten thousand times.
A flask of water remained perpetually full, a phenomenon that all marveled at. Although Zhiyi’s disciples were numerous, Yue was the foremost among them. At the Lushan Hermitage in Linhai, Zhi...

His life passed away as swiftly as a shadow or an echo. For twenty years, he had consistently and skillfully guided others through his gentle teachings. Shortly thereafter, he fell ill at Guoqing Temple and passed away while lying on his right side.
This caused the mountains to collapse and the earth to tremble; both monastics and laypeople witnessed and heard of these events (from the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Master Guān of Qiāntáng was born into the Sūn family of Fùyáng. After he had become a monk, he heard that Zhìzhě was expounding the Dharma at Fólǒng and went there to rely upon him as his teacher.
He specialized in reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* and was also capable of lecturing upon it. During the Zhengguān period, he traveled to Fǎrèn Temple in Yúháng.
While he was lecturing, one night he suddenly saw a divine being who said, "I am the deity of the shrine at Gaoting in Qiantang.

You, Master, once passed by the temple grounds, but as your disciple was on a pilgrimage, we did not meet. I have now come specifically to request the bestowal of the precepts. The Master immediately burned incense and recited the texts for him.
When midnight arrived the following day, [the deity] bathed and purified himself again, then summoned Dharma Master Hui to expound the meaning of the Three Contemplations (*sanzhuan*).
He then said, "This was personally received by me from the oral instructions of the Wise One (Zhizhe).
Having spoken, he sat in the full lotus posture facing west, recited the name of that Buddha as well as the honorific title of the Venerable Tiantai Zhizhe, and suddenly passed away (*Lingrui ji*).
During the Liang dynasty, Dharma Master Man and Dharma Master Kumārajīva translated the twenty-eight chapters of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in Chang’an.

Palace ladies of Chang’an requested that he lecture on the "Devadatta Chapter," which remained withheld within the palace. Consequently, what was transmitted in Jiangdong consisted of only twenty chapters.
Regarding the first fascicle: During the Liang dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Man, who lectured on the sutra one hundred times.

At Changsha, he burned his own body as an offering to the Dharma, and he placed this fascicle before the "Anchoring" (Anchi) fascicle; however, this was merely his personal arrangement and had not been heard of throughout the realm.

During the Chen dynasty, there was the Great Meditation Master Sengzhao of Mount Nanyue, who placed this fascicle after the "Jeweled Stupa" (Baota) fascicle. Later, when [the text] was compared with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it was found to be highly consistent.

[This] corresponds [to the original]. Now, however, the four great rivers have become conflated. Seeing the old edition from Chang’an, one knows that the two masters deeply grasped the intent of the sutra (from the *Fahua wenzhu*).
The Dharma Master Bhikṣu Fazhuang of Mount Lu was a native of Huainan. He left home to become a monk at the age of ten and became a disciple of Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu.
By nature, he was simple and unadorned; his ascetic practices brought him renown. Reciting the Lotus Sūtra was his constant occupation. Often, during the stillness of night, his neighbors...
Every time one heard the sounds of military weapons and ceremonial guards before the Master’s quarters, how could it be for no reason? (From the *Xu Lingrui Ji*).
Later, during the Northern Zhou dynasty, the Dharma Master named Huiming was summoned;

his surname was Guo, and he was a native of Jinyang. He held the Way in high esteem while remaining detached from worldly affairs, and was highly honored by the local community. At fifteen, he began reciting [the scriptures].

Within two weeks, he mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* from beginning to end. He then immediately shaved his head and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Repentance Ritual.
On the fifth day of the middle winter month in the third year of the Tianhe era, facing west, he sat upright in the full lotus posture;

beholding the Buddha coming to welcome him, he joined his palms and passed away peacefully. The entire assembly shared a dream that a celestial being descended to earth, with banners and streamers reflecting the sun. Furthermore, there were those who heard...
There were extraordinary music and rare fragrances, and those who praised him exclaimed, "Excellent!
(from the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Master Ming of Tiantai, whose former name was Fajing, was surnamed Zhu and was a native of Kuaiji. In his youth, he gathered sand to build stupas and used mugwort and wormwood to construct halls.
With palms joined, he called out the Buddha’s name. Suddenly encountering a monk on alms-round, the monk exhorted him, saying, "You should go to Mount Tiantai to leave the household life.
There, a Bodhisattva who is a primary refuge preaches the Dharma to transform the world. The youth immediately hurried there and attended upon Zhiyi as his disciple.
Zhiyi smiled and said, "By the power of past vows, we have now met. Thereupon, [the youth] remained at his side morning and night.
Ying was diligent and never slackened. The Master therefore instructed him to recite one volume of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* while concurrently practicing the ritual of repentance (*sādhana*).
Later, he accompanied Zhizhe into Mount Lu, where they immediately established the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Samādhi* within the Ruixiang Pavilion originally built by Tao Kan.

Suddenly, a monk appeared and said, "Your Dharma-name is not yet preeminent; it should be changed to Puming (Universal Radiance), for then you shall illuminate and comprehend the three periods of time. From then on...
He changed his name from Zong to Hui. Later, he returned to Guoqing Temple. His quarters lacked water; as the Master meditated upon it, a spring suddenly flowed from a rock.
Furthermore, while he was once casting a sixteen-foot statue of Vairocana, a mysterious person appeared and offered gold, after which they vanished.
Once, amidst the pine groves of Mount Chicheng, he manifested a body several tens of zhang in height. Master Zhangan Ding personally beheld him;
observing the Master’s spiritual activities from above, one could see that he was by no means an ordinary person (*Xu Lingrui Ji*).
Dharma Master Sui of Heyin, whose secular surname and clan are unknown, lived as a monk at Baima Monastery in Heyin. He maintained a vegetarian diet and wore simple cloth garments.

Every day he recited ten fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and, being well-versed in its profound meaning, lectured upon it for the assembly. One night, he suddenly dreamed of a person knocking [at his door].
Hù said, "I wish to invite the Dharma Master to lecture on the sutras for the ninety-day summer retreat. Sù declined, but when he was pressed repeatedly, he finally consented.
He felt as though he were neither fully awake nor asleep, when suddenly he saw himself in the shrine of the White Horse Mound deity, with one disciple also present.
From then on, he went there secretly every day; no one else knew of it. One day, while a monk from the monastery was passing beneath the shrine, he happened to see two high seats. Sù [saw this].
The master sat on the northern seat while his disciples sat to the south. They heard the sound of his preaching and also smelled a fragrant, exquisite incense.

Monastics and laypeople alike passed the news along, all declaring it a divine marvel. At the end of the summer retreat, the spirit bestowed one white horse, five white sheep, and fifty rolls of silk as a gift for the lecture.
The master offered prayers of blessing, accepted the offerings, and departed; his final destination was thereafter unknown. (From the *Liang Gaoseng Zhuan*)
From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*): Sengsheng, the abbot of Shengsi Temple in Chengdu.
A native of [Pei] in Shu Commandery; his secular surname was Yuan. He became a monk at a young age and was renowned for his ascetic practices during the time of Song [Yuan], the Governor of Chengdu.
Feng was invited to serve as the abbot of Sanxian Temple, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Once, while reciting the sūtra in the mountains, a tiger suddenly appeared and crouched before him; it departed only after he had finished a chapter. Later, during his studies and recitations, he frequently saw four divine beings attending and guarding him on his left and right.
Although he was advanced in years, his practice remained steadfast. When he fell ill, he immediately entrusted his affairs to his disciples.
The person sat in the lotus posture and passed away (*Liang Gaoseng zhuan*).
Master Xu of Gaochang was a monk of Gaochang whose virtuous conduct was rigorous; he ate vegetarian food and drank only water. Later, he entered Shu and resided at Liu Shi’s Tomb.

He occasionally practiced the dhūta austerities; even when tigers and rhinoceroses saw him, they did not harm him. He constantly dwelt in a stone grotto, reciting the three sutras: the Lotus Sutra, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sutra, and the Prabhāsa-rāja Sutra.
Suddenly, during one summer retreat, he passed away in the stone grotto while lying on his left side. Seven days later, his body had not decayed.
A fragrance assailed the senses. Every evening, he emitted light that illuminated several *li* around. The local people marveled at this and immediately erected a stupa over his remains.
He was a person of the Jin period (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

Dharma Master Yi of Kuaiji and Dharma Master Yiyi were both of the secular surname Zhu. At the age of thirteen, they entered the monastic path and devoted themselves diligently to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). They recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He resided at Waguan Temple. Later, he moved to Baoshan Vihāra in Kuaiji. In the second year of the Xianhe era, he fell ill; yet his recitation and study did not falter.
One night he dreamed of a monk who drew out his intestines and stomach to wash away their impurities. Once they were cleansed, the monk returned them to his belly.
Upon waking from his dream, he was immediately cured. The Emperor of Jin once summoned him to the inner palace, where he received the five precepts from him;

the imperial provisions and honors bestowed upon him were most generous. In the Dahe era, he passed away without illness. By imperial decree, a stupa was erected at Xintinggang to enshrine his remains;
this is the present-day Zhongxing Temple (as recorded in the *Lingrui ji*).
Regarding the Elder Dáshàng of Qiāngdì:
During the Lóng'ān era of the Jìn dynasty, while Sēnghuìdá was digging for licorice root north of the Lǒng Mountains, the Qiāng people were suffering from famine and were capturing and eating humans.
Dá was captured by them and placed within a stockade; they selected the fattest individuals to eat first. Dá was filled with extreme fear. One—
With his mind calling upon the name of Avalokiteśvara and reciting the "Universal Gateway" chapter (*Pumen pin*), he was captured until only Faxie and a small child remained;
their lives were destined for but one more day. Throughout the night, Faxie maintained his recitation without ceasing.

At dawn, a tiger suddenly emerged from the brush, its roar shaking the mountains. The Qiang people fled in terror, and the tiger then bit through the fence, making a hole, and departed. Faxie and the small child—
The child fled and managed to escape (from the *Taizong biexing yishu*).

Dharma Master Kuang of Wuxing—Dharma Master Zhu Fakuang—was of the Gao clan by secular name. He resided in Wuxing; his aspirations and conduct were lofty and eminent, and his observance of the precepts was profound and deep.

When his master fell ill, Huikang offered prayers and performed repentance rituals with sincere devotion for seven days and nights. Consequently, five-colored light illuminated the room, and the master’s illness was immediately cured.

Later, he resided in a stone grotto on Mount Qing at Qian, where he frequently remarked that the *Lotus Sūtra* contains the principle of unifying the three vehicles, while the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* is the cause for attaining the Pure Land. He constantly chanted these two scriptures and would preach them whenever there was an assembly.
In his daily life, he would recite [the scriptures]. When Xie An was the Governor of Wuxing, he went specifically to pay his respects.

Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty summoned him, commanding him to perform rites of purification and repentance to dispel an ominous star. Later, he moved to Changyuan Temple at Yuxue, where he rescued the common people from peril and suffering;

there were none who did not witness his efficacy. Those who frequently saw the Master while he was walking or sitting often observed that there were always several dozen ghosts and spirits by his side.

He was protected by attendants before and behind him. He lived to the age of seventy-six. The Court Attendant Gu Kaizhi composed a biography to record his virtues (as recorded in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Regarding the anonymous monk of Changsha:
in the second year of the Jianxing era of the Western Jin dynasty, more than one hundred li west of Changsha County, two stalks of blue lotuses appeared.
It grew on dry land, and both monastics and laypeople vied with one another to see it. Consequently, they dug the earth for a depth of one zhang and two chi, whereupon they discovered a brick coffin.
A lotus emerged from the broken section of the coffin. When Liu opened the coffin to examine it, he found a skull secured by cords;
the roots of the lotus had grown from between its teeth and cheeks. At that time, someone remarked: "In the past, there was a monk whose name and lineage were unknown who recited the Lotus Sutra."
He produced one hundred thousand fascicles. He transformed others without haste. His final instructions were that his followers should wear paper garments and use tiles for his coffin;
this was indeed so. Now, a temple named Lianhua has been built upon the site of the former post station (as seen in Hong Juefan’s *Wenzi Chanji*).

In ancient times, there were two monks from the Fanyang Wanghou Temple whose names have been lost. Reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* was their constant practice. When they first died, they were temporarily interred beneath an embankment.
Later, when they were reburied, their bones had all decayed, yet only their tongues remained intact. Furthermore, there was another monk in Yongzhou who also recited [the same sūtra].
Fahua lived in seclusion on Mount Bailu, where he was attended by a young boy who provided for his needs. When Fahua passed away, his body was placed beneath a cliff;
while all other remains had become desiccated, his tongue remained as it was before (from the *Sanbao gantong lu*).
Dharma Master Sengfayu of Jizhou:
Sengfayu was a native of Jizhou. At the age of fifteen, he resolved to leave the household life and became a disciple of Huisi.

Huisi’s observance of the precepts was rigorous and austere, and he practiced the dhūta ascetic disciplines. Fayu was upright and courageous, possessing a profound understanding of his master's path; consequently, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.

In the sutras, it is vowed that one should follow the example of Bhaiṣajyarāja by burning one’s own body as an offering to the Mahāyāna. At that time, Yao Xu, the Prince of Jin under the illegitimate Qin dynasty, was stationed at Puzha.
Fuyi reported the matter to the Prince, who said, "There are many ways to enter the Way; why must you sacrifice your life?
I dare not stubbornly oppose you, but I hope you will consider this well. Since Fuyi’s vow was firm, he immediately donned fragrant oil and wrapped his body in cloth, pouring [the oil over it].

Having applied oil and wax to his body, he recited the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" chapter and then set himself ablaze with fire. Monastics and laypeople vied with one another to witness this, all of whom were moved by grief and lamentation (from the *Liang Gaoseng zhuan*).
Dharma Master Hui-shao of Linchuan: his origins are unknown.
When he was a child, he would vomit whenever his mother fed him fish or meat; from then on, he abstained from pungent plants and meat.

At the age of eight, he left home to become a monk and mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. He was distinguished for his ascetic practices and strict observance of monastic discipline. Later, he followed Master Sengyao to reside at [a monastery].
At Zhaoti Monastery in Linchuan, he constantly reflected upon the gravity of the Buddha’s kindness and vowed to offer his own body as a repayment.

He then hired men to cut firewood, which he piled up to a height of one zhang against a stone chamber on Mount Dong. He carved a niche in its center and returned to the monastery to inform his master.

The Master admonished him, but he would not listen. Thereupon, he set a date to hold an Eight Precepts Retreat at the mountain. People from the entire district flocked there like clouds, filling the valleys and mountains.

When night fell, Sengshao himself performed the incense ritual; holding a candle and lighting firewood, he entered the shrine and sat down to recite the "Chapter on the Sacrifice of the Body" from the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*.
As the flames crept up to his forehead, the sound of the sutra could still be heard. Suddenly, the great assembly saw a star as large as a bushel measure.
He entered the flames directly and, in an instant, ascended to heaven. Everyone considered this an auspicious omen of his reception into the celestial palace.

Daoshao once said to his fellow students, "A *wutong* tree shall grow at the place where I burned my body; do not cut it down by any means. Three days later, it indeed grew there as predicted, which both monastics and laypeople found extraordinary.
This was the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*).

Dharma Master Qing of Mount Lu, whose secular name was Senghuiqing, was a native of Guangling. During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he resided on Mount Lu. His mastery of the sutras and vinaya was profound, and he maintained his monastic discipline with rigorous purity.

Whenever he chanted the *Lotus Sutra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, and other scriptures at night, he would frequently hear the sound of fingers snapping and voices of praise coming from the darkness.
Sheng once encountered a storm at Xiaolei; his boat was on the verge of sinking. Sengqing focused his mind entirely on reciting the sutras to seek safety and deliverance.
While the boat was amidst the waves, he felt as though someone were supporting and pulling it. In an instant, they reached the shore.
From then on, he devoted himself to recitation and study until old age without ever growing weary (*Fayuan zhulin*).
Dharma Master Sengdaojiong of Guangling, whose secular surname was Ma, was a native of Fufeng. Having left his home life, he took Dàoyì as his teacher.

When the master fell ill, he dispatched Daojiong and three others to Mount Huo to gather stalactites. After traveling several li into the cave, they had to cross a stream by stepping across wooden beams; three of them drowned.
The torch was exhausted once more. Sòng Jǐng habitually recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara.
After a short while, he saw a light like a firefly; he pursued it and emerged [from the water]. Furthermore, he once traveled south to the capital with four fellow students.
While crossing a river on ice at night, the ice broke in midstream. His companions were unable to cross, but Jǐng relied solely upon his recitation and invocation; suddenly, beneath his feet—
As he was carrying an object, he again saw a red light leading the way, and thus they reached Nanjian Temple.
On another night, while entering meditative concentration, he happened to see four men driving a precious chariot and inviting Sengjiong to board it.
As Jiong ascended the chariot, he suddenly found himself by the Shen Family Bridge in his home prefecture; by the roadside sat a man on a folding chair, directing the crowd.
He said, "Previously, I merely intended for you to know the Master's dwelling place. Why have you troubled yourself by coming from so far? You should be sent back immediately.

Once they had returned to the monastery, the assembly was entirely unaware of the Master’s coming and going. This was during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*).
Regarding the Dharma Master Ziming of the Song dynasty:

During the Jianchu era, there was a monk named Puming who entered the monastic life at a young age. By nature he was pure and simple; he always maintained a vegetarian diet and wore coarse cloth garments.

He made the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* his daily practice. When reciting, he used separate clothing and a separate seat, never mixing them with his ordinary attire. Every time he recited...
Upon reaching the "Chapter on Exhortation," he saw Samantabhadra standing before him riding an elephant. While reciting the *Vimalakīrti*, he heard the sound of music and singing from the air.
Wang Daozhen’s wife, a local resident, was at the point of death; she requested the Master to perform incantations. Just as he was entering the gate—
A patient was in a state of stupor when he suddenly saw a creature resembling a wild cat, several feet in length, emerge from a dog-hole; his illness was immediately cured.

Furthermore, once while he was walking by the water’s edge, a shaman said, "When the divine spirits see Master Ming, they all flee in haste" (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*).

The Dharma Master Hui of Yuezhou, the śramaṇa Fahui, was born into the Xiahou clan. From his childhood, he possessed extraordinary insight; once he had shaved his hair—its curls as green as a conch shell—his conduct became even more rigorous.
During the Daming era of the Song dynasty, he traveled east to the Cave of Yu and later retired to Mount Tianzhu, where he devoted himself to the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Throughout his life he was never indolent, enjoying a simple and austere lifestyle, subsisting merely on vegetarian food and wearing cloth garments. He resided constantly in a single pavilion, withdrawing from the affairs of the world for over thirty years.
Princes and nobles who halted their carriages at his gate could no longer obtain an audience with him;

only Zhou Yong, whose faith and understanding were both profound, was granted special access. At times, there were those who admired his virtue and came to pay their respects; some, through the mediation of Zhou Yong, were able to meet him.
[Recorded in] the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*. Dharma Master Senghou of the capital was surnamed Gong by birth;
his family had been people of Xiliang for generations. During the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, he arrived in the capital. Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*...
He recited the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* at a rate of one complete cycle every two days. He continued in this manner for nearly sixty years without ceasing.
Later, he established a stone chamber on a ridge behind the capital city as a place for meditation and recitation.

One day, feeling slightly unwell, he requested hot water for washing and rinsing his mouth, adjusted his appearance with solemn dignity, joined his palms, and passed away at the age of eighty-nine. This was the Master.
From the age of eighteen until his death, whenever the shadow of the sun shifted even slightly, he would pass the day in empty fasting (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*).
Dharma Master Jin of the capital was named Huijin.
He was the son of Yao from Wuxing. In his youth, he was a man of the wandering knightly way; it was only at the age of forty that he attained realization. Consequently—

Having left the household life, he resided at Gaozuo Temple in the capital, where he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). He took only the most simple and austere food and vowed to recite the Lotus Sūtra.

His mental exertion was so strenuous that whenever he took up the scroll, he would fall ill. Consequently, he resolved to produce one hundred copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as a means of repenting for his past transgressions.

Thereafter, he collected offerings daily; once the production of the scriptures was complete, his illness gradually subsided. Subsequently, he redoubled his efforts in chanting and upholding the text.

He dedicated all his meritorious deeds with the vow to be reborn in the Western Paradise. One day, he suddenly heard a voice from the air saying, "As you have vowed, you shall certainly attain rebirth there.
In the third year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, he passed away peacefully without illness at the age of eighty-five (*Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*).

Dharma Master Seng Huiguo of the Jingzhong Temple was a native of Yuzhou. From his youth, he abstained from meat and pungent vegetables. He resided at Waguan Temple in the capital, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and other scriptures.

Once, while in the latrine, he saw a ghost who paid him homage and said: "In the past, I served as a *vinaya-dhara* (steward). Because I was slightly lacking in accordance with the Dharma, I fell [into this state]."
"Among the *pūti-gandha* (feces-eating) spirits, there was once three thousand coins belonging to me, buried beneath a paulownia tree.

May the Dharma Master, out of compassion, take them to plant the seeds of merit for me. The Master then informed the assembly and retrieved the money, commissioning a copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in his memory.

Later, he suddenly dreamed that this ghost thanked him, saying, "I have already received a transformed retribution; it is far superior to what I experienced the day before. This occurred during the Taishi era of the Song dynasty (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*).

Dharma Master Yu of Mount Lu, whose posthumous name was Sengyu, was a native of Wuxing with the secular surname Zhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of twenty, and his religious practice was pure and complete.
He established Zhaoti Temple on the southern side of Mount Lu to reside there. He constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra without ever failing for even a moment. One day...

He said to his friends: "The reason for my lingering in the three miserable realms is due to my emotional attachments. Now that these emotions are about to be exhausted, it is fitting that I cast off this physical form.
Why should the path of the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja) remain so distant? He then piled wood to create a shrine, prepared a vegetarian feast, and took leave of the assembly.
On that day, rain and clouds fell in torrents, whereupon he made this vow: "If I have no regrets in relinquishing this body, may the heavens become clear and bright; otherwise, let it not be so."
It rained heavily. Having finished speaking, the rain indeed cleared. At night, he entered his niche, sat cross-legged with palms joined, and recited the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga-parivarta*.
Flames reached his body, yet he remained seated as if nothing had happened. The assembly saw purple vapors rising into the sky, which did not disperse for days.
He was forty-four years old at the time, which was the third day of the sixth month in the second year of the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty. Fourteen days later, [he passed away].
In the old room where Sengyu once lived, two paulownia trees suddenly sprouted; their branches and leaves were lush and abundant, growing straight upward so tall that they pierced through the roof.

Those who recognized them considered them to be twin *śāla* trees, manifesting the path to *nirvāṇa*. Because Sengyu had nearly attained this state, he beheld this auspicious omen, and was thus called the "Twin Paulownia Śramaṇa.
Zhang Bian of Wu Commandery, serving as the Assistant Secretary to the Governor for Pacifying the South, personally witnessed these events and composed [this account] for him.
The Eulogy says: Vast and profound is the subtle mechanism; boundless is the ultimate Way. In the cycle of birth and death, who can call anything the supreme treasure?
(I) From of old, Bhaisajyarāja manifested transformations beyond compare. Having heard his story in the past, now we behold this man himself. (II) Magnificent is this śramaṇa!
His wisdom was settled and his mind firm; he concentrated his spirit within purple qi. His traces were manifested beneath the twin trees (III). His virtue was delightful and his conduct noble.
Thus this composition is made, to evoke his faint likeness (IV). (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* of the Liang Dynasty)
Master Yiyi of Zhongshan was named Huiyi.
A native of Guangling, he entered the monastic order at Shouchun and later resided at Zhulin Temple. His character and integrity were exceptionally outstanding.

He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* with great diligence and vowed to cremate his body as a true offering to the Dharma. Among those who saw or heard of him, there were many who either reviled or praised him.

Initially, he ceased eating grain and subsisted on clarified butter and oil; later, he abandoned even the butter and oil, consuming only fragrant pills. Although his physical constitution was frail, his spirit remained alert and upright.
Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty held him in deep reverence and wonder, dispatching an envoy to admonish him to desist, but he did not comply. This was in the seventh year of the Daming era.

On the Buddha’s birthday that year, he established cauldrons and prepared oil at the southern foot of Mount Zhong. He then proceeded to the palace to take leave of the Emperor; upon seeing him, the Emperor changed countenance.

The Master repeatedly exhorted him regarding the Buddha-dharma before withdrawing. The Emperor personally came in his carriage to visit him, at which time the fourfold assembly gathered there in haste.
The Master then entered the cauldron. He wrapped himself in *karpāsa* cotton and doused himself with oil. Just as he was about to have the fire lit, the Emperor stopped him again.
Fayi remained firm and would not comply, saying, "What is this wretched body and lowly life worth compared to Your Majesty’s noble intentions?

I only pray that you grant twenty people permission to leave the household life, so they may serve as aids to the Buddha-dharma. The Emperor granted his request by imperial decree. Fayi held a candle and ignited it spontaneously; with palms joined, he recited the *Bhaiṣajyaguru*.

In the "Chapter on the King": When the fire reached his eyebrows and eyelashes, he could still hear its sound. The multitude witnessed this with such grief and distress that their cries shook the mountains and valleys.
Suddenly, the Emperor heard the sound of flutes and pipes in the air; a wondrous fragrance wafted through the day until he returned home.

That night, the Emperor again dreamed that Fayin arrived, shaking his monk’s staff, and once more instructed him on the Buddha-dharma. The following day, the Emperor convened a great assembly and ordained twenty persons.
The Imperial Edict for the Establishment of Yaowang Temple at the Site of the Cremation (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*):

Dharma Master Sengfazong of the Fahua Taisong lineage was a native of Linhai. In his youth, he delighted in hunting; once, while shooting in the Shan River valley, he struck a pregnant deer, which suddenly fell.

A son was born from her womb; even as she still held the arrow in her mouth, she licked her child. Zong repented, saying, "To crave life and love one's child is common to all who possess consciousness.

He then broke his bow and snapped his arrows, shaved his hair to become a monk, and supported himself by begging for alms. He ate but a single meal each day and prostrated before the Buddha during the six periods of the day to repent for his past transgressions.
He constantly chanted the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the sound of which reached the four quarters, and men and women alike [came to hear him].

More than three thousand people received the precepts of refuge from him. He expanded his dwelling to establish a vihāra, which he named the Fahua Terrace (Dharma Lotus Terrace) after the name of the sūtra he recited (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty).
Regarding Master Deng of Mount Lu:
Master Deng resided at Dalin Temple on Mount Kuanglu. He was thoroughly versed in the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, chanting it day and night without ceasing.
One day, he suddenly saw a silver palace in the sky gradually descending toward his room; it then suddenly transformed into a golden palace, and the Master entered it.
The Master remained seated, rising only for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) in this manner for three years. When Prince Jin’an heard of this, he issued successive edicts to welcome him.

Consequently, the Master briefly descended from the mountain. The Prince, together with the fourfold assembly, prepared incense and flowers and followed the Master to request the precepts. Sengde said, "It is too noisy and distracting during the day."
Their minds were largely distracted; they should have received it during the clear night.

When the time came for the master to formally recite the characteristics of the precepts and the Three Refuges, light suddenly emanated from his mouth, illuminating the entire assembly. Seeing this light, the multitude vied with one another to prostrate, creating a tumultuous commotion.
The Master remained silent, and the light immediately withdrew. The Master said, "I originally intended to receive the precepts; why must I witness such clamor and commotion?
The manifestation of this light was merely an auspicious omen for receiving the precepts, but it was not the primary condition for actually attaining them.

We shall begin again from the beginning. The assembly remained silent. The Master preached the Dharma once more, and the light appeared again. The assembly again broke into clamor, so he stopped for that reason. The next day—
He returned once more. The Master then took his leave and retired to the mountains. The golden hall that had appeared returned to its former state.
One day, he suddenly said to his companions, "Now I shall ascend the golden hall; I shall not return again. On that very day, he suddenly passed away (as recorded in the *Lingrui ji*).
Regarding Master Yuhangzhi:
During the Eastern Jin dynasty, there was a monk named Fazhi who built a hermitage on Mount Yuhang. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* morning and evening without ceasing.
A pheasant nested beside his hermitage; whenever it heard the sound of his recitation, it would fly and gather around his seat as if attending upon him.

He stood listening to the recitation for seven years in this manner. One day, he became emaciated and haggard. The Master patted him and said, "Though you belong to the feathered race, you have been able to listen to the sutras.
If you were to escape this karmic body, you would surely be reborn in the human realm. The next morning, the pheasant suddenly died. The Master buried it immediately.
That night, while the Master was resting lightly in sleep, he dreamed that a young boy bowed twice and said, "I am that pheasant. Because I listened to the Master’s recitation..."
He had escaped from among the feathered species and was now born as a male child in the household of the Wang family at the foot of the mountain;

even now, there were still pheasant feathers on his right armpit, which could be verified by anyone who saw him. Early the next morning, the monk arrived at the house and questioned them, and it was indeed so.
One day, when the Wang family was preparing a vegetarian feast, Zhi Fang approached the gate, and this boy suddenly exclaimed, "Our Master has come! The entire assembly marveled at this.

He brought it to show his resolve. Daoshi stroked it and said, "This is my pheasant-child. He then removed his garment and examined it thoroughly; indeed, there were three feathers of a pheasant beneath his armpit.
When he reached the age of seven, [Daoshi] permitted him to leave the household life. His parents consented. Upon reaching the appointed time, he entered the mountains.
At sixteen, he shaved his head. Because there were feathers under his armpit, he was named Tanyi (Cloud Wing). Daoshi bestowed upon him the Lotus Sutra, which he did not forget.
Regarding the single character "Yi" (Wing): when Master Zhi returned to stillness, Yi became the second patriarch of this mountain.
The Great Master Tianyi Feiyun’s dharma name was Tanyi;
his clan and lineage have already been mentioned in the preceding chapter. Having become a monk, he traveled in various directions to seek the Way.

He first visited Mount Lu, where he attained a thorough realization of the essential teachings under Dharma Master Huiyuan. Subsequently, he entered Guanzhong to pay homage to Kumārajīva as he was lecturing on and translating the sūtras and śāstras;
there he achieved unimpeded mastery and attained great eloquence. Later, together with his fellow student Tanyue, he traveled east to Kuaiji.
Arriving at Qinwang Mountain, he found the Five Peaks and Twin Streams distinct and magnificent in their grandeur; consequently, he hewed stones [to build a monastery].
He cleared away the weeds to establish a plan for mountain dwelling and devoted himself exclusively to reciting the Lotus Sūtra for nearly ten years.
One day, as the sun was about to set, a woman appeared, dressed in colorful garments and carrying a bamboo basket containing a white pig and two large garlic bulbs.
Standing before the Master, she wept and said, "I am the daughter of such-and-such a family from the foot of the mountain.
While entering the mountains to gather ferns, I encountered a fierce tiger on the road and fled here. The sun has already set; the vegetation is shrouded in shadow and jackals and wolves roam about.

I have no means of returning home. May I venture to beg for one night's lodging? The Master, citing matters of suspicion and impropriety, firmly refused her request. The woman then shed tears of sorrow.
"Alas! The Master, having no other choice, yielded to her request and provided a straw mat. She immediately began reciting the sutras upon it. When the third watch arrived, she cried out in distress;

her illness flared up and she claimed her abdomen was in pain. She hoped the Master would examine her. The Master administered medicine to her, but the woman’s pain only intensified. She called out incessantly, saying:
'If only you, Master, would press and massage the area around my navel and abdomen, I might find some slight relief. Otherwise—'"
She died immediately. "The Buddha-dharma takes compassion and skillful means as its foundation. Why did you, O Master, sit by and watch without extending a hand to save her?
The Master replied, "I am a monk who has received the Great Precepts. What principle allows me to touch a woman's body? She entreated him most earnestly.
He immediately wrapped his *khakkhara* staff in a cloth and, from a distance, began to stroke it with it. After a short while, he announced, "It is already unnecessary.

The following morning, the woman stepped out onto the courtyard; her colorful garments transformed into auspicious clouds, the pig changed into a white elephant, and the garlic blossomed into twin lotuses.
A woman, her feet treading upon lotuses, straddling an elephant and riding upon clouds, said to the Master: "I am the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Since you will soon return to my assembly, I have come specifically to test you; I observe the state of your mind as clearly as the moon reflected in water."
"It cannot be defiled. Having spoken these words, he vanished into the mists and departed. At that time, flowers rained down from heaven and the earth shook everywhere.

Among the local people who heard and saw this, there was none who did not offer praise. On that same day, Meng Gong Yi, the Prefectural Governor, was just rising at dawn to attend to his official duties.
Suddenly, auspicious clouds were seen billowing in the south, their radiance shining across the courtyard. Beneath the clouds, there was a faint sound of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments.
Upon inquiry, he learned of Master Puxian’s manifestation of his passing; he then reported the Master’s spiritual conduct to the imperial court.
An edict was immediately issued to establish a temple, named Fahua (which is the present-day Tianyi Temple). This occurred during the reign of Emperor Yijian of the Jin’an period.
This was the thirteenth year of the Xih era. The Master reached the age of seventy and entered parinirvāṇa on this mountain.

The monks then fashioned a statue based upon his true body (śarīra). During the suppression of the teachings under the Tang Emperor Wu, the assembly concealed the image within the trunk of a tree to the south of the temple, so that it remained undestroyed.
King Wusuku of the Wuyue Kingdom specifically conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Feiyun. (The Master’s life story is recorded in both the *Sengzhuan* and the *Zhulin*).
There is also an original biography and authentic record concerning Tiantai’s robes; all points of discrepancy therein have been carefully examined and recorded.

The Dharma Master Ming of Yuezhou, the śramaṇa Hongming, was born into the Ying clan of Kuaiji. He entered the monastic order at Yunmen Temple. His conduct was solitary and lofty, and he was esteemed by all.
He was one whom all looked up to. He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, practiced seated meditation, and performed repentance rituals, never ceasing throughout the six periods of the day.
He moved the spirits such that the water in his purification pitcher remained perpetually full; people said this was because divine youths were attending to him.

One day, while he was engaged in seated meditation, a tiger suddenly crouched before him; after a long time, it departed. Subsequently, he went to Shemoyan (Stone Old Woman’s Rock) in Yongxing to enter meditative absorption, where there was also a mountain...
A spirit came to cause him distress. Ming bound it with his waist-cord. The spirit apologized and begged for release, saying, "Henceforth I shall not dare to come.
From that time on, it ceased its tracks. This was during the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty (according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang*).
In the capital was the Dharma Master Senghuiyu.
A native of Huanglong, he devoted himself to study from his youth. He traveled to the capital and resided at Lingxiang Temple, where he visited and studied under renowned masters.

Whenever he heard people being praised or criticized, he would immediately plug his ears and refuse to listen. He recited such sutras as the Lotus Sūtra and the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, and also practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
One day, while lying down to sleep, he suddenly dreamed that three men knocked at his door; they were dressed in fresh and clean robes and hats and held canopies to welcome him.
When he questioned them, they replied, "The Dharma Master is due to die; therefore, we have come to escort you. Daoyu said, "My minor karmic conditions are not yet finished; you may [wait]."
"May it be extended by one year? He then gave his assent and departed. On that same day the following year, he again dreamed of the three men as before, and subsequently passed away.
This was also during the Qi period (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*).
Dharma Master Qi of the capital was the monk Faqi. His secular surname was Yuan. In his youth, he relied upon Zhiguan Temple to leave the household life. By nature, he was reverent and silent;

he took the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* as his primary practice. Whatever offerings or alms he received, he accumulated them to fund the creation of Buddhist images. His family resided as migrants in the capital.

The Master traveled extensively through the great markets. One day he returned home; on another, he went to Dinglin Monastery; and yet again, he was at Zhizhi Garden. On three subsequent occasions, investigations were conducted at these locations, and in each case, the Master was seen coming for his midday meal.
On that particular day, he immediately returned to his old room, where he suddenly lay down and passed away. His corpse remained fragrant and supple, and two of his fingers were curled inward.

The assembly examined these signs and concluded that he had attained the second fruit of the path (the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*). Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, deeply moved by such divine wonders, visited his monastery.
A vegetarian feast was prepared. By imperial decree, he was granted a formal burial (*Liang Gaoseng Zhuan*).
In the capital, there was the Dharma Master Bian;

during the Qi dynasty, there was also the Śramaṇa Chaobian from Dunhuang. From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and possessed profound stillness in his conduct. He resided in the capital, and later...

He traveled from the capital to Jiankang and then to Dongyue, where he sought out renowned masters. Upon returning to the capital, he resided at Dinglin Monastery, living in seclusion to cultivate his fundamental nature with the intent to spend the remainder of his life among the mountains and forests.
He recited the seven fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* once every day; his mind was so quick that his speech followed effortlessly, and he always had surplus energy.
He performed more than one million five hundred thousand prostrations before the names of the Thousand Buddhas, remaining within the monastery gates for thirty years.
In his later years, he passed away at the age of seventy-three. His entire body was interred to the south of the monastery.
Sengyou erected a stele to record his virtues (as recorded in the *Liang Gaoseng Zhuan*).
The śramaṇa Dharma Master Saṃghavarman was twenty years old when he left the household life to become a monk. His faculties were dull and he was utterly bewildered, not knowing how to proceed.

He resolved his will and vowed to recite the Lotus Sūtra in order to seek rebirth in the West. He committed one line per day, or sometimes even half a verse; thus did he persevere with diligent hardship.

Only upon reaching the age of eighty did he finally master one section of a scripture. One day, while sitting in meditative absorption, he suddenly saw a deity in vermilion robes holding an invitation scroll that read:
"The Heavenly Emperor respectfully invites the Venerable Dharmakṣema. The Master said, "Since birth I have been dull-witted;

I have merely recited the scriptures according to my capacity, praying solely for rebirth in Sukhāvatī. Although the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is a superior realm, it is not what I desire. The deity then took his leave.

He departed. On another occasion, he dreamed of a great stupa made of the seven treasures, and found himself situated on its fifth tier. From there, he gazed upon a city of the seven treasures whose stairways extended beyond all bounds.
Outside stood two *vajrapāṇis* holding vajras, and dozens of men dressed in blue robes held white fly-whisks to sweep the stairway.
Sengcheng asked about this, and the reply was: "This is the stairway to the precious city of the Western [Pure Land], coming to welcome you."
Tong awoke from his dream and immediately said to his disciples, "Take my robes and bowl and prepare a communal vegetarian feast for the assembly.
He further asked, "Did you all see the thousand Buddhas at that time? They replied, "We did not see them. He continued, "Did you perceive an extraordinary fragrance?
They replied, "We all smelled it. Having spoken, he passed away peacefully while facing west (from the *Lingrui ji*).
Dharma Master Yun of Jinling was a native of Yangxian.
His secular surname was Zhou. When his mother first conceived him, she saw clouds filling the room; consequently, he was given the childhood name "Yun" (Cloud).
At the age of seven, he left the household life and was given the monastic name Fayun. He was brilliant, elegant, and outstanding among his contemporaries. Liang...
Upon seeing him, the Master sighed and said, "My own spiritual brilliance is far inferior to that of Yun. This youth will surely become a pillar of the Great Dharma.

When the Master reached the age of thirty, he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*; his eloquence was as swift as a rising wind, and students flocked to him like the spokes of a wheel.

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty held him in high esteem and issued an edict appointing him as the head of Guangzhai Monastery. As for Fayun, from the time he first donned the robes of a novice, he had already held the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in profound regard, refining his mastery through repeated study.

Sengsi once went to a secluded rock cave to lecture alone on this sutra. He arranged stones as his disciples, broke off pine branches to serve as whisks, and both sang and guided the recitation while simultaneously engaging in difficult questions and answers.
Furthermore, his commentaries were layered and repetitive, with preceding and succeeding sections reflecting one another in profusion.

Once, while lecturing on this sutra at a certain temple, he was suddenly moved by celestial flowers resembling falling snow that descended from the sky and filled the air; they drifted into the hall, and he ascended [the seat].
The bowl did not fall. When the lecture was finished, he departed. At that time, Master Zhi’s Way transcended the mundane world.

Once, someone came to Yun and said, "I wish to understand the 'Lion's Roar. I request that you, Master, explain it for me. The Master immediately ascended the lion throne and analyzed the teaching in detail.
Zhi snapped his fingers and said, "Excellent! How subtle and wondrous! One day, because the heavens were parched with drought, Emperor Wu asked Zhi, "What plan can bring rain? Zhi—

It was said that since Yun could bring forth rain, one should invite Master Yun to lecture on the sutras. When Yun lectured on the *Lotus Sutra*, reaching the passage where "the moisture universally permeates," the heavens immediately poured down a great deluge of refreshing rain.
Yuan Ang, the Court Official, remarked, "In my home, there is a monk who receives regular offerings;

I have made a vow that he may attain the wisdom and understanding of Master Yun. Suddenly, he dreamed of a monk who said, "Master Yun had already lectured on this [sutra] during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha."
Sūtra: How could he be easily opposed? (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).

Later, during the Northern Zhou dynasty, Dharma Master Huiyuan was a monk of no shallow capacity. He stood nine chi and five cun tall, with a waist nine spans in circumference. When he ascended the seat—

He preached the Dharma, like thunder that startles the hibernating creatures from their slumber. At that time, Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty wished to abolish the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism.

He summoned all the śramaṇas to assemble in the palace hall. The Emperor addressed them, saying: "I have received the Mandate of Heaven to nourish and raise the common people. Throughout the ages, three teachings have been transmitted; I have examined them to determine their ultimate principles.
As for Confucianism, its rites, righteousness, loyalty, and integrity are beneficial to the world and must be established. Furthermore, the True Buddha has no physical image."
"Reverence for the Buddha remains in my heart. Yet these Buddhist stupas are magnificent and beautiful; they are truly insentient things—how could they bestow grace?

It is not worth preserving them. This is my intention. What do the virtuous masters think? At that time, more than five hundred monks turned pale and remained speechless. Huiyuan stepped forward from the assembly and said:
"Your Majesty says that the true Buddha has no image; this is indeed as you have stated. However, living beings who possess ears and eyes rely [upon such representations]."

"The sutras allow one to hear of the Buddha; relying on images allows one to manifest the Truth. If these were abolished, there would be no means by which reverence could arise. The Emperor said, "The True Buddha of empty space is known by all within themselves.

Huiyuan replied, "Prior to the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han, the sutras and images had not yet reached this land. How was it that [the people] did not know [of the Buddha] then? The Emperor had no reply.
Huiyuan continued, "If one does not rely upon the teachings of the sutras, consider that prior to the Three Augusts, written characters did not yet exist."

"Should one understand the Five Constant Virtues? The Emperor had no reply. Huiyuan said, "If you discard them on the grounds that images are insentient, then are the seven ancestral temples of the state not likewise insentient?
The Emperor said, "As for the seven temples, I do not consider them to be correct either.
Huiyuan said, "If you abolish the seven temples, you will not honor your ancestors; how then can you claim to preserve the Confucian teachings? If all three teachings are abolished, then..."
"How then will you govern the state? The Emperor had no reply. Huiyuan said, "Your Majesty has now used the power of the king to destroy the Triple Gem.
Hell makes no distinction between the noble and the humble; why do you not fear it? The Emperor said, "I only wish to bring happiness to the common people."

"How can you plead for exemption from hell? Huiyuan replied, "Your Majesty has transformed the people through false views; the common folk shall surely share Your Majesty’s destiny in the Avīci Hell. What joy could there be in that?
The Emperor grew angry and issued an edict for all the monks to withdraw, stating they should reconvene later.

From this point on, the Emperor practiced tyranny, and both the Buddhist and Daoist teachings were suppressed. Huiyuan then lived in seclusion in the Western Mountains of Jiji County, devoting himself exclusively to the recitation of the Dharma.

Huiguan and Vimalakīrti each recited [the scriptures] a thousand times; their principles were even more profound than those of Li Kui (the "Cave of Principle"), and they never abandoned their practice of the "raft.

Upon reaching the era of the Great Elephant (the Sui dynasty), they subtly manifested the Buddha’s transformation. At the beginning of the Great Sui, he was again ordained as a monk, his fame resounded at the imperial court, and an edict was issued appointing him as the Chief Śramaṇa of Luozhou to rectify and sustain the Buddha-dharma.
Although Huiyuan declined the appointment, it was not granted; he was thus installed in that position (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
The Dharma Master of Yangzhou, the śramaṇa Zhifang, was a native of the region of Shu. His fame spread throughout Yang and Yue, and his phrasing and meaning were pure and abundant.

While lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he reached the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," [describing] how the jeweled stupa was five hundred yojanas high and exquisite, measuring two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
He spoke, saying: "Why must the lands of the Buddhas of the past alone possess such lofty excellence? This blessed land of Yangzhou is also most magnificent.
For instance, the seven-tiered pagoda reaching to the heavens vies for radiance with the sun and moon; the nine-storied [pagoda] of Tongtai competes in color with the mists and clouds.
At the square wells, lotus leaves hang downward; at the circular cisterns, lotus flowers are spread askew. It was as if—
To the south of the abode of Anshizhi (An Shigao) and to the north of the settlement of Liniqie (Lokakṣema), what has been heard by ear and seen by eye may perhaps be compared side by side.
His spoken words formed such elegant compositions. At that time, there was the Dharma Master Baohai, who had previously expounded [the scriptures] before Emperor Wu;

on this day, he sat in the assembly and posed a challenge, saying: "In the sutras, it is said that the earth was transformed three times. This region was changed from impurity to purity. It is also possible to transform—"

Huihai asked, "In that case, do ordinary people become sages? Daofang replied, "Transformation Buddhas are exceedingly numerous; because they are humble, they must be widespread. Ordinary people and sages are naturally so; why trouble yourself to alter this?
Huihai further challenged him, saying, "If that were so, then sixty minor kalpas would be like the time it takes to eat a meal.

This would be something seen only by sages, while ordinary people could not see it. If ordinary people and sages both see it, then are ordinary people also sages? Daofang laughed and said, "Why such high seats [of argument]?"
He had previously said this, which was merely stating his own position and raising an objection against himself. Haijue (Haijue) made a slip of the tongue, whereupon [the other] quipped to him:

"If three wooden planks can ascend, what need is there for 'wisdom' (zhi) to be square? Fangxun replied immediately: "Since it is but tiles, rubble, and a muddy pond, how can it be called a 'treasure ocean' (baohai)?
The assembly dispersed with laughter (*Xu Gaoseng Zhuan*).
The Dharma Master Zhensheng Jinghui was a person of pure True Vehicle (Zhensheng) realization.

His family lineage had long been devoted to Confucian learning, yet he was born with innate wisdom granted by Heaven. He could recite eight thousand words daily, a feat rarely equaled by his contemporaries.

Eventually, his reputation reached the Emperor’s ears, and officials looked up to him in admiration. In the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era, an imperial edict concerning the Three Teachings was issued.
The Academician [Hui]jing debated at the Hongwen Hall. He was summoned to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*, while the Daoist Cai Huang lectured on the *Treatise on the Way*.
Cai Huang asked: "The scripture states that the 'Introduction Chapter' is the first. I do not understand to which section this 'first' refers. Jing replied:

"When the Tathāgata entered meditative concentration, emitted light, and rained down flowers, it served as the grand foundation for breaking through duality and established the gradual process for clarifying the One. Therefore, it is called [the Introduction]."
"Preface" (*xu*) refers to being at the head. "First" (*di*) means beginning. Since the preface occupies the very forefront, it is called "first.
Huáng said: "'Di' is 'ti' (younger brother). If one is a younger brother, one cannot be called 'one'; if one says 'one,' one cannot be called 'di.
These two words are contradictory. How can they be reconciled? Jìng said: "Did I not say earlier that 'di' means to occupy the foremost position and 'yī' means the beginning?"
The Master did not grasp what had been said before, yet he mistakenly presented a subsequent objection. Senghuang said, "Your words have not even left your lips;
how could there be anything to grasp? Jing said, "When a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, his voice shakes the ten directions. Yet the Daoist masters sitting here are as if lost or intoxicated."
Huang said, "How could one hear a jackal preaching the Dharma? Jing replied, "The celestial palaces are strictly guarded; by principle, the tracks of beasts are excluded from there.
The Daoist’s spirit was clouded, leading him to mistake a person for a beast. The celestial being was greatly pleased, and the entire assembly rose in joyful exultation and dispersed.
Such was the pivotal power of Jing in our teaching (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Regarding the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema:

At the beginning of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, there was a śramaṇa named Dharmakṣema from Huanglong. He was diligent in his practice and asceticism, and he constantly recited the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Accompanied by twenty-five disciples, he traveled west to India, enduring numerous hardships and perils along the way. Dharmakṣema...
His resolve became even firmer. Having reached Śrāvastī, he encountered a herd of elephants on the road. Exhausting his heart in devotion, he recited the scriptures with mindfulness;
thereupon, a lion emerged from the forest, and the elephants immediately fled in retreat. Furthermore, a herd of wild oxen arrived bellowing, intending to cause him harm.
He exerted his mindfulness with the same intensity as at the beginning. Suddenly, a large vulture flew toward him; startled, it dispersed and vanished without a trace.
Thus he was able to escape. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*, Master Lang).

The monk Falarong was accomplished in the recitation and upholding of the Lotus Sūtra. One night, he dreamed that he entered the underworld. The official of the underworld questioned him regarding his spiritual practice;

he then took up his brush and issued a judgment, saying: "The paths to the three evil realms are blocked, and the way to the human and celestial realms is opened. Behold the Buddha and practice with diligence; do not stop at the 'transformed city' (the provisional vehicle)."
One may show them the celestial palaces; they shall see their future place of rebirth (*Commentary on the Inscription of Auspicious Omens*).
During the Yongtai era of the Wei dynasty, there was a monk named Sengzhao at Danling Temple in Qinzhou. By nature he was leisurely and detached, and he always delighted in wandering.
Guan went to Mount Xing one day and saw a rock cave beneath a waterfall. He entered it and traveled for five or six li before emerging from the cave again.
Continuing northeast for several li along a rocky ravine, he suddenly saw a house where drifting dust reached his knees.
Looking around, he beheld a deep forest. After a short while, he encountered a monk about sixty years of age, whose eyebrows were over a zhang long and hung down in coils.
When he arrived at Eri, they received him with great joy. When asked about himself, he replied, "Three companions of mine came here to escape the world;
one has not yet returned, and another has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). He then inquired, "Who is the king today?
and so forth, before taking ears of grain, pounding them, and preparing a meal. A monk asked Zhaor: "What sūtra do you regularly recite? Zhaor replied, "I recite the Lotus Sūtra. The monk...
Shaking his head, the monk said, "Excellent! This is the work of sublime diligence. He then pointed to the sutras on the shelf in the eastern room and said, "These are the same ones I recite.
Would you like to hear them? Zhaohui joined his palms and replied, "Yes. The monk then began to recite them; the clarity of his voice and tone reached from night until dawn.
Zhaohui suffered from drowsiness, so the monk said, "Just sleep yourself; I am always like this. The next morning, food was again prepared, and Zhaohui expressed his gratitude.
He then took his leave and departed; the monk did not detain him, merely saying, "A fellow student of mine has gone out. If you should encounter him, he will surely bring about great enlightenment.
Once Daozhao had returned, he immediately sought out a companion and went back to search for him, but they could not find where he was (from the *Xu lingrui ji*).
During the Northern Wei dynasty, there was a Dhyāna Master named Cheng who upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with unwavering diligence.

At the end of his life, he was reborn as the fifth son of the Xie family in Hedong. From birth, he was able to speak of his past lives; he took no pleasure in remaining a layman and his mind turned toward [the religious life].
He became a monk. His father served as the Prefect of Sizhou, and he followed his father to the official post.

He then went to Qidi Temple in Zhongshan, where he suddenly recalled a place he had frequented in the past. He searched for his original disciple and said to him, "Do you perhaps remember when we crossed the water to go to Langshan?
The Master Chéng was my own self. In the room was a miraculous desk.
He was sent away to be removed [from the monastery]. His parents, fearing he would renounce the world, provided him with a wife. Thereafter, he forgot his past-life memories;
yet, he constantly gave rise to a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*) and remained seated in quietude with hands folded (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Dharma Master Zhanzhan of Qizhou:
A native of Qizhou, his innate nature was pure and profound; he was simple and upright in his conduct, regarding benevolence and compassion as his fundamental principle.
He resided at Xiancao Temple in a deep valley on Mount Ren-tou, where he constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* without ever ceasing for even a moment.
On the day of his passing, Master Zhi (Zhigong) reported to Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty: "A holy monk of the stage of *srotāpanna* from Xiancao Temple in the north has entered parinirvāṇa today.
When both the clergy and the laity heard this, they all paid him homage from afar. At the time of Tanzhi’s death, he was serene and free from any lingering affliction. He sat upright and...
Manifestation: He extended one finger with each of his two hands. At that time, a Brahman monk remarked, "The extension of one finger signifies the realization of the first fruit [of the path].

Monastics and laypeople alike revered him, and he was interred in a stupa at his home mountain in his entirety; birds and beasts did not defile it, and it remains there even now (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Dharma Master Xian of Jiangling was Sengxian of Wu Commandery.
Born into the Yan clan, he was spiritually gifted from childhood, and those who knew him marveled at his brilliance. He served Dharma Master Daoze;
Ze, whose conduct was both influential and outwardly manifest, held him in deep esteem. As Xian traveled among the lecture halls, his eloquence was as natural as heaven itself.

Chui. During the Liang dynasty, Emperor Gaozu issued an imperial decree for the "Collected Exegesis" at Xingshan Hall. The Emperor, valuing his sharp intelligence, bestowed upon him the courtesy due to a member of the imperial household.

Since his youth, he had recited the Lotus Sūtra more than six thousand times. One day, while sitting as if in a state of sleep, he dreamed of Samantabhadra, whose fragrant light illuminated him as the Bodhisattva personally rubbed the crown of his head.
He recorded this vision but did not transmit it. It was only when he reached old age that [the text] gradually became available.
The monk Chen lectured dozens of times on eighteen sūtras, including the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.

He composed commentaries for each of them, which were circulated among later students. Later, he entered parinirvāṇa and was interred at Mount Zhonghua in Jiangling (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

Dharma Master Huiguan of Nanjian Monastery served as a monk and was a leader among those who listened to Dharma Master Xian’s lectures at Nanjian Monastery. Later, he fell ill and remained in his room with the door closed, refusing to go out;
he devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* and offered sincere repentance. His illness subsequently abated, and from then on, he never ceased his practice.

Regarding his deeds: Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty held him in such high esteem that he issued an edict for him to reside at Nanjian Temple. There he extensively lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
his phrasing was rich and his arguments were robust, both exceeding all expectations. Thus, a contemporary proverb said: "The words of Jiakara, recorded by Huiguan.
People of the time copied his works as if they were pearls and jade (as noted in the *Lingshui ji*).

Chan Master Ren of Jingzhou, whose secular name was Sengfaren, was a native of Jiangling. He entered the monastic order at Tianhuang Temple and was fully endowed with the observance of the precepts. He specialized in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, reciting each daily twice.
As the assembly there was often noisy and distracted, he subsequently went to the foot of Fuchuan Rock in Jingzhou to practice the dhūta austerities in solitude.
He practiced meditation for thirty years. Since entering the mountains, he had sought no external protection; his intake of grain food was exhausted, and he sustained himself on fruits and water.
Sometimes he would eat only once every seven days. During one summer retreat, he consumed three *dou* of rice, yet even after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, five *sheng* still remained.
His meditation cell was barely large enough to accommodate his knees, and he never ventured outside. One day, an elephant suddenly appeared at the site of his cell;

ten days later, it fell ill and passed away lying on its right side. His robes and alms bowl had become as worn and decayed as dust; when the assembly estimated their value, they were not worth even ten *wen*.
This was during the Liang dynasty (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Dharma Master Yiqian Lin was the monk Faling of the Later Liang dynasty.
He was the son of the Yan family from Zhiyang. At the age of fifteen, his insight and discernment were remarkably extraordinary.

He left home to become a monk at Yuquan Temple, where he did not wear silk or cotton. Sustaining himself by begging for alms, he wore only coarse cloth as clothing and took the practice of meditation and mindfulness as his vocation.
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for a long time, his side never touching the bed. He traveled far and wide to seek out teachers, reaching places no matter how distant.
His countenance was serene and dignified; all who saw him paid homage to his lofty character. Once, while at Mount Dai, he encountered a county magistrate who asked him for official credentials.
Sengling was always carrying a case containing one volume of the Lotus Sūtra. He remarked, "There are written characters within this case, yet I cannot find them.
This enraged the magistrate. Sengling replied, "This sūtra is the track upon which all Buddhas tread; that I walk and practice it is precisely my own walking of the written characters.
The magistrate ordered him imprisoned and withheld food for seven days, yet he continued to recite the sūtra with single-minded devotion. The magistrate was moved by his sincerity.
He had a nightmare and subsequently performed a repentance ritual to resolve it. Later, he resided at Mount Mo, where he passed away while seated beneath a cliff.
People smelled a wondrous fragrance that did not dissipate for ten days (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Senglang, the Dharma-master Lang of Ezhou, was born into the Xu family and was a native of Nanyang. Having reached adulthood, he left the secular life and soon entered the monastic order.
He resided frequently at Ezu and habitually kept a monkey and a dog. The Master would eat from a wooden bowl; when his meal was finished, he would feed the leftovers to the two animals. He ate.
He had already donned a monkey mask and was riding a dog while carrying an empty bowl. He allowed the dog to roam and wander at will, showing no restraint or regularity.

He recited various sutras, taking the Lotus Sutra as his primary focus. With pure resolve, he chanted and maintained his practice; in a single sitting, he would complete seven recitations, even up to seven hundred and seventy times, the number being by no means small.
His voice flowed freely, sounding like the lute or the flute. When bystanders observed him, they watched and listened [in wonder].
Both were lost. Lang’s limbs were extended and bound according to his own whim; his appearance was like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs.

Sometimes he stayed in wine shops, drinking and eating meat, yet no one could fathom his origins. Thus the proverb says: "Fahua Lang, with five limbs both extended and contracted; pork filling his mouth and forehead.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī at a neighboring monastery who possessed deep understanding of the sūtras and śāstras, and who resided there to lead others through her lectures. Her listeners—
Clouds gathered. When Hui-lang heard of this, he said, "This is the work of a malevolent spirit; how could there be any righteous principle in it? I must go to investigate.

One day he arrived at that temple while the nun was in the midst of preaching. Lang then rebuked her with a stern voice, saying, "You little maid! Why do you not descend from your seat upon my arrival?
At the sound of his voice, the nun collapsed, yet she remained standing before the hall, perspiration flowing to the ground, motionless and upright. [He] asked:
His wisdom and understanding suddenly became as if he were dull-witted and deaf; only after more than one hundred days did he return to his original nature.
This occurred during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Dongyue Jianshi (Eastern Peak Master Jian):
Shi Xingjian of the Sui dynasty. His origins are unknown. He constantly practiced meditative contemplation and was renowned for his strict integrity.

On one occasion, while traveling through Taishan on business, he entered the mountain shrine at daybreak and spent the night there. An official said, "There are no guest quarters here; there is only the corridor of the deity."
[The deity] descended. However, those who had stayed there invariably died a violent death. Sengjian said, "It will do no harm. He then spread out some mugwort beneath the eaves for him to sit upon.
As Sengjian sat upright reciting the sutras for about one watch of the night, he suddenly saw the deity, whose robes and cap were most magnificent, bowing with palms joined toward Sengjian.

Sengjian asked, "I have heard that many who stay overnight here die. Could it be that you, O Dānapati, are harming them? The spirit replied, "Those who are destined to die arrive specifically for that purpose;
they die upon hearing the voice of my disciple, not because I kill them. Jian asked again, "Is it true, as the world’s tradition says, that Mount Tai governs the ghosts?
The spirit said, "My merit is meager; such a thing exists. Jian said, "There were two fellow monks who had already [died]..."
"Is he dead? Is he still here? The spirit asked for his name. One person had already been born into the human realm; the other was in prison undergoing retribution. The Master went to see him.
The spirit sent an attendant to lead him into the walled courtyard. He saw a man in the midst of fire, wailing and crying out;

his form had changed beyond recognition, and the stench of his scorched flesh and blood was unbearable. Unable to bear looking further, he immediately returned to the eaves below and spoke again with the spirit.
Sitting down, Sengjian asked, "Is it possible to save this monk? The spirit replied, "It can be done. If you can transcribe the Lotus Sūtra for him, he will surely be able to escape.
Subsequently, he took his leave of the spirit. At dawn, the temple official saw that Sengjian had not died and was astonished. After Sengjian departed, he hurriedly reported on his previous vow.
Once the transcription and binding of the sūtra were complete, he brought it to the temple. The spirit emerged as before; when Sengjian informed him of what had happened, the spirit said:

The Master was writing the titles for the transcribed scriptures when the deity departed. He had now been reborn among humans; however, this place was impure and unsuitable for housing the scriptures.
"I pray that you, Master, will return them to the temple so they may be offered there," he said, and thus took his leave of the deity (*Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).
Dharma Master Lun of Yuezhou was Shi Senglun.
When he was five years old, he saw white light filling his room. He subsequently went to Yunmen Temple in Yuezhou to leave the household life.
His primary practice was the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*. During the Kaihuang era, when the Buddha-dharma flourished greatly, the Master resided at Wuyang.
While the Master was attending a lecture at the Vinaya school, he suddenly saw five-colored light, like a chariot wheel, illuminating his heart center.

He immediately prostrated before the fifty-three Buddhas within that light; even as the light had not yet subsided, he further prostrated before the fifty-five Buddhas, whereupon the light finally withdrew.
At the age of eighty-five, the Master suddenly called to his disciples and said, "In the stillness of the night, I have attained liberation through all dharmas."
It is said that he had attained the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), yet he did not know that the Lord of Devas (Śakra) was coming to welcome him. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
On the day of his burial, the sky was exceptionally clear and bright; though there were no clouds, it suddenly rained down. Everyone marveled at this (from the *Xu lingrui ji*).
Regarding Dharma Master Chao of Qizhou:
