During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, there was a monk named Hui-chao whose conduct was preeminent. He constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra.

He had a disciple whose name has been lost, who was still at the age of *zhixue* (roughly fifteen years old) and was also proficient in the first three fascicles of the Lotus Sūtra. One day he fell ill and died in Qi, which is to the east of Tai.

The mountain was not far away. Sengchao went there to burn incense and fully explained his purpose for coming. Suddenly, the wooden puppet spoke, saying, "Your Reverence’s precepts and ascetic practices are so refined and rigorous;
how would I dare not inform you of what you ask? It then led him before the Lord of the Underworld. Sengchao asked, "Where is my disciple now?
The Lord replied, "Wangming is here; he has no place of rebirth yet. Sengchao said, "I wish to meet with him."
"No," [the Master] replied. The official immediately dispatched a messenger to lead [him] eastward for several dozen paces, where they indeed met face-to-face.

He then asked how his suffering and joy were. The disciple said, "I am merely under restraint; I feel neither particular suffering nor joy. However, I am mindful that the place of my next birth is not yet fixed;

I pray that the Master will elevate me and deliver me. The Master asked, "What meritorious deed have you performed? The disciple replied, "I beg to commission the production of one copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* and to provide a vegetarian feast."
One hundred scrolls. Once the Master had returned, he immediately transcribed the sutras and provided a meal for the monks. When the task was finished, he went again to visit the Prefect.

The Prefect received him as before. The Master explained what he had done. The Prefect said, "When the anonymous Master wrote these sutras, his calligraphy was so marvelous that they were only completed when he was reborn in a superior realm.
The Master asked, "Where was he reborn? The Prefect replied, "He has been reborn in the household of Wang Wu, the Prince of Qi Commandery, as a male child."
"It will be possible to go and seek him once he is three years old. When more than three years had passed, [the Master] went to inquire, saying, "The donor’s son wishes to see you.
The Wang family resisted and denied having a son. The Master then recounted the words of the Prefectural Governor (fujun).
His wife, who was at home, said to her husband, "If the Dharma Master's spiritual power is such as this, we may allow him to see the child. She then took her son in her arms.
He was settled outside the monastery. Upon seeing the Master for the first time, the boy ran into his arms and wept bitterly for a long while.
When he grew up, he resolved to leave the household life and returned to serve Master Chao (as recorded in the *Lingrui ji*).

The Chan Master Cizhi of Qizhou, whose secular surname was Sengxiao, resided at Cimeng Temple. From his youth, he followed the teachings of Chan Master Xinxing regarding the Buddhadharma of the Third Stage and practiced asceticism.
He constantly begged for food, wore robes made of discarded rags, and performed prostrations and repentance during the six periods of the day; wherever he stayed, he likewise...
Using this as a means of transformation, he proclaimed that those who chant and recite Mahāyāna sūtras would enter the Avīci Hell of the ten directions and must urgently perform repentance.

Later, while the Master was preaching the Dharma in Qizhou, there was a laywoman (*upāsikā*) there who upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and exhorted all those with whom she had a karmic connection to recite it together.
The Master said to her, "Your upholding of the *Lotus Sūtra* does not accord with your spiritual capacity; you ought to enter hell."
"Prison! You must immediately cease reciting; all others must likewise abandon it.
The leading *upāsikā* was not angry, but on the day of the Great Fast, when ten thousand people had gathered, she burned incense and made this vow:

"If I, while upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, do not accord with the Buddha’s intention, I pray that my body may be afflicted with a foul disease for all the assembly to see, and furthermore, that I may sink alive into hell. If...
"I uphold the Lotus Sūtra and act in accordance with the Buddha’s intent; I pray that the Dhyāna Master shall receive this retribution immediately.
Having spoken these words, Ci was instantly struck by a spirit; his voice failed him and he could no longer speak.

The one presiding over the assembly at the high seat to the west likewise lost his voice, and five elderly monks within the hall were also unable to utter a word. Those who had been reciting the scriptures beheld this...
A Different Account. Regarding the reading and recitation [of scriptures], it was twice that of former times (from the *Zizheng lu*).

Dharma Master Chong of Xiangzhou—Sengfachong—was devoted to the sūtras and śāstras, particularly excelling in the *Lotus Sūtra*. He authored a commentary in four fascicles. Once, he went to Lushan in Xiangzhou.
At Mount [Name], a mountain spirit transformed into a lady and went to Huichong to request the precepts. Consequently, she donated the mountain where she resided to establish a monastery.
Before long, her transformative influence had permeated the region of Xiang (from the *Xu lingrui ji*).
In the early Kaihuang era, there were two monks from Yangzhou and Qizhou. There was a monk in Yangzhou who had mastered the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* through recitation and took pride in his achievement.

On Mount Dongshan in Qizhou, there was a śrāmaṇera who recited only the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Samantamukha-parivarta*). Both men died suddenly and arrived together at the Netherworld. The King immediately sentenced the śrāmaṇera...

The king sat upon a golden throne and recited the sūtras he had mastered with great solemnity; he then seated the monk upon a silver throne and had him recite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, yet the king did not treat it with equal reverence.
When the recitation was finished, the king asked his officials, "Both men possess long lifespans," and he subsequently released them both.
The monk who had recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* relied on the fact that he had recited more, and feeling great resentment, he then inquired after the dwelling place of the śrāmaṇera.
"I hope we may meet again in the future. Once the two had revived, the monk recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* until they reached Qizhou, where he indeed found the śrāmaṇera.

When the monk asked him how it was that he had been able to find him, the śrāmaṇera replied: "Regarding this chapter I recite, I use separate robes and a separate seat; I burn incense and offer prayers of aspiration, and only then do I begin my recitation.
This practice has been constant without negligence, and there is no other technique involved. The monk then apologized, saying: "My transgressions are deep. As for what I have recited..."
Nirvana. [If one’s] deportment is disordered and body and speech are impure, one merely avoids forgetfulness.
As an ancient said, "Much evil is not as good as little good. This can be verified today. This is indeed diligence, but it is not a *pāramitā*. (From the *Zhi guan fu xing*)
Regarding Dharma Master T'ai of Meizhou:

During the Great Sui dynasty, there was a monk named Fatai. His surname was Lü. Having initially donned the robes of a Daoist for more than ten years, he suddenly grew weary of that school and turned his mind toward the Great Awakening.
He then went to Mount Bi in Meizhou, where he sought out a master to shave his head and receive the precepts, and began to recite the Lotus [Sutra].
He studied the sutra and immediately mastered it. He then personally transcribed one copy of this sutra, which manifested several miraculous signs.
Consequently, he paid two thousand coins to have it transported to Yizhou for binding and decoration. When the load reached Zuo Bridge, the bridge collapsed and fell into the water.

Although the servant escaped with his life, he lost the cloth-covered basket containing the sutra. Sengtai cried out loudly, "The money and goods are of little consequence; how could you bear to lose the sutra? Someone fished it out of the water.
He was to be granted two thousand [coins]. At that time, there was a man who dived into the water to search for them and recovered only the money and goods.

Sengtai continued his search by patrolling the area and suddenly saw a bundle in the city center. He tried picking it up and found it was a sutra. Supported by grasses and trees, it showed no signs of having been wet at all. He then had it restored and bound with cloth;
when it was returned to the temple for veneration, a wondrous fragrance was constantly perceived, gathering and lingering in its presence. It was truly marvelous.
His progress doubled. He made it his regular practice to recite one section of a scripture every night. At the monastery, there was Dharma Master Biao, who was lecturing and teaching.
At midnight, he went to observe [Taisi] reading; finding Taisi’s chanting too loud and bothersome, he wished to urge him to lower his voice.
Upon arriving, he suddenly saw countless divine beings before Taisi’s door, all kneeling with palms joined. Feeling ashamed and sweating, he withdrew (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
The Venerable Gōng of Chéngdū, whose secular surname was Zhōu, was a native of Chéngdū Prefecture. He followed the monk Shàotí at Shìsì Temple and formed a bond of study with the monk Huìyuǎn;

together they diligently pursued their learning until they became perfected vessels of the Dharma. After Huìyuǎn went to Chāng’ān to study the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, he returned to his hometown to lecture and teach, standing out as a preeminent figure.
Huiyuan was peerless. After Huicong left Jingzhou and Yangzhou to seek the Way and return, thirty years passed in separation.

During a night conversation, Huiyuan’s speech flowed like a stream, while Huicong remained silent and unable to respond. Huiyuan ridiculed him, to which Huicong replied, "By nature I am extremely dull-witted and have no understanding.
Huiyuan asked, "Can you not recite at least one sutra? Huicong said, "I can recite the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter). Huiyuan still held him in low regard.
Hui-gong said, "Although this scripture is small, it was proclaimed from the Buddha’s own mouth; I shall recite it once for my elder brother. Gong then spread out a seat and began the recitation.
As soon as he raised his voice, they perceived a fragrant aroma. Next, they saw celestial flowers falling in profusion and heard the clear resonance of heavenly music.
When the sutra was finished, these phenomena ceased. Hui-yuan prostrated himself and offered praise, saying, "I pray that you will remain to instruct me. Gong replied, "This was not by my power."
"This is merely the power of the Buddhas. Gong immediately brushed his sleeves and departed, and his final whereabouts remain unknown (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Master Yin of Jingzhou:
Master Yin’s dharma name was Fanyin. He resided for a long time on the eastern ridge of Mount Fuchuan in Jingzhou, making the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* his primary practice. Every...
Regretting that he had not yet mastered mental contemplation, he went to Songzi to seek guidance from Chan Master Fachang, from whom he gained a profound understanding of the essential principles.
One day, as he was departing to bid farewell to his old friend Hu Jinyi, he did not meet him; instead, he wrote on the wall that on a certain month and year he would travel far away.
Later, he suddenly said to the monks, "Today I shall take one long sleep, and tomorrow I will not rise again."

The multitude pushed open the door to look at him; he had already cast off his mortal coil from his right side. When they examined the date and month inscribed on the wall, there was not a single discrepancy.
(Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks)

Dharma Master Chong of Mount Lu, whose name was Fa-chong, was the son of the Bi family from Jiuyang. Disgusted with the world, he left the household life. He constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
his total count of recitations was so vast that it could not be recorded. He resided at Huacheng Temple on Mount Lu, where he further practiced *samādhi*, remaining aloof from worldly affairs.

In the meantime, he repeatedly exhorted the assembly of monks not to allow women to enter the monastery, saying, "Above, this would damage the Buddha’s transformation; below, it would cause the decline of secular reputation.
To those who did not comply, Sengchong said, "If the True Teaching cannot be practiced, it is right that I die early. Why worry that the local people will not uphold the precepts?
He then went secretly to Mount Xianglu, threw himself down to crush his bones, vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land. Someone saw the Master fall.
[The monk] went down and searched for him; it was indeed Chong. His body remained uninjured, and he recited the sutras as before. He earnestly requested to return to the monastery.
The monk, moved by his dying admonition, immediately ceased [interacting with] women. Six years later, he passed away. It was during the height of summer, yet his corpse did not decay.
"Like the fragrance of the orchid. During the Kaihuang era (*Xù gāosēng zhuàn*).
Regarding the Venerable Xiù of Huángzhōu:
during the end of the Sui dynasty, there was a monk named Xuánxiù who resided at Suíhuá Temple in Huángzhōu. He was pure by nature and gentle in disposition; he constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Whenever such extraordinary signs appeared, he did not regard them as strange. At a time of intense summer heat, a friend sent a messenger to summon him for the sake of cooling off.

When the messenger reached the front of the master’s room, he suddenly saw men and horses in full military array; terrified, he turned back. When the friend went there in person, what he saw was exactly as described.
As he turned toward the rear gate, armored soldiers were even more numerous, filling the air in numbers beyond counting. The fourfold assembly...
This was widely circulated; everyone said it was divine and miraculous (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
As for the Dharma Master Sengsheng of Qizhou:
Sengsheng, a monk of Qizhou, possessed the nature of a solitary cloud, originally having no fixed form. Whichever monastery he entered, he did not inquire whether [it was large or small].
There was no monastic community residing there; he sustained himself by begging for alms and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* a full one thousand times.

He then moved his staff and arrived at Lingyan Temple during the Kaihuang era. While he was engaged in recitation, one night he suddenly saw several dozen spirits prostrating themselves to listen to him.
Zhi-sheng asked, "Who are you? The spirits replied, "We are mountain deities who have resided here."
Seven hundred years had passed. Now, hearing the sound of the Dharma Master reciting the sutras, he came specifically to listen and receive the teaching.

He requested the Master to recite for him, and after a long while, he departed. From then on, he came regularly. The Master subsequently traveled to Fazang Temple in Xiangzhou to establish a Great Canon (Tripitaka).
There, he lit lamps before his eyes as an offering to the Mahayana, reciting without ceasing. Later, he passed away there (*Lingshui Ji*).
During the Daye era, there was the Dharma Master Liang of Suzhou.
A monk named Liang resided at Tiger Hill; he left home at the age of twelve to receive instruction, devoting himself exclusively to reciting the Lotus Sūtra.
Before even forty days had passed, he had mastered the entire text. He traveled south to Kuaiji, where, before the image of San-sheng at Shan County and at Mount Mao, he [established] a dwelling.
Before the altar, he lit a finger from each hand as an offering of the lamp of wisdom. He then returned to his hometown and resided at Beichan Temple.
One day, he suddenly requested hot water to bathe and took leave of his patrons; sitting upright, he passed away, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room (as recorded in the *Lingrui ji*).
Dhyāna Master Boji Xian:
The śramaṇa Huixian of the Kingdom of Boji left home at a young age and possessed great aspirations. He recited only the Lotus Sūtra;

whenever people sought blessings or made petitions, there was nothing that did not accord with their wishes. Upon hearing that the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) were being expounded, he went immediately to listen and receive its teachings. Once the Dharma entered his spirit, it took root there.

His wisdom and understanding increased ever further. Initially residing at Xiude Temple in his native land, he would lecture when there was an assembly and engage in pure recitation when there was not.

Hearing of his reputation from afar, people from all directions came to attend upon him. The Master grew weary of receiving guests and departed for Mount Danna in the south. The mountain was extremely deep and perilous;
Xian sat within it, specializing in his studies as before, until he passed away there. His fellow students carried his remains to...
In a stone chamber, a tiger devoured his body until it was entirely consumed; only the skull and the tongue remained.
After three years had passed, his tongue was red and soft, even more so than before, and later turned purple. When struck with a whip, it was as hard as stone.
Monastics and laypeople alike gazed upon it in endless reverence, and they built a stupa to mark the site. This was during the early Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Dharma Master Xi of Jingzhou, whose secular surname was Li, was born in Xiangyang. At the age of seven, he left home to become a monk at Qingxi Temple in Jingzhou.

There were more than forty people in the temple community; while Xi served as a śrāmaṇera, he performed the duties of a dhūta attendant. By day he would cook and prepare the fires, and by night he would engage in recitation and study.

Living in the mountains, he had no oil; he used firewood for illumination. Every evening he recited one sheet of scripture. Although he studied various sutras, he took the Lotus Sutra alone as his core principle.
Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty issued an edict for him to reside at Chan Ding Temple. In his later years, wishing to attain spiritual resonance, he vowed to recite the Lotus Sutra one thousand times.
Consequently, he did not remain in his former room but instead circumambulated the pagoda and temple grounds. Between heaven and earth, he vowed to fill [the gaps].
His original vows numbered eighty thousand and eight hundred. One day, the temple monks suddenly saw a white horse drawing a precious carriage enter the Xifang (Joy) Hall;

they pursued it, but it vanished from sight—a manifestation of his spiritual resonance. Later, he returned to Luoling to spend his final years. In the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he fell ill and summoned his disciples, saying:
"Impermanence has arrived; do not cause a commotion. The three realms are empty and illusory; they are but the single mind. Thus he addressed the assembly.

Suddenly, the sound of musical instruments and carriage wheels was heard to the north of the grove. [The Master] used this to announce his joy. Huixi said, "I have already renounced worldly retribution;
how could I be reborn in a place of pleasure? A moment later, a wondrous fragrance filled the room, and he passed away while sitting upright (*Xù gāosēng zhuàn*).
Finally, there was the Dharma Master Senghui of Zhongnanshan.
A native of Yongzhou, he delighted in the discipline of the Way from his youth. Possessing a firm and upright character and high integrity, he lived in seclusion at Baolin Valley on Mount Zhongnan.

There he applied himself to his studies and recited the Lotus Sūtra. Upon seeing the account of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja’s self-sacrifice, he desired to emulate him and privately gathered a pile of firewood.
Xuemu intended to carry out this practice. At the end of the Zhenguan era, during a quiet night, he recited the *Pūrva-yoga* of the Bodhisattva while burning them with fire.
As the smoke and flames blazed fiercely, he sat upright in the full lotus posture, his voice continuing as before.

At that moment, the assembly suddenly saw a great white light from the west flow into the mass of fire. After the burning was complete, they collected the remaining remains and immediately erected a stupa (*śarīra-stūpa*).
He erected a stupa and inscribed a stele upon a mountain to ensure his legacy endures. (From the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Dharma Master Niu-tou Tong was the śramaṇa Zhitong of Zizhou;
his secular surname was Chen. He entered the monastic order at the age of eight and became a disciple of Dharma Master Zhengdao.
He specialized in reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* and also lectured upon it. Residing at Mount Niutou, he maintained dignified deportment and observed the precepts.

He subdued the followers of Huang-Lao (Daoism). A pair of geese would frequently come to listen to his preaching of the Dharma. After he had lectured on the sūtra more than a hundred times, it emitted light on two occasions.

During the Zhenguan era, he passed away while separated from the rest of the assembly. The rooms and halls of the entire monastery shook and turned entirely white for the duration of a single meal. (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*)
[From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*]:
Dharma Master Min of Suzhou, whose name was Huimin, was a native of Hedong. At the age of nine, he left the secular world and devoted himself to pure conduct, reciting the Lotus Sūtra.

Within a single month, he had already passed [the initial period]. At fifteen, he requested the Dharma from Master Kuang of Silla; he was exceptionally brilliant and outstanding, earning the praise of veteran practitioners.
At fifteen, he returned to Shiguang Xing Temple in Haiyan, where he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Extraordinary fragrances and the snapping of fingers repeatedly manifested in the air.
The assembly gathered like clouds, all declaring it an auspicious omen. Later, he moved to Tongxuan Temple, where he gathered disciples and practiced the Way.

For seventeen years, his feet did not cross the threshold. At the end of the Sui dynasty, when the realm fell into chaos and famine struck the region of Wu, the fourfold assembly fled in search of safety;
yet Baoyun Min alone remained, persevering in meditation and recitation until death. During the era of the Great Tang’s enlightened rule, he resided at Nanjian Temple.

There, two rabbits and a tiger lived together in harmony. Three days before his passing, a rare fragrance filled the room. When the entire community questioned him about it, the Master said, "After I..."

"The sun must set; this is the constant law of birth and death for humans. Dwelling in this world is like drifting clouds; each should contemplate impermanence and strive early to attain liberation for oneself.
When the appointed time arrived, he indeed passed away in accordance with the natural transformation (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Regarding Dharma Master Huida of Lishan:
During the Zhenguan era, there was a monk named Huida who resided at Jinliang Temple on Mount Li. He was resolute in his aspirations and recited the Lotus Sūtra;

by the time of his death, he had completed it six thousand times. Whether walking or sitting, his majestic deportment remained constant and the sound of his recitation never ceased. As for his care for living beings, he was straightforward... [text continues].

His gaze was downward, his eyes cast low. Seeing an insect on the ground, he turned his body to let it pass. When someone asked about this, he replied, "The life and death of this creature and my own are not fixed;
until I have first attained perfect enlightenment, how can I treat it with contempt? Later, he sat cross-legged and passed away.

People said he had entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*). He remained for five nights; once he had finally departed, his body did not decay or emit any odor. Thereupon, they placed him upon a bier and interred him in a stone cave.
*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Middle Section.
During the early years of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Yisu in Liquan County, Yongzhou. From his youth, he had recited the Lotus Sutra until he had completed [the required number].
He recited [the scripture] one thousand times. One day, he fell ill and was nearing death. He then entrusted his friend Huikuo with these words:
"Although I have been reading and reciting this, my intention was to seek spiritual omens so as to inspire faith among the laity. After I die, bury me; after ten years have passed, you may exhume me.
If my tongue has rotted away, know that my recitation was without merit. If it still remains intact, you should inform the clergy and the laity to erect a stupa for me."

He manifested a spiritual sign and, having finished speaking, passed away. Later, his remains were exhumed according to his words; the flesh and blood had completely vanished, yet only his tongue remained incorruptible.
His bones and tongue were then enshrined in a stupa on the southern cliff of Gan Valley (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
The ancient master Senggaoci was a friend of Dharma Master Ren of Jianchu Monastery. He could recite the Lotus Sūtra by heart but was not proficient in the Vinaya.
One day, as he was nearing death from illness, Ren said to him, "I hope you will inform me of the place where you are reborn after death. Gaoci—

He said, "I have long lamented this matter. If there were karmic causes from the unseen realm involving good or evil, they would surely manifest as retribution. Yet after his passing, for two years, there was no news at all.
When the third year arrived, while Renzheng was visiting Jici’s home and the family members had all gone up the mountain, Renzheng sat alone in a state of daze when he saw Jici appear and tell him:
'At the time of my death, there was an agreement that I wished to inform you of long ago, but circumstances prevented it.'"
"Zhan said, 'I came late for this reason. I am now a minor official at Mount Tai, and I do not have much suffering.
Huiren asked, 'Throughout your life you recited the sutras and listened to the Dharma; how could you receive such a retribution? Zhiyi replied, 'It is precisely because of this that I am fortunate.
Otherwise, it would have been even worse. Having said this, he vanished. From this point on, Huiren redoubled his diligent practice. (As seen in the *Old Edition of the Lotus Sutra*).
During the Zhenguan era, a monk from Wuzhen Temple on Wangshun Mountain was traveling by night along the Lan River when he suddenly heard the sound of someone reciting the Lotus Sūtra.
The voice was faint yet carried far. At that time, the stars and moon shone clearly overhead, and looking out for dozens of li in every direction, there was no one to be seen. The monk...
He pricked up his ears in solemn awe and hurried back. He urged a companion to go and search for it; the sound of the sutra was then heard emerging from the ground. He immediately marked the spot.
When they dug there the following morning, they found a skull-bone amidst the accumulated earth. Its color was parched and withered, yet its lips and tongue alone were fresh and moist.
He took it back and enshrined it in a stone casket beside the hall. From that time on, he constantly heard [the sound] every evening.

The sound of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* drew men and women of Chang’an to view it in continuous succession. During the Kaiyuan era, it was suddenly stolen by a monk from Silla, who carried it away in a series of cases.
The temple monks pursued him, but he had already returned to his home country across the sea (*Tàipíng guǎngjì*).
Regarding Xuanfasi Monastery:
In the An-yi Ward of Chang’an there was Xuanfasi Monastery. This was originally the residence of Zhang Pin, a local man.
Pin once provided support for a monk who specialized in the recitation of the Lotus Sūtra for more than ten years. Suddenly, one of Pin’s subordinates slandered the monk, accusing him of misconduct.
Her maidservant killed her on account of some other matter. Subsequently, the household heard the sound of the *Lotus Sūtra* being recited, continuing day and night without ceasing.
Zhang realized it was due to his own grievous injustice; filled with remorse for what he could not undo, he donated his residence to establish this temple (from the *Tàipíng guǎngjì*).
Outside the city wall of Kuifeng, five *li* to the east of Jiangdong, lies Chishan Temple. As for its origins: in ancient times, there was a monk who established a hermitage at this site.
He would daily recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and was also able to lecture upon it. Suddenly, a pheasant would frequently come to prostrate itself before him.

He listened and received [the teachings] until the end of the fifth fascicle, after which the pheasant no longer came. Eight years later, a boy was born to a commoner family at the foot of the mountain.
When he reached the age of eight, he abstained from meat and refrained from play; he resolutely desired to go forth as a monk under that *śramaṇa*.

His parents granted him permission, and once he had departed, on a certain day while the *śramaṇa* was bathing, he ordered the boy to wash his back. Jian refused to expose his body. The *śramaṇa* asked him why, and he replied: "I..."

His previous incarnation was a pheasant. Because he had listened to his teacher’s recitations, he was reborn as a human being; even now, there are still pheasant feathers beneath his armpits, which is why he does not bare his shoulder.

Consequently, the monk bestowed upon him the first five fascicles of this sutra, which he could read as if they were familiar from former practice, but he was unable to master the final two fascicles.
From that time on, the mountain was named after the pheasant, and a monastery was established there; the monastery still exists today. (Categorized under Prohibitions Against Killing)

Dharma Master Cóng of Yangzhou, Sēngzhìcóng, resided at Bǎimǎ Temple in Yangzhou, where he specialized in the study of the Three Treatises (*Sanlùn*). Later, he crossed the river and settled at Ānlè Temple.
Encountering the collapse of the Great Sui Dynasty, he had no means to return home; he hid among the reeds by the river and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* for seven days without ceasing.
He was hungry. Constantly, four tigers would circle him in a submissive manner. Cong said, "I have not eaten for ten days; my life hangs by a thread. You may eat me.
The tigers spoke in human voices, saying, "To create heaven and establish earth—there is no such principle as this.
Suddenly, an old man appeared, carrying a small boat under his arm, and said, "If you, Master, wish to cross the river, board the boat immediately. As for those four tigers—
Upon seeing this, tears fell from his eyes. Sengcong said, "To uphold those in peril and rescue those in distress lies precisely with us today.
He then crossed to the southern bank along with the four tigers. As soon as they reached the boat, the boat and the old man suddenly vanished.

Sengcong led the four tigers to the west of the Xixia Pagoda, where he practiced walking meditation, recited sutras, and vowed never to sleep or lie down. He settled more than eighty people there; whenever there was an ominous event, the tigers would come to the rescue.
"Hou! By means of this exclamation, he was awakened. In the Zhenguan period, at the age of ninety-nine, on the Buddha’s birthday, he burned incense and prostrated before the holy monks.
Returning to his quiet chamber, he sat upright and passed away (*Xu Gaoseng zhuan*).
Fashi Faxiang of Qixia was a native of Yangzhou.
He stood eight chi tall, with a robust and imposing physique. He left home to become a monk at the age of sixteen and immediately devoted himself to diligent ascetic practice.
He mastered the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* as his primary spiritual vocation. Later, he established the Fahua Hall beside Xixia Temple, where he practiced...
The wise one practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* with diligent effort for twenty-one days and obtained great auspicious omens;

yet, knowing this, he did not speak of it. At one time, tigers were inflicting harm upon the people, numbering several dozen each day. Both monastics and laypeople established a great vegetarian feast (*mahā-śrāddha*) to avert the calamity.

Suddenly, a tiger entered the hall and seized a person to carry him away. The Master followed after it, calling out to make it stop, saying: "Why do you act so recklessly? A vegetarian feast has been prepared here today."
"Release this person. The tiger immediately released him. Thereafter, all the tigers gathered together; the Master struck their heads with his staff and preached the True Dharma to them.
From that time on, they no longer caused harm (*Xu Gaoseng zhuan*).

Dharma Master Cheng of Zhongnan, whose secular name was Sengcheng, was a monk from the region of Yongzhou. From a tender age, he displayed exceptional brilliance and entered the monastic life at Lantian Temple.

There he served as a disciple to the monk Senghong, who was himself a monk of divine and extraordinary character. Cheng followed his teacher’s instructions, reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* as his virtuous practice, and further engaged in its ritual observance.

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, he once dreamed that Samantabhadra exhorted him to transcribe the Great Teaching. He immediately ordered a scribe to copy the *Prajñāpāramitā* in eight sections and also transcribed the *Avataṃsaka*.
A bird of extraordinary color danced down and alighted upon his scripture desk. While he was copying the *Lotus Sūtra* by hand on an open space, he had to leave for some business;
before he could retrieve it, a torrential rain poured down. When he returned, the scripture desk remained exactly as it had been.
The others all drifted away and perished. During the Zhenguan era, he fell ill; his aspiration was to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
He then said, "Now a youth comes to welcome me; I shall depart immediately. Having spoken, light issued from his mouth and a wondrous fragrance filled the room.

He passed away peacefully while sitting upright. During one summer, the Master recited the Lotus Sūtra five hundred times; on other days he maintained his practice as well, yet still managed two more recitations. Even so—

Whenever he encountered people or guests, he would not cease until the entire *Jingbu* (Sūtra Section) was finished; during this time, he did not speak of other matters. It is roughly calculated that over ten years passed as he recited it more than ten thousand times (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Dharma Master Yan of Suzhou was the śramaṇa Zhīyán of the Tang dynasty. He was the son of Zhū of Wújùn; his mother was of the Zhāng clan.

She dreamed that she ascended to the *cakra* (finial) of the pagoda at Tōngxuán Monastery and sat there, after which the Master was born. At the age of eight, he left the secular life. His appearance was pure and elegant, standing out as extraordinary among his peers. At ten...

He recited the Lotus Sūtra through to the end twice; everyone called him a divine child. Upon shaving his head, he immediately went to the capital to listen to lectures, where his intelligence and wisdom were fully developed.
He subsequently lived in seclusion at Mount Wuyou in Suzhou. In addition to his lecturing, he practiced the Samantabhadra Repentance and recited the Lotus Sūtra three thousand times.
Even before the incense in the night burner had been lit, fragrant smoke would rise spontaneously; when the evening vessel was just empty, it would secretly overflow.
There were celestial youths who attended upon him like water [serving fire]. He further practiced the three kinds of pure karma and cultivated the sixteen profound contemplations.
He frequently gathered over five hundred people to establish fasts and lecture on the sutras every month; this continued for more than ten years.

He shared the same aspirations and vows as those at Mount Lu—how could they be different? Throughout his career, he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* thirty times each.
He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred times. When his end drew near, he exhorted his disciples and passed away in serene composure (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Dharma Master Ji-zang of Yuezhou was a native of Jinling.
He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and relied upon Dharma Master Lang of Xinghuang Monastery.

In all his inquiries and resolutions of doubts, he profoundly mastered their profound mysteries. Subsequently, he traveled through the Hundred Yue regions and took up residence at Jiaxiang Monastery, where he expounded the sutras, propagated the teachings, and received those seeking the Way.

The crowds gathered like clouds, and Emperor Yang held his teachings in high esteem. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Riyang Monastery. At that time, the assembly delighted in and venerated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

[the Master] immediately began to expound and analyze it. Hearing of his reputation, seekers arrived by the tens of thousands. He once transcribed two thousand copies of the Lotus Sutra and fashioned twenty-five Buddha statues.

Furthermore, he established the Samantabhadra Hall, where he personally engaged in meditation and recitation. When Emperor Wu of the Tang dynasty admired his virtue, he issued an edict for him to reside at Yanqing Monastery.

He founded Xing Temple. At that time, he was advanced in years and fell ill; the Emperor bestowed medicinal decoctions upon him. Knowing his end was near, Daozang composed the *Treatise on the Absence of Fear Toward Death*.
Its summary states: "Death arises from birth; therefore, one should fear birth. If I had not been born, how could there be death?"
Having completed these tasks, he suddenly bathed and changed his robes at dawn, burned incense, and invoked the Buddha before passing away peacefully while seated.

The Master lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* more than one hundred times; he also lectured on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* each several dozen times.
He composed commentaries and treatises that circulated in later generations (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Dharma Master Bā of Xiāngzhōu:
The monk Zhībā of Xiangyang was the son of the Zhang family. At the age of six, he entered the monastic order at Chángjì Temple in his native commandery. He recited [the scriptures] daily.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* consists of five fascicles. Within this sūtra, there are general principles and guidelines for its underlying meaning, which state:

"This sūtra is the great matter of the appearance of all Buddhas in the world. It cannot be fully understood unless one person attains the Way; therefore, I vow to uphold it until the end, in order to enlighten the ignorant and common folk.
Having thoroughly studied and mastered these teachings, at the command of Dharma Master Jizang of the capital, I have extracted [the essence] and recounted it once more. Part One.

He said, "The Vehicle is like a cloud; it is subsequently divided into three. Might one also consider the One Vehicle to be the rain, which is then divided into three? No one in the assembly could respond.
Huizang said, "Master Ba, this question of yours has profoundly grasped the essential purport of the sutras. He then entrusted him with the Great Dharma. Later, he resided at Qishan Temple.
He regularly preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* five times a year. One day, he suddenly took leave of the assembly; none could fathom his intention.
He immediately sat in the full lotus posture and passed away (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Dharma Master Huijiong of Bianzhou was named Huijiong. His secular surname was Bian. At the age of six, he requested permission to follow the Buddha; his compassionate parents marveled at him.

When they orally transmitted the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* to him, he mastered it immediately. At sixteen, he fulfilled his aspiration and entered Mount Tai to serve Dharma Master Daohong. Huijiong said, "I shall stand with arms folded..."

To remain silent in mountain forests is but one path for solitary self-cultivation; however, as for sustaining the remaining entrustment [of the Dharma], it cannot be accomplished without transformation and guidance.

He therefore traveled south and stayed at Huifusi Temple in Bianjing, specializing in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as his essential practice. He composed a commentary in five fascicles and constantly lectured upon it.
Every time he reached the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter, heaven would surely send down rain, which everyone found marvelous. This was the Dharma he preached.

He lectured on the *Yebao jing* (Sutra on the Retribution of Karma) from beginning to end fifty times. He also lectured on other sutras, which cannot be fully enumerated here. Later, he passed away at this very monastery.
On the day before his death, there was a rare fragrance and radiant light. Beholding it from afar, he said: "I pray that by virtue of this auspicious omen, I may be reborn in the Pure Land.
At the time of his passing, the well water happened to run dry; however, after several days had passed since his enshrinement, the water returned and filled it to the brim. (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*)
According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*),

Dharma Master Zheng and Dharma Master Zhizheng of the capital were both descendants of Emperor Ming of the Liang dynasty. They resided at the Great Zangyan Monastery in the capital and largely renounced positions of honor and rank.
He delighted in the Way and its practice. His family had served the Buddha for generations and was particularly devoted to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

All members of his clan, from the highest to the lowest, had mastered and recited it. He once composed a commentary on the sutra, searching deeply into several schools of thought and blending them with his own insights.

He compiled this work, submitted it to the Emperor of Tang under his own name, and frequently expounded upon it himself. His father, the Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, cherished the wholesome Dharma; from birth until old age, he recited [the sutra].

He recited them ten thousand times. He further ordered others to transcribe them, totaling over a thousand copies. Every day at the morning audience, he invariably had his attendants carry the scriptures before him.
Whenever there was a slight interval during his official duties, he would immediately proceed to chant and read them. His colleagues looked up to him in admiration, considering him peerless.
Since the Buddha’s transformation [of the world] flowed eastward, Xiao [Yan]’s *Lotus Sūtra* has truly served as a model for all under heaven (*Monk Biographies*).
The lay official Xiao Ziliang commissioned one thousand copies of the *Lotus Sūtra*. He dreamed of a person delivering a single scroll of the sūtra and saying that there was an error;
it was indeed in the fifth fascicle, the "Life Span" chapter, where the phrase "one speck of dust, one kalpa" was missing. This was the Dharma...
The ultimate principle of the Flower [School]. By practicing this phrase, he was moved by the auspicious omen of a white magpie soaring in response.

(This is from the commentary to the "Eulogy on the Auspicious Omens of Master Shou. Since Xiao Ziliang was surely the Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Household, he is included here for reference.)
Dharma Master Sengfajian of Changsha resided at Jianyuan Temple.
Having listened to Dharma Master Chong’s lectures, he attained a broad and profound mastery of the profound essentials of the teachings.

Furthermore, he constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra, having lectured upon it more than forty times. Suddenly, while at his lecture seat, a cluster of blossoms sprang up from each of the four corners; there were more than ten branches in total.
Yellow and white intermingled, measuring five or six inches in length, they resembled lotus flowers, their fragrance and light causing the petals to unfurl.
Some suspected they had been produced by dampness and moisture. After several more days, eight or nine such flowers grew again beside the lecturer’s seat and where the assembly sat;
they withered only after a month. Monastics and laypeople gathered to observe them, all declaring them an auspicious omen of the sutra lecture. The Master—
Later, he passed away in Changsha (as recorded in the *Lingrui ji*).

Dharma Master Xiang of Jiangdu, whose secular surname was Liu, was named Senghui. He constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and was also proficient in its profound meanings. Later, he traveled to the Jiang River at Huaiyang.

He resided at Zhigu Village in the capital. When the assembly requested him to lecture on this sutra, he was one hundred and one years old, yet his countenance remained as vigorous as that of a youth.
Suddenly, he addressed the assembly, saying, "I am about to depart. Having finished speaking, he joined his palms, sat upright, and passed away.
He was immediately interred at Tóngshān. Later, woodcutters frequently heard the sound of reciting the sutra at the burial site. One day, Sīmǎ Zhào Yuánkè...
Taking a path by the side, he looked back and saw a single lotus flower. Startled, he asked the villagers, who replied, "This is the grave of the former Master.
Huikê then ordered someone to dig it up. They found a heap of white bones, yet the tongue alone remained perfectly intact and was bright red;

the lotus root grew from that tongue. Witnessing this miraculous omen, the local prefectures submitted a report to the throne, and an imperial decree was issued to erect a stupa at this site in honor of him.
*Inscription for the Collection of Spiritual Auspiciousness*.

Dharma Master Baotong was one who cultivated the holy life with great diligence. He regularly recited the "Dhāraṇī Chapter" of the *Lotus Sūtra*, and he occasionally manifested spiritual wonders. At that time...
In Yangqiao Village there was a member of the Zhao clan whose wife had been possessed by a deity. He invited Tong to recite dhāraṇīs.
Once Tong arrived, the deity immediately manifested its form and said to him: "The deity resides within this village and ought to bring forth blessings; why, then, do you instead bewitch people?"
The deity said, "This is not your disciple's affair; it is merely a minor spirit under my command.
He then summoned the spirit before him and reprimanded it. Because of this, Lady Zhao’s condition improved. However, her illness soon recurred, and she spent the entire day chanting and singing.
She came again to report the matter, and Tong went once more. There he saw the punished spirit standing before the sickbed. Tong said, "I previously instructed you to cure her."
"How could I come again? If you do not leave, I shall recite a mantra to cause your head to split into seven pieces, like the branches of an *ari* tree.
The ghost then bowed its head and begged for mercy, saying, "There is no need for the mantra.
From that time on, his illness was cured, and the ghost never returned again (*Lingrui ji*).

Chan Master Sengyi of Suzhou resided at Kaiyuan Temple in Suzhou. While he was constructing a great Buddha hall, he suddenly saw a woman carrying her son who said to the Master, "My son is afflicted by illness;
I request that you recite one copy of the Lotus Sūtra. When the Chan Master had finished the recitation, [the woman departed].
Suddenly, a man dressed in red robes and wearing a sword came forward and bowed, saying, "The other day, my wife and children were afflicted by illness.

Having received the Master’s recitation of the sutras, they have now recovered. I have come specifically to express my gratitude. Hearing that the Master is constructing a hall, I respectfully offer ten thousand coins to assist you.
Your disciple is General Xu. The Master asked, "Where does your Excellency reside? Xu replied, "I reside in the Master's house."
After he had finished speaking, he vanished. The Master sent men to dig the earth in search of him; they then discovered a set of skeletal remains with a sword fastened across the body.
Everyone marveled at this extraordinary event. The Master immediately performed a sacrificial rite and buried them; it remains there to this day (*Lingrui ji*).

Shenzhao, the monk known as Zhao of Bianzhou, was a native of Bianzhou. At the age of nine, he encountered the chaos of civil unrest; his kinsmen perished, and he and his mother were left adrift with no place of refuge.
Before long, his mother passed away, whereupon he followed Master Mingzhi to enter the monastic order. In all that he heard and studied...
Nothing was left out; he took only the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as his virtuous practice. He had long kept a dog that followed him wherever he went.
When the Master fell ill, the dog wailed incessantly throughout the night, though no one knew why. Only after the Master passed away did everyone realize the dog’s omen.
Once the burial was completed, the dog lay down and wept for a long time; it died without eating (from the *Xu lingrui ji*).
Dharma Master Xuanzang of Jingzhou:

During the Jǐnglóng era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Xuanzang, a native of Jiangling. He entered the monastic path at a young age and became widely learned in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
He was particularly proficient in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, a work for which he was uniquely renowned. For fifty years, he recited it seven times daily. Once, while at...
While reciting scriptures in a purified chamber, he moved the heavenly beings to descend and listen. During his fasting and lectures, auspicious omens appeared in profusion.

Emperor Xiaohé, deeply honoring the Master’s virtue, held a ritual for breaking the fast at the Lin Guang Palace. Xuanzang submitted a memorial requesting to return to his hometown; the Emperor then bestowed upon him an imperial poem.
The hundred officials were all in harmony. This is recorded in detail in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*.
Regarding Chan Master Che of Jangzhou:

Master Che’s dharma name was Che; he was a native of Jangzhou. From his youth, he applied himself with diligence and hardship, mastering the *Lotus Sūtra*, and he constantly used this practice to guide others.
He transformed all things and subsequently constructed a hall on the western river to the west of Mount Gu. He established a monastery there;

though there was originally no water, one day the ground subsided and a clear spring gushed forth. Consequently, Fang Renyu, the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Qinzhou, requested a name for the temple, which was named after the "Subsiding Spring" (Xianquan).
The Master was also skilled in the recitation of dhāraṇīs, which frequently produced miraculous responses. The second year of the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty...
In the second month of that year, knowing that he was about to die, he entrusted his disciples with final instructions and passed away while sitting upright and composed.
At that time, the weather was clear and bright; flowers fell like snow, fragrant and without wilting. The branches of the trees and the leaves of the grass turned white, as if colored with vermilion.

This phenomenon extended for over two *li* and did not disappear until three days later. Three years after his passing, his seated body remained undecayed. The master’s diligent exertion of merit is truly difficult to fathom.
(Record of Auspicious Omens).
Dharma Master Yi of Shanyin expounded the Great Meaning.
He was the son of the Xu family of Xiaoshan. From birth he was exceptionally gifted; at the age of seven, his father taught him the books, and he memorized them daily.
He could recite several thousand words from memory. At twelve, he followed [his teacher] at Lingyin Temple in Shiyin, where he mastered all the scriptural teachings as soon as he opened a volume;
people held him in awe and respect. During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, an imperial decree was issued to recruit monks. The Master was ranked first in the examination on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Thereafter, he studied and lectured extensively at Chengxin Temple. During the Kaiyuan era, he lost a close relative and subsequently entered Mount Tiantai.

At Fulong, he perused the Tripitaka to repay his parents' toil; he visited Zuo Xi to receive the teachings of *zhiguan* (calm abiding and insight), through which he attained a transcendent realization of the mind and thereby fulfilled his great task.
Throughout his life, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and the *Mahā- and Kṣudraka-vinaya* as his primary practice.
At the time of his death, everyone heard the sound of celestial music playing in the air (*Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).
The Dharma Master Xiu of Tiantai was surnamed Liu and was a native of Dongyang. By nature, he was upright, lucid, and eminent;
he entered the gate of Dharma Master Sui—the tenth patriarch of the Tiantai school—and fully mastered his transmission. Students flocked to him in succession. His household...
His outer shoes were always kept full. Daily he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Prabhāsa*, and other scriptures, practicing the path during the six periods of the day.

As he grew old, he became even more steadfast. Every year he performed the forty-nine-day repentance ritual (*saptasaptāha-pratikramaṇa*), which corresponds to the fourth samādhi, "Following One’s Own Intent," within the system of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Later, he entrusted the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) to his disciple Wuwai. He passed away at Chánlín Temple during the Huicháng era and was subsequently reinterred.
At the Golden Ground of Fulong, the disciple Liangwen opened the tomb and performed cremation.
He recovered over one thousand grains of śarīra, which he enshrined in a stūpa (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).
The Biography of the Great Song Monk Ji Sui from Mingzhou, titled "End of the Lotus": Ji Sui’s secular surname was Zhang. His origins were unknown.

He entered the service of a master at De-run Temple in Mingzhou; this temple was formerly the study hall of Kan Ze, the Grand Marshal of Wu (it is the present-day Cixi Dong Puji Temple). The Master...
He was upright, honest, pure, and refined by nature, and did not engage in frivolous socializing. He was taught the *Lotus Sūtra* by a master;

he recited it as if it were his own lifelong habit, to the point that all who witnessed it were struck with awe and admiration. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, his lips never ceased their recitation, and he remained diligent until old age.

In the second year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, while sitting in the full lotus posture, he passed away in a state of profound composure. In an instant, seven blue lotus flowers sprouted from his mouth, fragrant and pure.
Upon being viewed from afar and nearby, people were struck with awe. Thereupon, a niche was constructed and he was interred beneath the Eastern Mountain.

After more than twenty years had passed, light frequently appeared within the stupa. When it was opened for inspection, his physical form remained as if alive. Consequently, he was invited back to the temple and adorned with lacquer and hemp cloth;
to this day, his true body still remains (as recorded in the biography). Regarding those seven stalks of lotus flowers, I once inquired about them with the elder monks.

All say that he was still present previously, until he was lost during the banditry of the Jianyan era. Nevertheless, as the Master’s true body remains, the ancient hall stands solemn and profound, and former sages regard him with awe.
Some have even composed poems to commemorate his enduring virtue. Zhang Ang’s poem says: "His name remains renowned in the annals of monks;
The incense and lamps within the cloud-cloaked niche are deep. This body is no longer the same as it once was, Yet it is indestructible."

Fundamentally arising from the mind: the gates are tranquil, the lakes and mountains are azure; in the courtyard, the cypresses and junipers cast shadows in the cold. May future generations continue this legacy;

the True Teaching rolls like golden scrolls. Sengbao Chong’s poem says: In the past, I recited the White Lotus Sutra; The spirit has shifted for nearly several hundred years. The physical body remains in this place;
Where in heaven does the true nature abide? The lake moon waxes and then wanes; The mountain flowers fall and yet bloom again. Only you, Master...
Gongde Gu (Merit-Bone). Seated upright as if in tranquil meditation (two poems are found on stone inscriptions).

The Dharma Master Sengshousu of Jingzhao was of exceptionally noble character and possessed peerless vigor and acumen. Residing at Daxingshan Temple in the capital, he constantly engaged in recitation.
He took this as his urgent task. For thirty years, he did not step beyond the boundary of his dwelling. He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* thirty-seven thousand times.
Every night, weasels would come to him in a state of docility to listen to the sutra; during his fasts, crows and magpies would come to his palms to take food.

During the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, a monk named Youxuan left him a verse of praise, saying: "Thirty springs for thirty thousand Lotus Sutras; for half a lifetime, one has not stepped [beyond the bounds]."
"Yuanmen Chen" (Dust at the Monastery Gate) is an excellent verse from the *True Record* (*Da Song Seng Zhuan*).

The Venerable Sanbai of Jiahe, whose name was Yuanhui, was a descendant of Lu Ji, the Interior Historian of Pingyuan during the Jin dynasty. He possessed brilliant insight from his childhood and became refined as he grew older.
Run left the secular world and received the precepts. He subsequently entered Mount Wutai to pay homage to the sacred traces.

Upon his return, he resided at Jianxing Monastery, where he resolved to maintain the "three whites" (vegetarian diet). During the Huichang era, he encountered the suppression of Buddhism; however, under Emperor Xuanzong, he returned to the monastic order.
In the Xiantong era, he escorted the Buddha-relics to Fengxiang, where he practiced asceticism by burning off his left thumb while reciting the Lotus Sutra from memory. His finger...
He was reborn again. Throughout his life, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* countless times. Regarding the "three whites": these were white rice, white water, and white salt.
Furthermore, his body did not lean to one side, his mouth recited the True Sutra, and his mind did not falsely follow external conditions; these three were clearly pure.
Because he enjoyed this auspicious reputation, the people of Wu called him the "Monk of the Three Whites" (*Dàsòng Sēngzhuàn*).
Dharma Master Chu of Wenzhou was Shi Hongchu of the Tang dynasty;
he was a native of Yongjia. Both Chu and his brothers possessed vast and noble capacities, and all were delighted to leave the secular world.

Their parents likewise wished for this, and so they followed one another’s example, privately and diligently reciting and studying the Lotus Sūtra. At that time, Dayun Temple was in a state of ruin and neglect.
Emperor Zhaozong issued an imperial decree to rebuild [the monastery], which the Master completed. Upon its completion, he lectured and recited there.

The Taizu of Liang bestowed upon him purple robes and a monastic title, but the Master declined and would not accept them. At that time, Zheng Shuo presented him with a poem which said: "The purple robes on the rack remain idle and unworn."
He would sit for long periods gazing at the golden characters on his desk. By nature, the Master was broad-minded and compassionate;
his face never showed a trace of anger, his eyes did not look askance, and he never spoke recklessly.

When he reached the fiftieth recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, a single lotus flower suddenly sprang up in the lecture hall, with layered stalks and overlapping petals, its fragrance exquisite and pervasive. The assembly marveled at this extraordinary occurrence. Furthermore, he drew blood to transcribe this sūtra.
One fascicle. To this day, the Yongjia family has treasured it generation after generation (*Dàsòng Sēngzhuàn*).
Dharma Master Sēnghóng of Jǔ in Yuèzhōu was the elder brother of Duke Chǔ. He entered the monastic order at Longgōng Temple in Yuè and was thoroughly proficient in the Lotus Sūtra.
Because of this, he attained liberation. Later, he went to Chang’an to study the Vinaya. While reading the inscription on the Huidu Monastery stele, he could take in two lines at once with his eyes.
When someone saw him and requested that he recite it back, he did so without missing a single character; his powerful memory was of this sort.
The Master recited the sutras day and night. He frequently saw spirits and deities attending to him, sometimes adding incense or lighting lamps for him.
During the Changxing era of the Li Tang dynasty, he passed away while sitting in meditation without illness.

At the third watch of the night, he knocked on the door of his shrine with his hand and said, "I have come back because my spiritual affinity for the Buddha-land was interrupted by my friends who found my robes and vestments impure. Once I have changed them, I shall sit again and depart. Seven days passed.
The crown of his head remained warm. After his burial, a tiger would frequently circle the stupa and wail (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).
Dharma Master Huì of the Eastern Capital was named Zhēnghuì.
His secular surname was Bāo, and he was a native of Wŭjùn. He left home at the age of thirteen at Longxīng Monastery; his character was grave and tranquil. He divided [his time]...
Yin was competitive by nature. Within a year, he had thoroughly recited the Lotus Sūtra and made this his constant practice, reciting two sections daily.
At nineteen, he shaved his head. From then on, whenever there were lecture assemblies in the Yi, Luo, or Jin regions, he attended them all.

During the Tianyou era of the Tang dynasty, he arrived at the Imperial Capital and took up residence at Xiangguo Monastery, where he lectured on the Lotus Sūtra about ten times; yet, people did not yet accord him with respect.
Thus one knows that even the sale of rare treasures has its own timing. Later, he met with Kong Gong, the military governor of Songzhou, who looked up to the Master’s noble conduct.
Kong Gong immediately provided a stipend for the Xita Monastery and established a lecture hall for the *Lotus Sūtra*. From this point on, his reputation flourished.

The Master further perused the Great Canon to broaden his insights and knowledge; as for the secular classics and the various works of the hundred schools, he paid them no heed. He exhorted [his disciples]:
His disciples said, "The doctrines of heterodox schools muddle and disorder our true nature; why must we study them?

We simply wish to let out the lion’s roar, not the cry of a jackal. Later, as he was about to pass away, he personally prepared his bath and purified himself, then ordered that the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha* be chanted.
While prostrating to the Buddha, he suddenly raised his palms in homage toward the sky and said, "I trouble the various sages to clear the void and come to welcome me. Disciples, this is enough."
At that time, the sound of celestial music was heard by all. He passed away after a brief moment (*The Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).
In the northern lane inside the city gate of Tanzhou, there is Qingyi Temple. In ancient times, there was a monk whose name has been lost who resided at this site.

He recited the Lotus Sūtra, and each time he did so, miraculous responses occurred that were not fully recorded in the world. On one occasion, he was moved by the appearance of two youths dressed in green who attended upon him.
After his death, he was buried, and suddenly two lotus flowers sprouted from atop his tomb. When they opened them to examine them, they were found to have emerged from his own tongue-roots.
At that time, the local prefectures verified these facts and submitted a memorial to the imperial court; consequently, the temple was granted the name "Green Robe" (Qingyi).
This temple was built there (as recorded in the *Lingrui ji*).
Regarding the Stone-Wall Sūtras at Gushan Temple in Hangzhou:
Gushan Temple is located on West Lake in Hangzhou. The *Lotus Sūtra* inscribed upon a stone wall is situated within the temple. It began in the tenth year of the Yuanhe era.
In the second year [of the Changqing era], when Yan Huifu served as Prefect, the monk Huiming first conceived this intention.
It was finally completed in the fourth year of Changqing, during the tenure of Bai Juyi as Prefect. The stone slab was six feet five inches high and fifty-seven feet six inches long.
Those who contributed funds included Yan Huifu, Bai Juyi, and [the people of] Lake... (Hu).
Cui Xuanliang, Prefect of the Province; Wei Wenque, Prefect of Muzhou; Wei Gongli, Prefect of Chuzhou;
Zhang Yu, Prefect of Quzhou; Li Liang, Prefect of Suzhou; Yuan Zhen, Prefect of Yuezhou;
and Chen Hu, Prefect of Chuzhou—these prefects requested that I provide this inscription. I observed how the followers of the Sangha have caused [this record] to be engraved upon stone.
The inscription was engraved upon the stele, for it was intended to ensure immortality.

Now that the stele is inscribed and the scripture is carved in stone, and furthermore, the nine feudal lords have vied with one another to contribute funds to this sacred site—speaking from a proximate perspective, this may be called manifesting the distinction of the school and achieving immortality;
speaking from a remote perspective, one knows not after how many tens of thousands of years the earth and heaven shall grind against one another.
Yin and yang clash with one another; fire and wind strike against each other; names and forms perish together.
Thus, the Four Seas and the Nine Provinces are but a single minute speck within the great void. How, then, can one know what does not decay?
Reflecting upon this, the followers of the Sangha have found their justification. Recorded by Yuan Zhen, Censor-in-Chief (from the *Tang Wencui*).
The Stone-Wall Sūtras at the Fǎhuá Monastery in Sūzhōu.

At the Fǎhuá Monastery of Chóngxuán Temple in Sūzhōu, Buddhist sūtras were engraved upon a stone wall. Now, as for the revelation, instruction, awakening, and entry into the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas:
it delivers the boundless through definitive meaning and extends infinitely through the Perfect Teaching (Yúanjiào). Nothing is more venerable than this.

In realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), in composing the *Avatāra-mukha*, and in abiding in inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*), nothing surpasses the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

In gathering the four types of birth and the nine classes of beings, and in entering *nirupadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa* where, in truth, there is no one who is delivered, nothing is more preeminent than the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
In destroying transgressions, accumulating merit, and purifying all evil realms, nothing is more urgent.
Regarding the *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya Sūtra*, one should maintain mindfulness and accord with its vows to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; nothing is swifter than the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

For clarifying right contemplation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), nothing surpasses the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra*. For elucidating self-nature and recognizing original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*), nothing is deeper than the *Tathatā-dharmaguhya Sūtra*.
For emptying the dust of dharmas and relying on non-intellection, nothing exceeds the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*.
These eight kinds of sutras comprise all twelve divisions [of the canon], totaling one hundred eleven thousand six hundred and fifty-seven words.
They contain the essential tenets of the Three Vehicles and exhaust the secret treasury of all Buddhas. This stone wall consists of four layers;
it is one *xun* high, fifteen *zhang* long, and one *chi* and eight *cun* thick. Above and below it are covered with stone lotuses. Therein...
Sekizan (Stone Deity) firmly protects its front and rear; fire and water cannot burn or sweep it away, and wind and sun cannot shake or dissolve it.

This is what is called the bestowal of the unsurpassed Dharma, which shall endure until the end of the future. Composed in the second year of the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty and completed in the third year of the Dàhé era.
The śramaṇa Qinghuang devised the plan, and the monk Qiuyuan transcribed it. Written by the Governor of the Capital, Bái Jǐyì.
He praised it with these words (from the Bai Juyi Changqing Ji):
"Recently, I traveled to Tiantai to pay homage at the ancestral pagodas.
Upon arriving at Guoqing Temple, I heard that the temple’s storehouse preserves various extraordinary relics; therefore..."

I request that you open the incense burner; what emerges is truly vast. For now, I shall briefly cite four examples. The first is a sandalwood incense case containing images, approximately one foot in height.
Inside are carved and engraved the holy countenances of the eight manifestations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, numbering over seven hundred in total.
Their exquisite craftsmanship is truly beyond compare. This was commissioned by Zhiyi for Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty to receive the [vows of] Bodhi.
First is the *Lotus Sūtra* bestowed upon me at the time I received the Bodhisattva precepts;

second is the *Golden-Character Lotus Sūtra* handwritten by the Venerable Master (Zhìzhě), a complete set whose calligraphy is so pure it seems almost divinely fashioned—this was produced by my ancestor in Jinling under the imperial decree of Emperor Xuandi of the Chen dynasty;
third is the *Heart Sūtra* on palm leaves from India, which a Brahman monk brought from the Great Sui dynasty and presented as a gift to the Venerable Master. Fourth...
It is said that King Qian of Wuyue transcribed the Lotus Sūtra in gold ink; it was exquisite and meticulously calligraphed. The colophon at the end reads:
"Respectfully transcribed by the King of Wuyue, Qian Chu. This sūtra consists of twenty fascicles, and this is one of those twenty.

Now, I have further seen the "Eulogy on the Auspicious Omens of the Offered Lotus Sūtra" by Chan Master Shou, which was praised and commended by the King of Qian. Consequently, an imperial decree was issued to have it transcribed in gold.
One hundred copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—how truly marvelous and extraordinary this is!
While it is well known that many emperors and kings throughout antiquity have propagated the Buddha-dharma, I have never heard of such diligent effort in transcribing it.
This is surely because he did not fail the entrustment of Vulture Peak, but came specifically to China to serve as a point of refuge for all sentient beings. —Master Zong

I, Xiaozi, have here compiled and arranged [this work], recording with my brush what I have long cherished in my heart from past observations, wishing that those who have not yet heard it might now hear it.
Thus, I have taken up the pen to record it.
Record of Manifested Responses from the Lotus Sūtra, Volume Upper;
Record of Manifested Responses from the Lotus Sūtra, Volume Lower.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongxiao of Shizhi in Siming.
Chan Master Fada of Hongzhou was a native of Hongzhou.
He left home at the age of seven and recited the Lotus Sūtra. After shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he went to pay respects to the Sixth Patriarch, Chan Master Huineng of Caoxi.
The Patriarch said, "If you do not prostrate yourself on the ground when paying respects, how is that any different from not paying respects at all?"
The Master observed him and said, "In your mind, there must surely be some lingering attachment. Fa-da replied, "I have already recited the *Lotus Sūtra* three thousand times.

The Master said, "Prostration is the root for breaking the banner of pride; why has your head not yet reached the ground? He continued, "Now you are named Fa-da (Dharma-Attainment), yet you recite diligently without ceasing.
You recite in vain, merely following the phonetics of the scripture; though your heart calls itself a Bodhisattva, you believe only in the Buddha’s wordlessness. [The *Lotus Sūtra*...]"
[The Master] spoke from his mouth. The Patriarch asked again, "What is the central tenet of this sutra? Da replied, "This student is dull-witted and does not understand.
The Patriarch said, "The central tenet of this sutra is the causal conditions for transcending the world; it is the single great matter: the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
Do not misunderstand this. "Opening, showing, awakening, and entering" are the Buddha’s own knowledge and vision; we have no share in them.
Since he is already a Buddha and fully possesses knowledge and vision, what need is there to further open it? You should know that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is simply your own mind.

There is no separate entity; it is merely that you obscure your own radiance and, out of craving for sensory objects, exhaust others by urging them to arise from samādhi and repeatedly exhorting them to rest.
You merely take this fixation of thought to be your merit—how is this any different from a yak that loves its tail? Da said:
"If it is as you say, then there is no need to recite the sutras? The Patriarch said: "What fault is there in the sutras? How could they hinder your mindfulness? Listen to my verse:
When the mind is deluded, [it wanders]...; when the mind awakens, it turns the *Lotus Sutra*. To recite for a long time without clarifying oneself is to become an enemy to the meaning.
Without-thought, thought is precisely right; with-thought, thought becomes deviant. When neither [thought nor non-thought] is reached, one forever drives [the Way]."

The White Ox Cart. Having received this instruction and enlightenment, Huineng joyfully spoke a verse: "Three thousand sections of scripture have been recited, yet one phrase from Caoqi has been lost.

If I do not understand the ultimate meaning that transcends the world, how can I cease the madness of successive lifetimes? The sheep, deer, and ox carts were provisionally established; the goodness of the beginning, middle, and end is now proclaimed.
Who would have known that within the burning house, there was originally the King of Dharma? The Patriarch said, "Only now may you truly be called a practitioner of mindfulness."
This refers to the monk Da. Having received the profound essence of the teachings, he never ceased reciting and upholding them from that time onward;
this is clearly seen in the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) concerning Chan Master Niu-tou Shanrong.

The *Xu sengzhuan* (Continued Biographies of Monks) records the monk Faxiong. His secular surname was Wei, and he was a native of Runzhou. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations, and he himself was extensively versed in the classics and histories;
however, he lacked any intention to serve the world through them. One day, while casually reading the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he attained a clear understanding of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

He thereupon abandoned Confucianism and fled into Maoshan, where he changed his scholar’s robes for the monastic black. For twenty years, he devoted himself exclusively to investigating the mysteries of this Way.

He was diligent and untiring. During the Zhenguan era, while he was lecturing on the Lotus Sūtra for over a hundred members of the fourfold assembly at the Ox-Head Stone Grotto, snow accumulated to the brim of the steps.
Suddenly, two blossoms appeared amidst the frozen ice, shaped like lotus flowers.
His radiance was like the color of gold. He remained visible for seven days before finally vanishing.

Furthermore, when the official Xiao Yuanshan requested that he lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he caused the earth to tremble so violently that the bells, chimes, and incense tables all swayed out beyond the temple grounds; yet [Tanhui] remained serene and unaware of it.
Furthermore, Liu Yuxi composed the Stele Inscription for the Master’s Stupa, stating:

"The Master’s divine efficacy moved Heaven such that springs gushed forth from the foot of the mountain, white snow gave birth to lotuses, a giant serpent was subdued, and a herd of deer listened to the Dharma. Moreover, during the Master’s tenure at Niutou, [birds] brought flowers in their beaks...
[omitted]. The Fourth Patriarch, Chan Master Xinxing, perceived auspicious vapors over that mountain; upon visiting it, he indeed beheld [the Master]."
There were many traces of his [enlightened] activity. With a single word, he attained awakening and transmitted the Great Dharma of the Buddha.

From then on, as he preached the sutras in accordance with conditions, they all resulted in miraculous efficacy. Thus we know that in ancient times, Chan and the Teachings (Dharma) were used in mutual support;
nowadays, however, this is not the case.

Regarding Mount Tiantong Jingde Chan Monastery in Mingzhou, where Chan Master Taibai resided: during the Western Jin dynasty, there was a practitioner of the Buddha who established a shrine upon a cliff.
For nearly four hundred years, until the twentieth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, the eminent monk Faxuan consulted ancient records and cleared away the thickets and brambles.
Having discovered ancient traces, he constructed a vihāra at the eastern foot of the mountain. Wan Qirong, a *zhengzi* of the Secretariat, first erected a Prabhūtaratna stūpa in the southwest corner;
it rose steeply several *ren* high. Faxuan resided there, reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* daily.
It is said that he was once moved by celestial spirits; a divine youth would ascend and descend upon the clouds to present him with heavenly food as offerings.
Whenever the Master traveled around the stupa at night to practice the Way, those who saw him from afar perceived his body to be equal in height to the *cakra* (spokes) of the stupa’s pinnacle.
Initially, his mother, the Lady, had dreamed that the Goddess Śrī led her to the palace of Mārīci, after which she conceived the Master. This is the one known as Chan Master Taibai.
The temple possesses a record composed by Fan, which details these events (as found in the *Sīmíng Tújīng*).
The nun Jì of Zhùzhōu was named Dàojì and styled Zǒngchí; it is unknown where she was from. She received the Dharma from Bodhidharma. Upon examination...
As for the transmission of the lamp: Bodhidharma did not find resonance with the Emperor of Liang, so he went to Shaolin and sat facing a wall for nine years.
One day, he addressed the assembly, saying, "I wish to return west to India. You should each speak of what you have attained. At that time, Daoyu said:
