"As I see it," [Huineng] said, "I do not cling to words and letters, nor am I separate from them, yet I employ them as the Way. The Master said, "You have obtained my skin.
Nizi Tongzhi said, "What I now understand is like Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha:
having seen it once, one does not need to see it again. The Master said, "You have obtained my flesh. Daofu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates are..."
"There is. Yet, in my state of realization, there is not a single dharma. Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my bones. Huike prostrated and stood in his place.
The Master said, "You have attained my marrow. Bodhidharma then transmitted the Dharma to Huike and departed from that dwelling.
Although Huike’s realization had not yet reached the level of attaining the marrow, his resolve to practice it remained undiminished; he immediately withdrew to live in seclusion at Lake Zhou.
At the summit of Byeon-ryeong Peak, she recited the *Lotus Sūtra* day and night until she had completed one hundred thousand fascicles. For nearly twenty years, she did not descend from the mountain.
Later, she passed away into stillness (*parinirvāṇa*), and her entire body was enshrined in a stūpa at the site where she had lived in a thatched hut.

In the first year of the Dae-tong era, a single blue lotus flower suddenly appeared inside the stūpa. Monastics and laypeople marveled at this; upon opening it to see, they found that the nun’s physical body remained incorruptible.
The flowers emerged from her tongue-root, and within them, she obtained a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra*. The local prefectures recorded these facts and submitted a memorial to the throne.
By imperial decree, the Fa-hua Temple (Fahua Si) was established. To this day, during the Great Song dynasty, the temple’s name has been changed to Guanyin Yuan (Avalokiteśvara Monastery);
thus, it is named after the *Lotus Sūtra*. The nun’s stupa still exists. During the Chunxi era, the abbot monk Jingran re-established the ancestral hall.
He offered incense and lamps. The inscription on the stone records that the Master’s original name was Baoyu;
his surname was Tang, and he was a native of Anji in Wuxing, Huzhou. His mother was of the Mei clan, and her pregnancy was accompanied by auspicious omens.
He immediately loathed pungent foods and impurities. Once born, as soon as he reached the age of ten, he set his mind upon the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*).

He subsequently left the household life at Nitzongchi Fahua Temple, vowing to recite the Lotus Sūtra. Within three months, he had mastered it thoroughly. From then on, he daily maintained the recitation of seven sūtras.

When he reached the age of twenty, he went to the capital to receive the full precepts. At that time, Emperor Suzong dreamed one night of a monk from Wu province reciting the Lotus Sūtra, from whose mouth five...
The color of his light was radiant, and his Wu-dialect pronunciation was clear and resonant.

When he ascended to the court the following morning, the Emperor issued an edict for more than two hundred monks from the capital who were able to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* to enter the inner palace together. The Emperor examined them, but none were the one he had seen in his dream.

At that time, Bao Yu was about to enter the pass. The warden of the pass asked him the purpose of his long journey, to which he replied: "I am skilled at reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*; I have come to receive the precepts."

He was then ordered to perform a memorial service. The Emperor immediately issued an edict summoning him for an audience. The Emperor said, "The voice and countenance of the one I dreamed of are exactly as they were.
He then commanded [him] to take a seat and recite the sutra. When they reached the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing," light of five colors emanated from the corners of his mouth.

The Emperor was greatly delighted and said, "The light I beheld in my dream is this very one. As soon as the scripture was finished, he presented him with a broth made of the seven precious gems and ordered a separate incense altar to be built for him specifically to receive the precepts.
He bestowed upon him the name Daguang (Great Light) and enfeoffed him as the *sthavira* (Elder) of the realm.

He resided in the capital for three years, devoting himself exclusively to recitation. Furthermore, by imperial decree, he performed rites at Qianfu Monastery; after forty-nine days, the Sanskrit [text]...
His voice was pervasive and reached the ears of the sages. He resided separately at the Lantian Monastery, but was subsequently summoned to reside at Zisheng Temple.

Because his compassionate mother was in the region of Wu, Huiguang submitted a memorial requesting to return home to repay her kindness; the imperial decree did not grant permission. Later, he adorned his head with a jeweled crown and wore the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* upon it while reciting it.
Shortly thereafter, an imperial edict permitted him to return. Huiguang submitted a petition stating: "If I return to my hometown, I have three wishes: first, to attend to my parents' needs."
First, [the request] of the elderly mother; second, the petition to ordain monks throughout the empire; third, the desire to construct and expand Fahua Temple.

By imperial decree, all were granted: one official edict from Huzhou, one string of government currency, one imperial decree, one Many Treasures Stūpa, one Maitreya image, one copy of the Lotus Sūtra, one set of [ritual] implements, and one male slave.

He was accompanied by a single attendant. Having returned, he built a hermitage along the pine-lined path of Fahua Temple to dwell in. Daily, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* to repay the great kindness [of the Emperor].
In the final winter month of the first year of the Yongzhen era, he went to bid farewell to the Regional Inspector, Yan Fang, saying: "I have said my goodbyes."
"I am departing. Human life is impermanent, like a dream or an illusion. Having said this, he returned to the temple and sat peacefully until his passing.

A wondrous fragrance wafted about for three days without fading. He was buried beside the hermitage. At that time, the assembly all declared that the Master was the reincarnation of the nun Zongchi of the Liang dynasty.
Who can possibly fathom the transformative manifestations of such a perfected being? Upon seeing the stele erected by Master Ran, I [wrote this].
If one consults the *Great Song Biographies of Eminent Monks*, that work treats Dàguāng and Bǎoyù as two separate individuals; this is an error resulting from insufficient investigation.

Now, I shall further extract and supplement the text of those biographies. While the Master resided at Lántián, a monk of the monastery previously dreamed that a celestial youth descended and announced:
"The sound of Dàguāng’s recitation of the scriptures reaches as far as the Summit of Existence (Bhavāgra); this is no trivial matter. One day, as Guāng was feasting...
While sitting at the site of enlightenment, he saw a divine being descend from heaven and massage his heart with his hand.

From that time on, his spiritual power became even more manifest, and his body and spirit remained free from fatigue. Once, while the Master was walking in the mountains, he suddenly fell into a dragon well;

he immediately called to mind the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and vowed to recite this chapter one hundred thousand times. Suddenly, he felt as though he were being lifted out by a divine being, and he emerged unharmed. Later, an imperial edict was issued.
He resided at Ziseng Temple, which had been built by Empress Wende. The temple was suddenly struck by fire, yet among the rubble several volumes of sutras were found, not a single character damaged.
He reported this matter to the throne, and an imperial decree was issued for the temple to be rebuilt. Having personally examined these scriptures, he redoubled his diligent practice.
Subsequently, he requested to return to the region of Wu; once there, he went first to Wucheng, where the Chancellor Li Xun was serving as Regional Inspector of Wu.
Xing was intoxicated. While [he] was holding the *sūtra*... [he] spied upon Master Guang as he sat in meditation and recited the scripture. When Guang rose, the radiance from his face...
[his] patched robe had not been washed for forty years, yet the fragrance of his precepts was profound and pervasive. He ate but one meal a day; for seventy years he did not...
He violated the rule against [reciting] at improper times. Although Minister Yi Sang-so was sparing in his faith toward the Buddhist gate, he was deeply devoted to this master.
He personally composed an inscription for a stele, titled "Epitaph for the Miraculous Virtue of the Great Virtuous One Who Recited Scriptures by Imperial Decree."

The Great Master Danyuan of the Western Capital, whose secular name was Chujin, was born into the Chen family of Jingzhao. His mother conceived him after dreaming of various Buddhas; thus, he was truly the son of the Dharma King.
At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly life and left home to become a monk at Longxing Temple in his native prefecture. Subsequently, he paid homage to the Tripitaka and explored its depths...

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was in his hand; he recited it through from beginning to end, the cadence of his voice flowing like a stream. After receiving full ordination, he ascended the hall to listen to lectures, whereupon he suddenly grasped the entire treasury of the Dharma.
Once, while chanting this sūtra during a quiet night, as he reached the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," his body and mind became utterly tranquil.

Suddenly, he beheld the jeweled stupa before him, with the emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha arrayed throughout the expanse of space. From that time forth, he never again emerged from meditative concentration.

He resided in the chamber for six years, reciting the scriptures with a vow to erect this stupa as a response to the divine manifestation. Once his sincere devotion was expressed, donors and believers arrived in great numbers.

He immediately began the restoration; at the site where the foundation was being laid, every night the assembly suddenly heard the sound of celestial music and the fragrance of extraordinary incense wafted through the air.
Since the Master’s realization had accorded with the Buddha-mind, he was immediately moved to appear in the Emperor’s dream. The Xuanzong [Emperor] beheld...
Beneath the name "Dharma" (Fa), there is the character for "Gold" (Jin). When he ascended to the court and was questioned, his responses were entirely sincere and authentic.

His reputation spread throughout the capital, and he was immediately sought out in accordance with a dream. Consequently, fifty thousand coins and one thousand bolts of silk were granted to him for the purpose of construction.
Furthermore, the Emperor personally inscribed the plaque for the Many Treasures Stupa (Duobao Ta) to be enshrined therein. [Regarding] the stupa affairs... [and] the repentance rituals.
Immediately, five-colored clouds and vapors gathered above the stupa.
Not far from here, I wish to assemble seven monks to unite our resolve and recite [the scriptures] day and night beneath the stupa.
He caused the incense smoke to be unceasing and the sound of the Dharma to be inexhaustible, with various musical instruments accompanying it.

Every spring and autumn, he would assemble forty-nine fellow practitioners to perform the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Subsequently, he received an imperial edict permitting this to become a permanent practice.

Within the meditation hall, the number of *śarīra* relics obtained was particularly great; one day, while painting an image of Samantabhadra, he was moved by the appearance of nineteen *śarīra* relics.
He drew [the characters] from the tip of his brush. Furthermore, he pricked his fingers to shed blood and transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Caryā-dharma-sūtra*, and other scriptures.

He also inscribed thirty-six copies of this wondrous sūtra in gold to enshrine within the precious stupa. Additionally, he transcribed one thousand copies to distribute among the masses for their recitation and upholding.

When his efforts in seeking donations were complete, on the seventh day of the seventh month in the second year of the Qianduan era, he passed away peacefully in the right lateral position at the age of sixty.

The Prince of Heaven (the Emperor) mourned for him deeply, and an imperial envoy came to offer condolences. His stupa was erected at the Fahua Aranya to the west of the city. From his childhood, the Master had been content with a simple and austere life;
he did not wear silk or flossed cotton, but was satisfied with coarse hemp and shoddy for warmth. He ate but one meal a day and endured rigorous study through three winters.
His virtuous conduct was so manifold that it cannot easily be recorded in full. In the thirteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, Dou Wenchang submitted a memorial stating:
During the Tiānbǎo era, Chǔjīn established a pagoda for the state and founded a Lotus Sūtra practice hall (*fǎhuá dàochǎng*).

More than sixty years have passed since then, and the sound of the monastic community’s prostrations and recitations has never ceased. Yet, having passed through four successive dynasties, his virtuous deeds had never been formally honored.

By imperial decree, permission was granted to bestow the posthumous title of Chan Master Zàiyuán (The Master’s life story follows the *Fēixí* stele in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*; his spiritual wonders are recorded in Cén Xūn’s inscription; as these accounts were gathered from different sources, they vary and contain some discrepancies).
Regarding his life and passing (now combined with the two accounts to complete the full record):
Dharma Master Zun of Suzhou was praised for his extraordinary conduct and pure aspirations; his glory shone brightly.

Regarding the practice of the threefold contemplation within a single mind (*ekacitta-trisamādhi*)—which does not concern [the specific details of] □□□□□□□□□□□—he took the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*) as his fundamental principle.
Because he had extensively transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he established a Scripture-Reading Hall at Zhizhong Mountain in Suzhou.

On the first day he resolved his mind; on the second day he laid out its foundations. Without exceeding the proper sequence, the halls and pavilions were completed by transformation. This was in the first year of the Dali era.

The provincial governor Wei Yuanfu and others all witnessed these extraordinary wonders. They jointly submitted a memorial to the throne, by imperial decree of which the site was specially designated as the Fahua Daochang (Lotus Sutra Monastery).
From the region east of the Yangtze River, seventeen such establishments were founded, all through the efforts of Zhi [Zun].

Furthermore, he recruited fourteen monks of refined conduct to constantly recite this sutra as a means of repaying the Emperor’s grace. He also cast an image of Śākyamuni and erected a stūpa for Prabhūtaratna.
He fashioned a statue of Amitābha Buddha and transcribed the Three Great Treatises, which overflowed the boundaries of his practice hall.

Later, while practicing the Lotus Samādhi at Lingyan, he suddenly beheld a great radiance shining upward toward the heavens; his body remained upright in right mindfulness, as if standing solemnly within the light.
On another day, he asked Master Yan of Jingxi: "The light of wisdom flows forth from the mind—is this not the result of diligent resolve?"
Furthermore, while at his home temple, he entered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* meditation hall and personally beheld this body sitting in mid-air.

Those who had previously attained realization recognized this as a sign of the purification of defilements. When the Master finally passed into *parinirvāṇa*, the two masters Yì and Hàn of the mountain temple both dreamed that the main hall collapsed;
this was truly a portent of his departure (from the *Dàsòng Sēngzhuàn*).
Regarding the Dharma Master Yun from Xihe:
During the Zhenguan era, there was a Dharma Master named Tanyun who left secular life at a young age and specialized in reciting the Lotus Sūtra.

When only two fascicles remained, he retired to a secluded place on Mount Heng to complete that portion of the sūtra. There, he happened to meet the Chan Master Yin, who said to him, "As for reciting the sūtra..."
It is not that he does not take the Way as his object of focus.
He constantly recites [the scriptures], maintaining the rhythm and receiving this instruction. He practices it with solemnity.

Having reached the stage of Wutai [Mountain], for twenty years he wore tattered robes and took but one meal a day. As for the scriptures he previously recited, his mind and mouth no longer focused upon them.

For thirty years, he recited it without missing a single character. Later, he also became thoroughly proficient in both volumes. He constantly desired to transcribe a copy of this sutra with perfect purity, but for several years he was unable to do so.
Suddenly, he encountered a scholar who said, "I am skilled at copying; I shall establish the rules for the style and write it for you.
He wrote it in the stone chamber, entering in the morning and emerging in the evening. [Fahai] deeply marveled at what was being done. Before even ten days had passed, seven fascicles were complete.

He understood them all. The Master was pleased with him and prepared a meal to express his gratitude; suddenly, the man vanished. Later, during a period of banditry and chaos, he concealed the scriptures in a mountain cave.

When the rebellion was quelled and he went to retrieve them, they had been left beneath some trees; the boxes and wrappers were already rotted away, yet the scrolls themselves remained as they were originally.
Subsequently, he passed away while seated on Mount Pingyao in Xihe at the age of over eighty. The Master had lived in seclusion within the mountain forests for sixty years.
He had no desire for fame or profit. He did not maintain lay attendants (*śrāmaṇera*), nor was he registered in the public records. He did not carry out official duties;
he was truly an eminent gentleman of upright integrity and pure detachment (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).

Dharma Master Zhang of Dongjing, whose courtesy name was Fuchu, was a native of Kaifeng Prefecture. His father, Peng Yin, was a prominent farmer of the district who, beyond his worldly affairs, constantly recited Buddhist scriptures and further explained their profound meanings.
His mother, Lady Xing, dreamed that she entered a Buddhist monastery and reached out her hand to grasp a vessel of the Way.
Consequently, she became pregnant. Her father, perceiving that his son was extraordinary, vowed while she was still in her womb that he would enter the monastic order.

At the age of eleven, he entered the Way. His teachers instructed him in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Aparimitāyurjñāna-rāja*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*. Before long, he had mastered them thoroughly.
Upon reaching maturity, he studied the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* under Dharma Master Lang, exerting himself with great vigor within the waters of the Dharma. Day by day, his progress was remarkable.
For over twenty years, he never ceased for even a single day.

He composed verses [and practiced] until, upon his passing into nirvana and cremation, when the smoke had subsided and the fire was extinguished, his tongue remained unburnt. Previously, his father had been reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
after his death, it was burned, yet his tongue likewise did not decay. That both son and father shared this same miraculous sign is truly rare (from the *Great Song Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

Jìlún, the Śramaṇa and Chief Registrar (Sēnglù) of Bìngzhōu, was the son of the Cáo family of Jínyáng. From his youth, he possessed resolute ambition and sought with determination to leave the household life.

His original teacher taught him the *Lotus Sūtra*, which he recited at three sheets per day; even then, he was startled by his long-standing karmic predispositions. After becoming a monk, his study of this sūtra became thorough, and he mastered its meaning.
His traces were exceedingly profound and mysterious. Consequently, he compiled the *Fahua jing chao* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) in three fascicles.

When the Liu family occupied the regions of Bing and Fen, they held his Way in high esteem and appointed him as the Right Street Monk Registrar (*youjie senglu*). In managing the assembly, he balanced leniency with severity, such that none dared to oppose him.

One day, he manifested illness and expressed his vow to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. After his death, the crown of his head remained warm for half a day before cooling. During the cremation, śarīra relics [were found].
He was resplendent and pure. People from near and far vied with one another to request his presence for offerings (*Dàsòng Sēngzhuàn*).
Regarding Dharma Master Ying of Wutai:
During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Shenying. He was a native of Cangzhou. He recited the scriptures day and night without ever flagging. He traveled everywhere...
The monk Sengzhi traveled to Mount Wutai. One day, while wandering through the Xilin (Western Grove) section of the monastery, he suddenly saw a courtyard with a plaque inscribed "Fahua" (Lotus).
Sengying walked slowly inside and beheld a stupa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha; it was magnificent and splendid, exactly as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
There were also statues of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra made of jade and stone, exquisite and radiant, divinely sublime.
His merits are rarely fathomable. The scale and layout of the monastery resemble those of the ten temples on Mount Tai. [The text here is fragmentary:
...having finished [the construction], Daoying went out from the temple and encountered a multitude of monks, none of whom were those he had previously seen.
After traveling for about thirty *li*, [he found] not a single possession [among them]. Daoying wept bitterly and said: "This is truly the Great Sage awakening me."
Thus, he established a hermitage at the site where the Many Treasures Stupa had appeared in a semblance and resided there. He then made a vow, saying:

"I shall establish a temple upon the foundations of this transformed courtyard to repay this spiritual response. Thereafter, as the days and months passed, donors and believers gathered like a forest.
He then traveled nine hundred li from Yizhou to procure jade and stone, using them to fashion two Bodhisattva statues whose craftsmanship was peerless.
Upon seeing this, once the monastery was completed, it was renamed Fahua. Fanyi was appointed as the Dharma-abiding master (shouzhu).
Its orderly arrangement was as if it had been cut with scissors (from the *Dàsòng Sēngzhuàn*).

The Master Lin, who served as an attendant at the capital, was surnamed Fan and was a native of Yanzhou. His father did not favor the Triple Gem; whenever he saw a monk, he would invariably scold him and spit upon him.

The Master’s childhood name was Lín’ér. From a young age, he felt admiration for monks and consequently fled his home to enter the monastic order, taking refuge at Guang’ai Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
In the temple, there was a monk named Zilin who had been ordained for eleven years when he suddenly thought of returning home to visit his kin.

His father had lost his sight, and his mother had been dead for three years. Desiring to repay her for her nurturing care, the master went to the shrine of Mount Tai to seek his deceased mother’s whereabouts in the netherworld.
He immediately spread out his mat and, with single-minded devotion, recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, vowing to see the Heavenly King Tianqi. The King took pity upon him...

He pleaded earnestly and manifested his form to question him. The neighbor said, "It has already been a year since my mother, Lady Wang, passed away and completed her mourning period; why is she here now?
The subordinate official replied, "Lady Wang is currently imprisoned and undergoing suffering. The neighbor asked, "What crime has my mother committed to bring this upon her?"
The King said, "When Master Sheng was alive, he ate many chicken eggs. Furthermore, he took the head tumor of Bai Fu and sat upon it;

for this reason, you are bound by your karma and there is no way to release you. If you go to Mount Mao to pay homage at the Aśoka Stūpa and [prostrate] at Changshan Temple, you may perhaps find mercy. He then knelt and wept in lamentation.
He prostrated himself in worship until forty thousand bows had been completed. Suddenly, he heard the sound of someone calling out his name.

Looking toward the sky, he saw his mother within the clouds, who said to him, "By your power, I have been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; therefore, I have come to inform you. Having spoken, she vanished.
Today, atop the peak behind Yūrwang Temple, there is the Ch'wi-mi Hermitage, which was the place where the Master resided. Later, the Master extensively commented upon the scriptures.
The treatise states: His reputation for eloquence was widespread. Emperor Suzong summoned him into the inner palace to serve as an attendant.
Praising his quick-wittedness in debate, the Emperor bestowed upon him purple robes and appointed him as an Official of the Imperial Presence (*Dàsòng Sēngzhuàn*).

Dharma Master Chao of Mount Lu, Seng Jingchao, had long maintained the precepts. His character was upright and straightforward; he did not seek to curry favor with his interpretations. Dwelling on Mount Lu, his constant practice was solely the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Having completed two full recitations of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, performing one prostration for every single character, he then burned off one of his fingers.

He made offerings, and next he prostrated before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. His practice of burning his fingers was likewise. Thereafter, śarīra relics emerged from within his flesh, numerous and perfectly lustrous.
Whenever there were those who sought them, they were obtained wherever one sat or walked upon the ground.
He passed away at his hermitage during the Tiānfú era of the Shí Jìn dynasty (as recorded in the *Dà Sòng Sēng Zhuàn*).
The Dharma Master Zhen of the Capital: The Dharma Master’s name was Hongzhen.
He was the son of the Chunyu clan of Huazhou. In his youth, he awakened to the fetters of the mundane world and resolved to seek liberation from it.
His resolute character rose high like a solitary crane among the clouds. When his teacher bestowed upon him the wondrous Dharma, he mastered it at once; he had recited it since birth.

He recited [the scripture] approximately ten thousand times. Regarding his donning of armor and so forth, he later went to the court to submit a memorial, requesting to burn his body as an offering to the Buddha’s stūpa.
The imperial decree did not grant permission. Zhen sighed that while his wholesome roots were weak, demonic obstacles were particularly strong.
He subsequently withdrew to Guang’ai Temple, completely renounced his robes and bowl, and performed an untimely almsgiving. Suddenly, he sat peacefully and passed away after several days had elapsed.
His facial features remained as if he were alive. When he passed away, his tongue remained intact and grew even more vividly red. The people of the Yi and Luo regions revered him as a Buddha.
This was during the Liu Han period (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).
An anonymous monk from Tanzhou during the Qianyou era of the Later Han dynasty was a man who constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and spoke no other words.

King Wenzhao of Changsha treated him with exceptional honor and respect, summoning him to the Tiance Palace at the Xiangxi Monastery to provide for his needs. However, his speech— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; this translation reflects the available portion.*
The events were strange and extraordinary. One day, he summoned the monks in charge of the hall and ordered them to quickly fold up the Buddha images and move them to the two side aisles.

The assembly all thought he had gone mad and looked at one another with smiles. A short while later, he entered the main hall himself, took his place upon the Buddha’s seat, sat solemnly, and passed away.
The clergy and laity throughout the entire prefecture revered him and marveled at this. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*)
During the time of Qian Wusuku, the Prince of Xuancheng, there was a monk named Zixin who resided at Ruiying Monastery. Once, while entering the Xuancheng Mountains to gather medicinal herbs,
he traveled several li through a cave until he suddenly saw a thatched hut by a stream beneath some pine trees, where a monk with snow-white eyebrows sat wrapped in his robes.
While he was practicing seated meditation, there was a novice monk named Xin who struck the *qing* (stone chime). The monk opened his eyes and asked, "By what cause have you come here?

Xin then struck fire to brew tea as they waited for evening. Xin requested that the monk look after him during the night; the monk immediately ascended to the summit of a pine tree and entered a large nest to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*.
His voice was exceptionally clear and resonant, making it a pleasure for all to hear. After a short while, [the bird] suffered greatly, causing people to take pity on it.
Terrified, he cried out, "Go quickly! Go quickly! Upon peering closely, it was revealed to be a tiger or a leopard. The following day, a new [monk] arrived to reside in this place.
He observed that the grass was withered and the surrounding area was utterly devoid of human presence; thus, it was not a suitable dwelling for the Master.
Furthermore, he gathered yellow grain to provide as food and bid him farewell, saying, "Sir, eat this; you shall never lack for food throughout your life. The new [monk] then returned.
He arrived at the monastery; more than a month had already passed. When he went there again, however, he had forgotten the way (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).

In Chengdu Prefecture, there was a monk who had achieved great merit in reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*. Even though the two uprisings led by Wang Jun and Li Shun occurred in Shu, [the monk remained steadfast].
Nor did he suffer any harm. One day, he suddenly saw a mountain servant who said, "Master, you have been invited for a morning recitation of the scriptures;

we shall welcome you at the Medicine Market. When he arrived, [the master] was already there. He was led into the valley and over the ridges, through several layers of misty greenery, until they reached a mountain pavilion spanning a stream—this was his dwelling.
The servant came out and said, "Master, you have invited the teacher to recite the scriptures. Because of old age and illness, I arose late. If—"

Upon reaching the "Chapter on the Precious Stupa," he requested to be informed of the Master's arrival. The Master informed him. Sure enough, the Senior Scholar emerged, dressed in rustic clothes and carrying a staff of sorrel;

his two eyebrows hung down to his shoulders. He bowed silently, burned incense, and listened attentively. When they entered the hall for the meal, there were mats of rattan and chopsticks of bamboo, with millet rice and *qǐ* and *jú* greens.

He did not season it with salt or curd, yet it was as delicious as nectar. When the meal was finished, he offered a *xuan* of gold as a donation. The servant said, "The Master sent word that you had come from afar;
I was unable to go and see you off. The servant then escorted him on his way. Midway through the journey, the monk asked, "What is the Master’s surname?"
He replied, "My surname is Sūn. What is my name? I then wrote the two characters "Sīmāo" (Sīmiǎo) upon the monk’s hand.

The monk sighed in amazement; I suddenly vanished. He searched for three days, but ultimately lost my trail. Upon returning to check the alms-gift, there were one hundred gold coins, five or six of which were half-iron.
From this, my body became light and free from ailment for a single meal. This occurred during the Yuánxǐ era of the Great Song dynasty.
He was one hundred and fifty years old in his middle age. He traveled extensively through the capital cities and later disappeared into seclusion (from the *Sanyo roku*).
Regarding Dharma Master Ang of Xiangzhou:
there was a Dharma Master named Daoyang who resided at Kaiyuan Temple. He regularly lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*. One day, during the course of a lecture...
Suddenly, he saw the banners, streamers, and music of the various holy ones descending from the sky. They announced, "We have come specifically from the Tuṣita Heaven to welcome you.
Daowang replied, "The heavenly realms are the very root of birth and death; I have never wished for them. What I desire is only the Western [Pure Land]."
Having finished speaking, he vanished. After a short while, the clear and resonant sounds of music from the west were heard, different from what had been heard before.
The Master said with joy, "The time has come; I shall now depart. Farewell, all of you! Be diligent in mindfulness of Amitābha and be born together in the Pure Land.
Having spoken, the incense burner fell from his hand, and he passed away on the high seat with eyes closed. The fourfold assembly deeply admired him.
[From the *Brief Biographies of Those Reborn in the Pure Land*]:
The Chan Master Zhijue of Hangzhou, whose name was Yanshou, was a native of Yuhang.
From his early childhood, he knew how to revere the Buddha Vehicle; by the age of twenty, he had mastered the recitation [of the scriptures].

For the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he wrote five lines at a time, completing it in just sixty days. At that time, there was a sheep that knelt to listen to him. He once served as the official in charge of tax collection for Beiguo;
whenever he saw fish or shrimp, he would buy them to release them. He even embezzled government funds, using them all for the purpose of releasing living beings.
When the matter was discovered and he was sentenced to death, King Qian sent an envoy to observe him, instructing that if he showed fear, he should be executed; otherwise, he was to be spared.
He immediately abandoned it. When he was brought before the blade, his expression did not change; consequently, [the executioner] felt ashamed of his crime.
Thereupon, he went to Cuiyan in Mingzhou to enter the monastic life. King Wenmu granted him the tonsure. He once practiced the Lotus Samādhi at Guoqing Temple.

At night, he saw a divine being enter carrying a halberd; the Master rebuked him for entering without permission. The spirit said, "Only after long cultivation of pure karma does one reach this place."
In the middle of the night, while walking on his path, a lotus flower suddenly appeared in his hand as an offering from Samantabhadra. He then reflected upon two vows:
first, the vow to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* constantly for the rest of his life; second, the vow to extensively benefit all sentient beings throughout his entire existence.

Recalling these two vows, he again took pleasure in meditative stillness, yet could not decide between them. He therefore made two lots: one said "single-minded dhyāna-concentration," and the other...
He said, "Reciting the sutras and the 'Myriad Good Deeds'—if one wishes to achieve success in either of these two paths, one must draw lots seven times.
He then offered sincere prayers to the Buddhas and patriarchs and drew at random; on all seven occasions, he drew the lot for "Reciting the Sutras" and "The Myriad Good Deeds."
With single-minded devotion, he cultivated pure karma and subsequently went to Mount Tianzhu, where he recited the sutras for three years.
During his meditative contemplation, he saw Avalokiteśvara pouring nectar into his mouth; from that time on, he was endowed with the eloquence of Avalokiteśvara. He first resided at Xuedou.
Later, during the Yongming era, his assembly reached two thousand people; he was then hailed as Maitreya’s descent into the world.
He practiced with great diligence, performing one hundred and eight daily rites. Throughout his life, he recited the Lotus Sūtra approximately thirteen thousand times.

He composed the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred fascicles, which was subsequently ordered by imperial decree to be included in the Tripitaka. Upon falling ill during the Kaibao era of the Great Song dynasty, he burned incense and addressed the assembly, adding:

He sat in the lotus posture and entered meditative stillness (his life story is recorded in detail in the *Great Song Biographies of Monks*, the *Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha*, and the *Jewel-Bead Collection*. He used official funds to purchase living beings for release; this is seen in the *Complete Works of Dongpo*).

During the Taiping Xingguo era, the Dharma Master De of Sizhou was a monk from Jiangnan named Huide. Having left secular life, he was diligent and modest in his conduct and adorned himself with virtue.

He had mastered the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and thereby received full ordination. From then on, although he ascended the lecture hall, he remained dedicated exclusively to the practice of recitation and upholding the scriptures until his later years, when he traveled abroad.
At Sishang, he paid homage at the Sengqie Stupa. The Great Song dispatched an envoy bearing banners and flowers as offerings. De swore an oath that he wished to offer his own body by burning it.
First, he gave away his robes and alms bowl and established a vegetarian feast; next, he clothed himself in paper garments, wrapped his body in wax, and took leave of the assembly of monks.
Holding a pair of candles in his hands, he ascended the stack of firewood. He ignited the flames and recited a scripture. As the fire flared high, his body—

As he leaned to one side, the sound of chanting scriptures was still heard; among those who witnessed this, there were none who did not feel profound grief and sorrow. When the remaining bones were collected, Śrī was found in particularly great abundance.
He was dispatched to return with a report, which moved the Emperor to show his emotion (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*).

Dharma Master Yan of Hangzhou, whose secular surname was Liu and whose given name was Shaoyan, was the son of a family from Yongzhou. He entered the monastic path at the age of seven; he read all the various scriptures and classics as if they were his own private studies.
Traveling through various regions, he arrived at Hangzhou and hung up his staff at Suixin Temple. There, he constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra without ceasing, day or night. Suddenly—

A lotus flower was miraculously born upon dry land; the entire city gazed upon it in wonder. Yanqi stepped over it and immediately made a vow to emulate the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja by performing self-immolation.
At that time, the King of Qian held him in profound reverence and tried to detain him earnestly, but he refused to stay.

Shortly thereafter, he went secretly to the Cao’er River to cast himself into the waters to feed the fish’s bellies. Yet, as he threw himself in, he did not sink; it was said that a divine being had supported his feet. Just then, a fisherman...
The King of Qian immediately constructed Shangfang Monastery and summoned him to reside there. During the Kaibao era, he fell ill;
refusing medicine, he gave his final instructions, saying, "I have recited the Lotus Sutra twenty thousand times. I am certain that my destination shall be the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

Now, fortunately, my wish is fulfilled. Having spoken, he passed away while sitting upright. His funeral rites were performed with official provisions, and his body was cremated at Longjing Mountain, where relics were obtained.
The śarīra relics were beyond counting; his bones remained as lustrous as polished jade. He was then enshrined within a stone sarcophagus in the Shadow Hall (yingtáng).
Sun Chengyou, the Grand Preceptor, composed the inscription for the stele (*Dàsòng Sēngzhuàn*).
The Venerable Chuyun of Mount Heng was born at the end of the Tang dynasty. He possessed supreme conduct; he once drew blood to transcribe one copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It measured seven inches in length, four inches in width, and half that in thickness. He fashioned a sandalwood case to enshrine it.
This was the *Fuyan Sengzang* (Tripiṭaka of Three Lives). Furthermore, eight characters were inscribed upon it, saying: "If this scripture is opened, I vow to be like Maitreya.
During the Huángyòu era, a nobleman visiting the mountain saw it; suspecting it to be a fabrication, he sent someone to pry it open with pliers.
Blood as thin as a thread emerged from it. In an instant, wind and thunder shook the mountains, and smoke and clouds entered the hall.

They held onto one another, unable to see each other, and the phenomenon did not cease for days. The nobleman was greatly alarmed; he surrendered his heart in repentance, sighing, "How great is the power of such a vow!
I once traveled there to pay my respects and examined it closely; the blood-thread remained exactly as before. Chan-yue Guanhui composed a poem in praise of it.

He said: "To scrape off the skin and prick the blood—how truly bitter is such suffering! Yet for the sake of transcribing the *Text on the Three Assemblies at Vulture Peak*, my ten fingers have been drained dry until the seven fascicles were finished.
Hereafter, those seeking the Dharma will find no one like me. This account appears in the *Línjiān Lù* (Record of the Forest).
During the Chunxi era, the Minister Fan Chengda visited this temple and requested to see this scripture, praising it with a verse that begins: "The Buddha-son’s true Dharma-body, radiant..."

Radiating purple-gold light that scatters and fills the worlds of the ten directions, it gathers into seven scrolls of scripture; these seven scrolls pervade as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
Trembling with joy, they proclaim the wondrous Dharma—neither gathered nor scattered; this is the vision of the Eye of the Dharma.

Dharma Master Guang of Qizhou, the monk Daoguang of Yongle Temple in Qizhou, was a man of pure and simple character whom the local community revered. He once drew blood to mix with ink and transcribed one copy of the Lotus Sūtra;
the slanting strokes and dots were as even as rain falling from the sky, as orderly as [the rows of] grain above.
The fish in the rapids are all accomplished through the power of diligent practice and perfumed by the fragrance of knowledge and vision;

otherwise, how could they be so subtle and wondrous? Furthermore, within the space of a single hair-pore, one beholds eighteen thousand Buddha-lands, and in a single kṣaṇa, one enters the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meaning.
This is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Whether walking, speaking, remaining silent, or moving, [one should always maintain this].
It was not for personal enjoyment. After I returned from the north, I beheld the sutras he had transcribed and observed his conduct;
as he conversed with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, how could he have harbored any worldly thoughts? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"To never allow one’s thoughts to merge with the worldly mind is great diligence. Guang took this as his principle (*Shimen Wenzishan*).

In the capital, people spoke of the *Lotus Sūtra*, saying, "The *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Lotus Sūtra," yet no one knew where it had come from. He traveled through the capital; at first, he was seen at the Jingde Juzhi Monastery.

His appearance was strange and ancient; he gazed straight ahead without blinking, and the flow of words from his mouth was so rapid that it could not be understood. It was said by tradition that he was reciting [the sūtra].
Because he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he was thus named after it. He ate and drank without discrimination, and both monastics and laypeople labeled him a "mad monk.

When Emperor Renzong’s succession had not yet been established, [the Emperor] offered silent prayers during a night incense offering, saying: "Tomorrow, let the Great Master Fahua come to the Huacheng Hall for a vegetarian feast.
The following morning, the Emperor donned his ceremonial robes and waited. Suddenly, a report came in stating that Fahua himself had arrived.
He hurried along the path through the right side gate toward the inner palace. The Emperor stopped him, saying he could not enter, but the Master laughed and said, "The Emperor has invited me here.

Once they arrived, the Master ascended the imperial couch, sat cross-legged, and finished receiving the offerings. The Emperor said, "Because no heir apparent has been established, the high ministers all say that my life is drawing to a close and question whether an offspring will exist or not.
Great Master, please resolve this for me. The Master sought a brush and wrote "Thirteen, thirteen" several times.

[The Master] spoke of the "Ten Practices," but no one understood their meaning. Later, when Emperor Yingzong ascended the throne, it was revealed that he was actually the thirteenth son of Prince An-yi of Pu;

thus his words were finally verified. As the Master was about to pass away, he said: "Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have perfected the land of Jetavana and manifested my body to propagate the teachings.
Now I am returning south. Having spoken these words, he entered nirvana (*śānta*). (From the *Sengbao zhuan*)

At Shangfang Temple in Longquan, Yuyao, along the Yao River, there was a monk named Shaoben. It is unknown when he lived; his sole religious practice was the dedicated recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
At that time, there was a monk from Huqiu named Xiuya who composed a song to praise his deeds. The words and meaning [of this song are as follows:]...

Brilliant and transcendent throughout all time. Although the records of Master En’s deeds have not been transmitted in formal biographies, a close examination of this song is sufficient to reveal the merit of his recitation and study.
It says in brief: “The mountain colors are deep and profound; pine smoke mists the air.
Beneath the empty forest, upon a flat-topped rock, sits a monk. With legs crossed and staff resting across his lap, he recites the White Lotus Sutra from dawn until—”
At evening, turning left and right, tiger tracks and wolf tracks—ten fragments, five pieces—strange flowers were strewn about in profusion.
Having met by chance, we had not yet come to know one another deeply; we did not know whether these were people of old or people of today.
As for this Tan Yan and this Tan Yi, it is said that even if people of the world see the Master’s form, who among them can see the Master’s mind? Even if people of the world recognize the Master...
Who among men can truly know the Master’s name? The Master is a King of Physicians who carries out the Buddha’s command; he comes to treat the maladies of the weary world.
He can cause the mad to find composure, the defiled to become pure, the heterodox to become upright, and the ordinary to become sages.

If this is so, not only should people revere him, but it is fitting that even dragons and ghosts should move with praise and song. How could those who turn their backs on awakening and align themselves with the dust of the mundane world [fail to do so]?
Without prostrating in formal greeting, I take refuge [in him].
During the Jianzhong Jinggu era, there was an ancient Chan master named Lingfeng Sǒu (The Old Man of Lingfeng). When he was thirteen years old, he heard from others...
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* until he felt as though he had returned home from a long journey. Thinking upon it, within a few months his mastery of the text became thorough.

His elder brothers said he was fit for instruction and stopped him, ordering him to read Confucian texts; however, his eyesight immediately worsened and did not recover. He then prayed to the Bodhisattva Saṃgha, and suddenly dreamed that a thunderbolt struck his eyes.
While still asleep, he cried out loudly. The crowd looked on in alarm, and his eyes were already healed. Thereupon, he sought to leave the household life and become a monk.
He tested this scripture by reciting it aloud; when he reached the title, his hair fell out. He subsequently traveled south for thirty years, during which time he ceased his recitation.

In his later years, he reflected upon it again, and upon resuming his recitation, not a single character was omitted. Furthermore, he attained a profound mastery of the scripture’s purport and realized the ancestral intent of the Patriarch who came from the West.
Moved by the Buddha’s deep kindness, he extracted the essential themes of each chapter and composed thirty-two verses. The title of the first verse is as follows:

Transcending speech and thought, it is called the Wondrous Dharma; primordially pure, it is likened to a lotus flower. The provisional teachings converge into the ultimate reality as the true skillful means, universally removing the grit from the eyes of all beings.
The final summary verse says: Where there is no speaking, the sutra is spoken; where there are no traces, the traces are transcended.

Where there is no saying, the words reveal the profound mystery. If, by chance, one strikes the essential point and opens the eye of the mind, The assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa remains as solemn as ever.
Chan Master Shi Zu’ke of Mount Lu was styled Zhengping.
He was the son of Su Bogu of Western Sichuan and the younger brother of Yangzhi. He resided at Mount Lu during the Chongning era.
Having observed his family’s scholarly tradition from childhood, he joined the Jiangxi school of poetry. Possessing profound intellect and vast talent, he did not fall short of the ancients.
One day, he was suddenly struck with deep reflection and said: "My countenance is turning toward autumn; I have been devoted solely to poetic composition.

Suddenly, as if the demon of death has come to seize me, how shall I confront this adversary? He therefore questioned a venerable elder: "Among the secret scriptures of the *Pitakas*, which is the most supreme?

The elder replied, "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is certainly to be trusted among all the sutras. He then immediately read it himself and subsequently declared: "This scripture is indeed [the one]."

[The Buddha] took [the flower]. He stopped [the old flowers], and a fragrant wind blew away the withered blossoms, raining down fresh and beautiful ones instead—this single couplet is quite in accord with the underlying intent.

[If one] were to lightly utter these words, one would immediately contract the disease of *kāmalā*; the entire body would become scorched and foul-smelling, making it impossible to approach, and only after more than thirty years would one pass away.
Therefore, within the monastic community (*saṃgha*), such a person may be designated as having leprosy. As the Sūtra says: "If one sees someone who receives and upholds this sūtra..."

This reveals his transgressions and evils: this person shall suffer from leprosy in the present life; by this one may verify that the Buddha’s words are not false (as noted in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*).
The Great Master Rizhao of Hangzhou was named Shan-sheng.
His lineage descended from the Zhong family of Qiandang. He entered the monastic order at the age of ten and mastered the Lotus Sūtra by fifteen.

At seventeen, he received the tonsure and traveled to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) for thirty years to seek the Way, where he associated with eminent scholars and realized monks; he possessed a profound understanding of Buddhist learning.

During the Tianxi era, an imperial decree was issued to the Monastic Registrar (Senglü) to commission Changjian and others to provide commentaries on the *Fayin ji* (Anthology of Dharma Sounds), an imperial composition.

The Master was selected for this task. Upon its completion, he was granted a master title and returned to his hometown. During the Kangding era, he entered Tianzhu Mountain and resided at the Rujian-an (Daily Contemplation Hermitage) of Chan Master Shixian.
He did not descend from the mountain for over ten years, reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* ten thousand times. When I arrived in Qiantang...
I encountered him in the mountains; he was robust and vigorous, his speech as it had been in the past. One day, he set down a letter saying, "My wishes are fulfilled;
I am about to depart from this world. You must bury me beneath a stupa. I pray that you, sir, will bear this in mind. Later, he indeed passed away.
I have therefore composed an inscription for him, which says: "The mountain moon stands tall—such is the Master’s mind. The mountain spring flows coolly..."
Ah, Master’s zither! Its nature remains; who can distinguish between past and present? I have recorded this briefly upon the peaks of India.
(Recorded by Fan Xingwen; found in *Shengsong Wenhai*).
Master Duan Shizi of Huzhou was named Fadan;
his secular surname was Qiu, and he was a native of Wucheng. From the time he was weaned, he abstained from meat.

Before reaching the age of twenty, he underwent the examination for the monastic precepts and shaved his head, enrolling at Jiekong Monastery on Mount Wu. Initially, he followed Jingjue of Xiangfu Temple.
The Dharma Master studied the Three Contemplations of the Tiantai and Hengzhou traditions. Later, he traveled extensively to study under various masters and attained the Dharma lineage of Huanglong.

He entered the world of teaching, moving through three successive appointments until he reached Xiyu, where he constantly let out the "lion's roar" and performed the "lion’s play," leading people to call him "Master End.
Later, he retired to Guiyun Hermitage on Mount Wu, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* day and night. He composed a poem which says: "Old age..."
In my agitation, my spirit becomes even clearer. Deep into the night, I recite the Lotus Sutra in a secluded chamber. My children and grandchildren will surely resent me when they wake up;

thus, I strike the stone slab three or four times. About a li from the mountain front lies the grave of my mother. In the early morning, I walk slowly and return after reciting one volume of the sutra.
The people of Hu lake vie with one another to request that I recite for them, yet I will only open the scroll once I have received five hundred coins.
Mushu counted the coins and took them away, distributing them to those suffering from hunger and cold. He was fond of singing the *Yufu Ci* (Songs of the Fisherman);
when the moon was bright, he would chant them until dawn. In Zhe, there was a monk named Touhou; even the scholar-officials were content with his delusions.

In Xiu, there was a mad monk called Buto who deceived the world with his sermons. The Master exposed both of them as being through and through. Yushou Lao composed the opening address for his formal installation.
The Commentary says: "Pushing over and turning back; kicking over and not relying. Before the seven-fascicle Lotus Sutra has been recited, the single cry of the Fisherman is first heard.
Upon hearing this, the Master ascended the seat and chanted: "Originally, I was but a lone fisherman of Xiao and Xiang."
From the east, from the west, from the south, and from the north, the great assembly acclaimed him as excellent. The Master said, "I observe the Dharma of the Dharma-King;
such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King," and then descended from his seat. Later, due to illness, he passed away at the age of seventy-two.
The people of Eastern Wu enshrined him as a "Scattered Sage" (Sansheng). (The Master’s recorded sayings are also found in the *Sengbao zhuan*.)
The Master Jingjiao of Mingzhou was named Ying;
he did not use the character for "upper" (shàng). He resided at Guangyan Monastery in Jiangdong, Mingzhou.

He was a disciple of the Venerable Fazhi of Yanqing, who had inherited the teachings and contemplations and reached their profound source. Therefore, people referred to him as the "Master of the Teachings" (Jiaozhu).
He once transcribed seven fascicles of the Lotus Sūtra using silver ink; for the characters representing Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he substituted gold ink.
His calligraphy was robust and forceful, almost transcending the realm of ordinary brushwork. Encased in jade rollers and lapis lazuli cases, those who beheld them were struck with awe and reverence.

The Master eventually passed away at this monastery, and his tomb and stupa still remain. Although the sūtras have endured through the passing of years, they remain intact and perfectly preserved. During the Jianyan era, the monastery...

The barbarian invaders had utterly devastated [the land], yet this sutra alone was recovered from among the ruins. During the Chunxi era, there was a Dharma Master named Falian who served as the abbot.
One night, while he was fast asleep, he suddenly heard a clamor like the voices of thousands or tens of thousands of people.

Startled awake, he saw that the abbot’s quarters and adjacent rooms were ablaze; the fire had already penetrated the roof. His sutra, however, was protected by being placed upon a small stand atop a pillar.

[The scripture] was placed above; [the monk] braved the flames to retrieve it from below, yet it remained almost entirely undamaged. Alas! That these two scriptures emerged unscathed from such fierce conflagrations is verified by this:
distantly, it is due to the merit of the Mahāyāna and the protection of devas and nāgas; proximately, it is sustained by the firm vows and conduct of the Dharma Master.
As the Buddha said: "Those who read this scripture cannot be burned by fire. This is a clear manifestation of that truth (Zongxiao personally heard Master Lian say this).

Seng Kejiu of Kaiyuan Monastery in Mingzhou was known as "Jiufahua" (Lotus Sutra Reciter Jiuzhou) because he constantly recited the Lotus Sutra. Throughout his life, he dedicated the merit of his recitations toward adorning the Pure Land with virtuous benefits.
In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away while sitting upright and composed, free from illness; three days later, [his body remained intact].

Suddenly, he revived and said, "My spirit has already traveled to the Pure Land. The features of that land are identical to the adornments described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations).
Within the lotus pedestals of the seven-jeweled ponds, the names of those destined for rebirth there are inscribed. On one pedestal made of purple-gold, it was written:
'Xun Fahua of the Guangjiao Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture, Great Song. I have already been born therein."
Furthermore, one golden tablet identified Sun Shierlang of Mingzhou; another golden tablet identified Jiu Fahua of Mingzhou;
and yet another silver tablet identified Xu Daogu of Mingzhou. Having finished speaking, he returned to his seat and departed. Five years later, [the results were realized].
The nun Xu indeed passed away while sitting in meditation. At the time of her death, a wondrous fragrance was perceived filling the room. Twelve years later, Sun Shierlang also passed away;
at that time, the sound of celestial music was heard. Such auspicious signs occurred in succession, and all people looked up to them in reverence (from the *Longshu Jingtu Wen*).
The Master of the Dharma at Fàn Monastery in Suzhou was named Jìngfàn.
A native of Jiāhé, his secular surname was Cè. His mother dreamed that light filled her chamber and she beheld a divine being resembling a Buddha;
consequently, she conceived him. When he was only ten years old, he left home to become a monk and shaved his head at Shèngguǒ Monastery under the tutelage of Zhànqián.

The second Dharma Master studied the teachings and received their transmission. Initially, he resided at Wuliangshouyuan (Infinite Life Monastery), where he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* more than ten times.

During the Daguan era, he gathered twenty-seven monks to perform the *Lotus Repentance*, dedicating twenty-eight days for each session consisting of preparatory and formal practice. He conducted three such assemblies in succession;

through his pure and diligent devotion, his spiritual resonance reached upward, and he was moved by the manifestation of Samantabhadra bestowing upon him the *karmavācanā* (the ritual of ordination). [He] called out...

The reputation of the bhikṣu Jingfan resounded like the tolling of a bell. At that time, Wang Gongdu, the Magistrate of Changzhou County, personally witnessed these events and inscribed them upon stone as a record.
Furthermore, he once dreamed of a man in yellow robes who invited him to enter the underworld. There he saw the King, who ordered the registers to be inspected.
It was found that the bhikṣu Jingfan had recited the Lotus Sūtra throughout successive kalpas; the King immediately dispatched an envoy to escort him back.
One day, while in meditative contemplation, the entire assembly saw a deity clad in golden armor kneeling before the Master.

Furthermore, during a period of repentance at another location, he was visited by the god Vaiśravaṇa, who inspected the assembly and had already identified those whose observance of the precepts was not pure;
subsequently, their repentance rituals were indeed found to be incomplete. At that time, a maidservant of Ying Gong, the Governor of Gusu, was possessed by a malevolent spirit.

He was troubled by demons and requested the Master to bestow the precepts upon him; the malevolent spirits were immediately extinguished. Lady Ge requested the Master to confer the precepts as an offering for her deceased husband;

she saw her husband circumambulate the Master three times before departing. Seeing the Master’s spiritual conduct, Jia Gong, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, appointed him as the Dharma Master for the region.
The Master maintained the precepts for over forty years. After his passing, he cremated his body, and five-colored śarīra relics were produced (*Beizhu Ji*).
Dharma Master Daoshi Ruogan of Mingwu Temple in Huzhou was a native of Shiwu Town.
His secular surname was Qian. He entered the monastic life at Jiahui Monastery, where his conduct was preeminent and the fourfold assembly held him in high esteem.
In the eighteenth year of the Xiangshu era, he once gathered one hundred thousand people to practice the Pure Land path. His...
The Exhortation Proclamation states: I, [Name], humbly reflect that birth and death are boundless and the cycle of rebirth knows no rest;

only by returning to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) can one avoid retrogression. For nearly twenty years, I have secluded myself among the mountains, where life and death are like dreams and illusions.
I have not entered cities, but have constantly studied the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, reciting them one hundred times daily, totaling six million fascicles. I vow—
Together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, they adorn the Pure Land. Those who enter the assembly each recite the Buddha’s name one hundred thousand times.
Those who first attain the Way shall successively deliver one another. When their lives end, whether earlier or later, they each hold a blue lotus flower and are reborn in the Pure Land.

One day, the Dharma Master Kōsō came to visit. After they had finished their meal together, which consisted of three flavors, he suddenly asked for a brush and wrote a verse, then sat upright and passed away.
Kōsō served as witness; it was a most extraordinary event. The cremation took place exactly at noon, when the sun was at its zenith.

Relics (śarīra) were scattered forth, their brilliance dazzling to the eye. Monastics and laypeople vied with one another to collect them, yet even the bones were no longer to be found. Alas! Such was the Master’s recitation.
It has never existed in the world before. All who have seen or heard of it do nothing but offer words of supreme praise (*Ratnagunasamcayagāthā*).

The Dharma Master Baopu of Wenzhou, the śramaṇa Qibaopu, was born into the Xu family; his ancestors were from Hengyang. From childhood, he harbored the aspiration to leave secular life and received full ordination.

At Shousheng Monastery, he was simple and dignified by nature and possessed clear discernment. Upon embarking on his travels for study, he stayed in the region of Baiyue, where he beheld the life and conduct of Chan Master Tanyi of Tiandi Mountain.
Struck with deep admiration and longing, he resolved to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* for the rest of his life.
From that time until his return home, he withdrew from worldly affairs and devoted himself single-mindedly to its proclamation and maintenance, continuing until the first year of the Zhihe era.
On the seventh day of the twelfth month, he bathed, changed his robes, and passed away while reciting the name of the Buddha.

During his lifetime, the Master would either read and chant aloud from various Mahāyāna sūtras and dhāraṇīs, or the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; he would also transcribe them with blood from his own body or prostrate before each character.
These details are all recorded in a separate collection and are not recounted here in full. At that time, many literati who visited his stupa left behind poems in praise.
Now, I have briefly transcribed three chapters; thus, a small portion of the Master’s meritorious conduct may be seen.
A poem by Zhou Kan of Yongjia says: "Flying frost and flying dew, cold sky and cold night; night after night at midnight, the ice freezes the balustrades.

The Purple Emperor and the celestial hosts join their fingers, listening as he recites the characters. As the characters reach the rising sun, Changji of Tiantai says: 'The golden lion incenses the empty void.'"
In the hall, the sound of the sutras blends with the pure tones of the *qing-shang* scale like the resonance of pines. The west wind blows, the moon sets, and the cold night stretches long.
White lotuses fill the heart with fragrance. Furthermore, a person whose name was not recorded said: "You must have personally received the prediction [of Buddhahood] at Vulture Peak;

The flavor of the *amṛta* (clarified butter) fills the field of your mind. Though the kalpa-stone of the human world must eventually crumble, It cannot destroy the lotus upon our Master’s tongue. (From the *Zhizhuang Ji*)

Dharma Master Yunqi Qingbian of Nanying was born into the Zhou clan of Qiantang. Having entered the monastic order, he specialized in the Tiantai teachings and penetrated the profound depths of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

His reputation spread far and wide; he presided over seven sites of practice, and his followers gathered like clouds. During his tenure as the abbot of Nanying, he served as the Chief Secretary (Shushi).
Jiang Yingshu presented him with a poem that said: "The Master of the Way re-expounds the Lotus Teaching; the family tradition of Fulong is excellent—listen well! The Master once remarked:
"I have observed that regarding the One Vehicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, many former sages have praised and described it, yet I have not heard of anyone who has propagated it through verses.
In the past, the Great Being Shanhui’s hymn on the *Vajracchedikā* was truly not bad. As for myself, in my youth I delved into the Six Classics."
The scholars of the hundred schools delighted in composing phrases and sentences; though I am now old and exhausted, I feel no shame in offering my words on this matter.

Accordingly, I have set forth twenty-eight chapters, each assigned a verse. Regarding the "Introduction Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta), I say: "One and many, profound and wondrous—rarely seen in years past."
Cloud shadows and flying blossoms—how wondrous their forms! Maitreya and Mañjuśrī, both eloquent in speech, have revealed that one must personally receive the ancient dignified deportment.
As the "Expedient Means" chapter says: "The heavy gates lack keys; sighing at their difficulty to enter, a master hand knocks them open until they are passed through everywhere.
Dense leaves and withered branches suddenly fall away; standing tall in its lofty character, it battles the pure wind. This verse was originally circulated in printed editions.
I have briefly recorded one or two instances for the sake of practice, so that those of like mind may look up to them with reverence.
During the Daguang era, there was a Dharma Master named Yuan Ying of Wuxing in Huzhou who transmitted the lineage of Fulong; his mastery of the doctrinal studies was vast and profound. I once...
Upon examining the master’s catalog of teachings and writings, he found that they were exceedingly numerous.

Among them was a work titled *The Collection of Miraculous Omens of the Lotus Sūtra Continuation* (*Hokke-zoku-reishū*), which had not been seen by the world. He subsequently searched for it everywhere and indeed obtained it. It consists of two fascicles;

the more than one hundred individuals recorded therein are categorized into ten sections: first, testimony by Samantabhadra; second, accomplishment of wondrous causes; third, veneration by spirits and deities.
Fourth, beasts and birds bowed in reverence; fifth, his aspirations were fulfilled; sixth, transformation Buddhas came to welcome him; seventh, he was reborn in the Pure Land;
eighth, as a karmic reward, he was born in heaven; ninth, his faculty of the tongue remained unimpaired; tenth, fragrant light manifested as an auspicious sign.

This is truly because the Buddha Vehicle is one, yet the responses it evokes accord with individual capacities. These numerous auspicious signs could not have been known by the world had it not been for the Master’s comprehensive synthesis. At the very end, the Master...
The concluding chant says: If one takes the true reality (*dharmatā*) as the *Lotus Sūtra*, then all sūtras and all practices are none other than the *Lotus Sūtra*.
If one takes rarity as a miraculous omen (*prātihārya*), then this body and all other bodies are none other than miraculous omens.
It is precisely for this reason that I have now collected these various extraordinary accounts. I pray that those who see or hear them may all obtain what a son of the Buddha ought to obtain.
Master Ya of Hangzhou:

Master Ya was a native of Qiantang. He registered his studies at Jingzhu Monastery and relied upon National Teacher Haoyue of Tiantian Temple, thereby inheriting the transmission of the Three Contemplations of the Tiantai and Jingxiu traditions.
However, he had no intention of engaging with the secular world, saying: "What is the use of pursuing empty fame? It is far better to cultivate reality."

His speech was pure but his conduct was turbid, a state censured by the sages and saints. He subsequently chose to reside at the Tianwangyuan (Heavenly King Monastery) on the Southern Mountains, dedicating himself exclusively to the practice of recitation.
Throughout his life, he read the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* five times, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* four times, and the *Amitābha Sūtra* ten times.

He performed three hundred thousand prostrations to Śākyamuni Buddha and circumambulated the True Body Stupa ten times, performing three prostrations for every single character when worshipping the *Lotus Sūtra*.
After three cycles, he had prostrated himself before Amitābha Buddha one million times and recited this Buddha’s name five million times.

At that time, the Imperial Commissioner Yang Jie, admiring his diligent cultivation, presented him with thirty stanzas of praise for the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Anle guo zan*) that he himself had composed.

The Master, wishing to guide beings without end, subsequently depicted the true likenesses of the three grades and nine ranks, accompanied by eulogistic inscriptions, which were carved upon stone at Jingzhai Monastery.
Throughout his life, he never sat with his back turned toward the west; such was the nature of his sincere devotion.

Later, he passed away while sitting upright without illness, moved by a rare fragrance that filled the room and celestial music that filled the sky. All people said it was an omen that the Western Sage had come to welcome him.
[From the *Ratnagrantha*]: Dharma Master Wò of Hangzhou, whose secular name was Wei Wò, was the son of the Jin family of Qiantang.
Having left the secular life at a young age, he applied himself diligently to the wondrous scriptures and passed the mid-level examination.

He immediately entered the stream of the Dharma. Resolving his mind in profound stillness, he shut his door and declined all worldly affairs. He recited this sutra five thousand times by oral chanting.
Beginning in the second year of the Kangding era, he commenced reading the Tripitaka; at the conclusion of each volume, he would recite the Heart Sutra five times.
When one collection was completed, the Heart Sutra had been recited five hundred times. He did this three times over the entire Great Canon. He then read the Avataṃsaka Sutra two hundred times.

Five thousand fascicles of the *Sūtra of Radiant Light*; one hundred treasuries of the *Heart Sūtra*; twenty treasuries each of the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*, and the *Great Compassion Mantra*;
three thousand fascicles each of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*; two thousand fascicles of the *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas*;
and ten million recitations of the Honored Name of Amitābha. May all these roots of goodness be dedicated with a single-minded resolve toward the adornment of the Pure Land. I pay homage.

In the autumn of the first year of the Ningyuan era, he fell ill. He formed a mudrā and passed away while seated. His age was eighty-nine. During the cremation, his teeth and rosary did not turn to ash.
Master Lingzhi Dazhi, admiring the Master’s virtue, inscribed this: "I have observed throughout the three dynasties that eminent monks were devoted solely to meditation and the recitation of sutras.
That they manifest such extraordinary signs at the moment of death—is this not because their spirits are merged with the void and stillness, and their vision is fixed upon the sacred realm?"
This is what one relies upon. As for the essential gateway to liberation, nothing precedes this. An ancient worthy said:

"If one serves the Buddha through the ten categories of monastic affairs without [this practice], one merely wastes a hundred years. I address those who have come to study: can you not resolve to emulate them? (*Baozhu ji*)
The Master Yi of Yuyao was a man of extraordinary character.
He was born into the Du family of the Yao River. He renounced the secular life at Longquan Temple. During the Huangyou era, he received full ordination through the "Universal Grace" (Puen) ceremony.
He studied the Tiantai teachings in the Two Zhe regions. Once his studies were complete, he returned to his former residence, where some [disciples] requested him to serve as the abbot.

He urged them [to remain], but they all resolutely refused to comply. In his later years, he closed his quarters and severed ties with worldly affairs, devoting himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.

He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* five thousand times and the *Sūtra of Universal Worthy’s Contemplation* and the *Amitābha Sūtra* ten thousand scrolls; the number of times he invoked the Buddha’s name is beyond calculation.
In the first year of the Chongning era, he suddenly fell ill. Summoning his disciples, he burned incense and declared, "The time for my birth in the Pure Land has arrived."
"Indeed. You shall mount a vajra-pedestal and follow the Buddha westward. I pray that you exert yourself in cultivation; then we may meet again.

Having spoken these words, he formed the mudrā of the Buddha with his hands and sat down, passing away peacefully. Upon cremation, his tongue and rosary were found uncorrupted, causing all who saw them to revere and marvel at him (from the *Ji-zhi-yuan ji*).
The Venerable Sengsichong of Qiantang was a native of Qiantang.
At the age of fifteen, his parents wished to arrange a marriage for him, but the Master deeply loathed the prison of the household life.
He immediately fled to Lingyin Mountain in India (Tianzhu) and entered the monastic order at Fajian Temple. He resolved to practice with diligent austerity;

every day he left the city to solicit offerings for the monks, and at night he did not sleep, devoting himself exclusively to reciting the Lotus Sūtra. When he reached the age of twenty, he took the sūtra with him to the examination and was immediately selected among the monks.
From then on, he daily maintained the two divisions [of the Vinaya], while at other times he would chant the Buddha’s name. Some call him—

A disciple said, "Reciting the sutras is sufficient; why must you also invoke the Buddha? The Master replied, "If one wishes to be reborn in that land at the end of life, how can one not fix one's mindfulness upon it?

One day, he was afflicted by a wind-illness and said, "Last night I already saw the assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all saying they have come together to welcome and guide me. In two days, I shall depart. His disciple Zu’an said:
"I fear this may be a demonic realm; you must not follow it on your own.

The Master said, "When my life comes to an end, if a lotus flower grows from within my chest, that shall be the sign of my departure for the Pure Land. Two days later, at dawn, he ordered An to strike the sounding gong and said:
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas had already filled the void. The assembly together praised the Buddha when he suddenly passed away.
Upon examining his body, it was entirely cold, except for a palm-sized area on his chest which remained warm and supple, appearing like a blooming lotus flower.
Thus, it truly accorded with what had been prophesied (from the *Ratnaguhya-saṃgraha*).
Dharma Master Zhào of Xiuzhou was a native of Dongyang. From birth, he was exceptionally distinguished; his aspiration was to become a monk.

Since entering the Gate of Emptiness, he never lay down to sleep, reciting and chanting day and night. In less than a month, he had mastered both the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prabhūtaratna Sūtra*. At the age of... [text fragment ends]

Having passed the age of twenty, he passed the state examination on the scriptures and was ordained. Since then, he has carried his books to the monastic academies, where he fully mastered the Way of the Three Contemplations of the Tiantai school.
He successively presided over famous monasteries, until in his later years he settled at Chaoguo Monastery in Huating.

During the Yuanfeng era, he gathered more than twenty thousand people to form a religious community (*shè*), emulating the spirit of Donglin and admiring the teachings of the Western Paradise. He once dreamed of Amitābha and the two other holy ones. Master... [text ends]
Kneeling, he asked: "I have spent my life reciting the sutras, hoping to be reborn in the Pure Land. Will this wish be fulfilled? Guanyin pointed and said: "The Pure Land is not far;
