if you have the vow, you shall be reborn there. Do not doubt it further. Again, while reciting the sutra during a quiet night, he saw Samantabhadra in a dream.
Thereupon, he resolved to create an image of the Bodhisattva and vowed to recite ten thousand copies of the Lotus Sutra as an act of adornment.
His karmic retribution was pure. He recited other scriptures beyond count. Suddenly falling ill, he said to the assembly, "In my illness, I have seen extraordinary signs;
the time for the Pure Land is certain. He then passed away with his feet crossed. Upon cremation, his tongue remained unburnt.
It was supple and moist as if alive. The śarīra relics streamed forth, alternating between red and white; can this not be said to have been sustained by the power of diligent exertion?
(From the *Zhīyuán jí*)
Dharma Master Zhan of Wuzhen was surnamed Jiao and named Weizhan.
His family had been natives of Yongjia for generations. His mother dreamed one night that she had swallowed a precious stupa and subsequently conceived him.

In his youth, he left the secular world and devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*. He received ordination through formal examination and studied under Master Qin of Dongling and Master Hui.
Gong Jueyu and Gong Puci were both rigorous and meticulous in their practice, fully attaining the profound mysteries [of the teachings].

During the Jianyan era, they preached the Dharma at Shousheng Monastery and composed records such as the *Guangming ji* and the *Huguo ji*. Whenever they performed Buddhist rites, miraculous responses invariably occurred.

They recited one volume of the *Lotus Sūtra* daily and chanted the Buddha’s name twenty thousand times. On ordinary days they slept little; whenever it reached the twilight hours during the height of summer, they would...
He sat upright with his fan resting against the edge of the grass, reciting the Lotus Sūtra and giving food to mosquitoes and gnats.

His disciples, seeing that their teacher was advanced in years, requested that he cease this ascetic practice. The Master said, "How can these wriggling creatures possibly create for themselves the superior karmic conditions of the Lotus Sūtra?"
He caused those who had bitten him to plant the seeds of the Mahāyāna, vowing that they might attain liberation in every lifetime.

Later, he retired to a mountain hermitage and for several years diligently cultivated pure practices. One day, he fell ill; sitting upright with solemn composure, he passed away. Wherever the smoke from his cremation reached, there were śarīra relics.
When members of the gentry and commoners requested them, they all obtained what they wished for. Duan Shizi once studied under this master. There was...

He wept for him in verse, saying: "What cause has this mountain monk for such sorrow? It is because I remember my virtuous friend in the woods. The ten thousand scrolls of the Lotus Sūtra remain incomplete;
Yet, with conditions ripened throughout the ten directions, he has already manifested his divided bodies. Before the courtyard’s ancient tree, yellow leaves drift down;
Beyond the clouds, the moonlight fills the sky with its pale orb. If you ask where my master has gone, His spirit has already taken rest within the boundless realms."
(*Ratnasaṃcaya*). Dharma Master Mingzhi of Mingzhou, whose posthumous name was Zhongli, was the son of the Chen family of Ning.
His mother dreamed that a solar disc pierced her breast before he was born; from his early childhood, he was extraordinary.
[He was] extraordinary. He was subsequently ordained as a monk. At the age of nine, his teacher gave him the *Lotus Sūtra*; upon reading it once, he attained a profound spiritual realization.

During the Jiayou era, he passed the examination at the Kaifeng Prefecture and received full ordination. He followed the teachings of Guangzhi of Yanqing Monastery in his native district, serving him diligently and receiving the Way;

can one not say that the depth of his realization was great? Later, he was invited to reside at this temple, where he remained for ten years from beginning to end, extensively opening the dharma seat for instruction.
Every year, he selected his disciples to perform the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* repentance ritual. One day, while in meditative contemplation, he suddenly beheld a great boat;
though the assembly wished to board it, they could not, yet the Master alone traveled back and forth within it. From that time on, his wisdom and understanding gushed forth like a spring.

He lectured on the *Fahua xuanyi*, the *Fahua wenju*, and the *Mohe zhiguan* each several dozen times. In his daily life, he appeared as if unable to speak, yet when lecturing, his eloquence was powerful and resolute, such that all who heard him were moved.
He forgot his fatigue. Throughout his life, he recited the Lotus Sūtra ten thousand times; other aspects of his spiritual practice are not easily recorded in full.

Once, while suffering from illness, he twice smelled a wondrous fragrance. He then summoned all his disciples and said, "Each of you should advance in your cultivation so that we may meet again within the assemblies of the Buddhas.
Having spoken, he sat facing west and passed away. Chao Shuo-zhi, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, composed a stele inscription to commemorate his virtue.
This is truly a literary treasure of the Fourfold Clarification (Sishiming).
The Dharma Master Wufei of Mingzhou was named Faqiu;
his secular surname was Zheng, and he was a native of Yaojiang. He entered the monastic life at Longquan Temple at the age of seven during the Zhenghe era.
The *Zhongzhong Lianjing* (Middle-of-the-Middle Lotus Sutra), Volume [Number]. At the age of fifty, he shaved his head and passed away at Mount Qingxiu in Ming.

The Master’s demeanor was elegant and refined, and his wisdom surpassed that of others. He remained indifferent to joy or anger toward all things; his speech and laughter brought forth the spirit of spring.

Initially, he studied under the guidance of Zhiyong at Guangyan Monastery; subsequently, he traveled extensively to seek instruction at the gate of Huijiao at Sutai. Thus he diligently pursued his studies.

Ren, undaunted by cold or heat, fully attained the subtle, untransmitted essence of the Tiantai school. Continuing his travels among the clouds and waters, he visited Dahui at Shuangjing Mountain and received profound certification of his realization.
Before long, his own school urged him to emerge from seclusion for the sake of others;

he resided at Qingxiu Monastery for seven years, establishing a lecture hall and attracting a vast assembly of disciples. The master and his followers were harmonious and dignified, truly embodying the refined atmosphere of the ancient monastic groves.
On the mountain is Lion Rock (*Siṃha-śilā*), where he constructed a chamber of fearlessness and dwelt therein.
He constantly recited ten sutras; of the *Lotus Sūtra* alone, he completed twenty thousand recitations. Its secluded and profound realm was said to be a place no one could reach.
Master Xuexi Hiyuan once lamented him in verse: "The silken shrine flickers as the incense smoke fades; The seven fascicles of the Lotus Sūtra rest upon his tongue."

The limbs of this withered-wood body rest cold upon the window-sill; the sound of flowing springs falling strikes the teeth with chill. Through both peril and ease, his integrity remained unchanging until the end;

yet even for the three robes worn during the fasts of the伏 (fú) and 臘 (là) months, he alone found it difficult to maintain. He still harbored regret that from this point forward, the "ox-horn" branch [of the lineage] had begun its decline, and that the torrential flow of eloquence from his mouth in discussing the profound mysteries would no longer surge forth.

At that time, there was He Gui of the Ministry of Personnel, who, out of respect for the Master’s reputation as a teacher, formed a friendship beyond the mundane world with him. Once, when [He Gui] was ill...

On the anniversary of the Master’s death, [the author] ordered the Master to ascend the seat and recite the Lotus Sūtra. Moved by his sincere devotion, [the author] composed the "Record of the Ichijō Hermitage" to commemorate the Master’s virtues.

The Venerable Master Zhao of Hangzhou,名思照 (Sīzhào), was a native of Qiantang. After becoming a monk, he traveled extensively through monastic academies to investigate the teachings of the Chan school.

Once his understanding had gained renown, he immediately established a regimen of practice. Every night at the fourth watch, he would rise to cultivate pure karma by reciting the names of the Buddhas without weariness.
Upon hearing the voice of his master, the Bhikṣu Dài could not rest in peace. In the past, the Bhikṣu Dharmakara made forty-eight vows;
the Master likewise emulated him. He then held the incense burner and declared: "The Buddhas of the past did not thwart the vows of the Buddhas of the present;
how could the Buddhas of the present contravene the vows of the Buddhas of the past? His self-confidence was such as this. He once drew blood to transcribe one fascicle of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

He performed one prostration for each character, continuing until he had completed ten recitations. In this manner, he eventually paid homage to over two hundred and seventy volumes of scriptures, including the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
He read the *Lotus Sūtra* one thousand times and the *Amitābha Sūtra* five thousand times.
Furthermore, for nearly thirty years, he exhorted both monastics and laypeople to form assemblies for the practice of mindfulness and pure karma. One day, he experienced a spiritual inspiration.
He fell ill. One night he dreamed of a sixteen-foot golden body. From then on, every day he took turns inviting seven monks to assist him in completing ten recitations of the Buddha’s name.

When the seven days were complete, he leaped up, joined his palms, and together with the assembly, called upon the Buddha’s name in a resonant voice. After a long while, he counted his fingers and made a mudrā, then suddenly passed away while seated.
During the cremation, his teeth and his rosary remained unburnt, a sight witnessed by all; it was certainly not a matter of flattery or fabrication. (From *Baozhu*)
[Collected].
In the early years of the Xiangxing era, there was the Venerable Nan of Hengzhou. A monk named Zunan resided at Falun Temple in his native commandery; from the time of his tonsure, he...

He devoted himself exclusively to ascetic practices. He transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* more than ten times, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred fascicles, and the *Amitābha Sūtra* fifty thousand fascicles.
He continued such transcription for twenty-seven years, remaining constant from beginning to end. He constantly kept Amitābha in mind, vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land.
In his later years, his blood was exhausted and his body withered; yet, though he was without illness, he was still able to walk and sit. One—
He went to visit the Abbot one day. Upon meeting, neither spoke a word; suddenly, he sat upright with eyes closed and passed away.
Examining his intent, it appears he wished for the Abbot to certify his final affairs. During the cremation, five-colored śarīra relics welled up from between his eyebrows in countless numbers.
Monastics and laypeople requested them, and all obtained as much as they desired. How great! This son of the Buddha has exerted such arduous effort that he now rivals Maudgalyāyana.
Ancient and rare was his peer. At the moment of his passing while seated in meditation, how could he not have returned to the Western Paradise? (From the *Baizhu ji*).
The Great Master Qing of Mingzhou resided at Guangfu Monastery in the city.
His monastic name was Keqing; his secular surname was Yang, and he was a native of Ningbo. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and mastered the recitation of the scriptures.
Fahua. At twenty-two, he underwent tonsure according to the *Caijing*. His master possessed a spirit and skeletal frame that rose with clarity;

his aspirations were beyond the common. He maintained dignified deportment and was prudent in speech. He recited Buddhist scriptures daily with a constant routine. In his leisure time, he perused secular classics.

He was skilled in poetic composition and adept at the "cursive saint" (caosheng) script. In his later years, he abandoned these for a day, diligently cultivating pure practices (*śukla-karman*). He read through the entire Tripitaka once.
For nine years he practiced the Lotus Repentance, remaining constantly within it whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining; thus he perceived no faults or afflictions in the world.
One day, falling ill, he summoned his disciples and said: "My great task is about to conclude; you should practice the Way with diligent application."
"Do not disregard my words. Throughout my life, I have never violated the precepts in my spiritual cultivation. If I have truly attained the Way, there will surely be a marvel at my death.
After several days, suddenly a single stalk of *zhicao* (mushroom) grew from the top of the bed’s leg; it was white in color and its patterns resembled a lotus flower.
Seeing this, the Master said, "This has appeared while I am still alive; the time for my departure has arrived. He then wrote a verse:

There were no scriptures to be recited and no Buddha to be contemplated. Today, as he was about to depart, he called upon everyone to bear witness. He set down his writing brush, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away.
The people of the commandery came to receive his feet and gaze upon him; even the Governor, Imperial Censor Qin Gong, inclined his heart and desired to see him.

He then dug into the earth and offered flowers to the image above. Upon seeing that the soil was dry yet the flowers were lush and their stems and trunks possessed extraordinary forms, he marveled for a long time.
He presented incense as an offering and returned home. An ancient worthy once praised him, saying:

"Having read through the entire Tripitaka, and having practiced repentance and cultivation for nine years, he has already realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra; white lotuses have truly grown upon level ground. This was indeed during the Shaoxing era.
This is the sixteenth year. The monastery has a record of these events, and the flowers still remain. I now transmit and transcribe them together.
Dharma-transmitting monk Yanshi, abbot of the Raoyi Chan Monastery at Shimen in Siming, Mingzhou, left secular life in his youth and recited [the scriptures].

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: having passed the examination at the age of twenty, he received imperial grace and entered the monastic order. From that time on, for sixty years, he never forgot it in thought or speech.

While staying yesterday as the head monk (*śrāmaṇera*) in the quarters of Tiantai Monastery in Shaoxing, on the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month of the fifth year of the Qiandao era, a strange flower suddenly grew from the seam of a bamboo mat beneath his desk. It was bluish-white in color and had two petals.
The slender stalk closely resembled a lotus flower; it grew daily more flourishing until it reached a height of about one foot.

When it was removed, on the fourteenth day of the sixth month, another branch emerged, also with two leaves and measuring four inches in length. This auspicious omen was extraordinary, and its beauty spread widely throughout the world.

In the commandery, there was a Vice Governor of Wukang named Zeng Xun, who was fond of the arts and held the Way in high esteem. He recounted the original circumstances of this event and had them carved into woodblocks for printing.
This work, consisting of only three thousand fascicles, is now being recorded once again, in the hope that it may endure and not perish.
Dharma Master Chengzhao of Mingzhou was of the Chen clan from Cixi;
his secular name was Juexian. "Chengzhao" was the honorific title bestowed upon him. He was naturally gifted from birth.
Rui left Sushu at Jingjin Monastery. There, his teacher bestowed upon him the Lotus Sūtra; he read it once and mastered it by heart.

After donning the black robes of ordination, he first entered the quarters of Mingzhi at Yanqing Monastery, and subsequently ascended to the gate of Huijue at Tiantai Zhizhe Monastery. Through earnest inquiry and close reflection, there was no aspect of the teachings and contemplations of this single school that he did not penetrate and understand.
When the assembly requested him to reside at Baolin Monastery, he lectured on the three great commentaries of the Lotus Sūtra in continuous succession.

He lectured and expounded the teachings, bestowing the Way without a single idle day. During the spring of the Jingkang era, there was a great drought; the Master preached the sutras before the Dragon King and the heavens, and immediately a rain fell for three days.
Within a hundred *li*, all rejoiced. Both monastics and laypeople, moved by his spiritual wonders, erected a "Banner of Radiance" (*Prabhāsa-dhvaja*) to serve as a permanent marker of his presence.
He subsequently moved to the Dharma seat at Yanqing Temple, where he propagated the ancestral teachings; the doorways were filled with visitors. In the eighth year of the Shaoxing era...

In his later years, he retired to Pao-lin Monastery, resolving to spend the remainder of his life there. Beyond his outward guidance of disciples, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was his sole essential practice;

he never failed in his daily recitations, eventually completing ten thousand recitations in total. He constructed a chamber deep within the abbot’s quarters, naming it the "Hall of the Wondrous Lotus" (*Miaolian Tang*), where he dwelt alone.
This was his only concern. His aspiration was set upon returning to the West; he maintained the four recitations of the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

Seventeenth, regarding the treasury of the three pure mental actions (*citta-śuddha-karma*), one may say he was single-mindedly focused. Later, he suffered a slight illness; while preaching the Dharma for the assembly, he passed away peacefully.
Liánbù composed a stele commemorating his virtues, which states: "On the day Master [Yì] presided over Yánqìng Temple, Master Rìyuètáng first arrived to study under him.
The Master recognized him as a vessel of jade-like quality (*húlǎn*) and immediately said to him: 'You shall surely reside on this mountain. Later, it indeed came to pass."
This accords with his words. As Yuet-tang was about to pass away, he told his disciples: "The stupa of the old master Cheng-zhao lies amidst the weeds of Bao-lin.
People often hear the sound of him reciting the Lotus Sūtra during the deep stillness of the night; this matter is particularly extraordinary."
"Moreover, since the Master dwelt on this mountain and upheld the teachings with great vigor, after my passing you should build a separate stupa at the ancestral mound to relocate his remains there.
When [the disciples] went to request and welcome [the relics], they saw that the Master’s sacred bones were bound by a single cord,
their color like that of bronze.
The Dharma Master Yuet Tang of Mingzhou was named Huixun;
his monastic title was Yuet Tang. His secular surname was Chen, and his ancestors were originally from Yongjia.
His grandfather resided on Mount Qushan in Mingzhou. His mother once dreamed that a monk came to her home to solicit alms, and subsequently she conceived. When he was still a child...
At the age of seven (*zhāo*), his deportment was exceptionally outstanding; consequently, he left secular life to follow the teachings of Śākyamuni and enrolled at the Zuoyin Monastery.

His master taught him the *Lotus Sūtra*, and after ascending to the reading desk just a few times, he could recite it from memory. This astonished everyone who accompanied him. After donning the black robes of a monk, he returned to visit his relatives. His grandmother admonished him, saying:

"Now that you have left the household life, you should conduct yourself as a monk like my disciple Zhong of Wenzhou. You must not harbor attachment to your parents' home when there is no business there.
Receiving this instruction from his teacher, he resolved his will upon study. Initially, he stayed at the Dharma seat of Chengzhao at Yanqing Temple.

Upon seeing him once, the Master recognized his potential. At that time, Cao’an resided as the First Seat; the Master approached him from the north to seek instruction, exhaustively mastering the essentials of his teachings.

Desiring further to seek out diverse insights, he traveled extensively throughout the two provinces of Zhejiang before returning home. There, he encountered Master Yuanbian, who was presiding over Nanhu and expounding the fundamental tenets.

The Master’s intellectual understanding was exceptionally sharp; he attained realization upon meeting him face-to-face. Toward the end of the Xiangxing era, he passed the selection and took up residence at a monastery.

He held [the office] and was successively transferred four times until he reached Yanqing Temple. Upon that towering Dharma-seat, surrounded by a dense assembly of ten thousand fingers, people regarded his unrestrained eloquence in proclaiming the teachings as being equal to that of Pūrṇa;
how could this not be so? Although the Master engaged with sentient beings through external conditions, his internal practice became even more diligent.
He made it a constant routine to recite the seven fascicles of the Lotus Sūtra daily; even during extreme cold or intense heat, or when suffering from illness, he never slackened.

Ten years have passed since he arrived here. His conduct and speech were both perfectly fulfilled. One day, he fell ill; his complexion indicated that his departure was imminent. His disciples requested him to preach the Dharma.
The Master said, "How can there be any preaching of the Dharma? He then asked for a brush and wrote a verse to inform the assembly.

Suddenly, he recited the Buddha’s name and formed the two-knotted Amitābha mudrā. Sitting in the full lotus posture, he passed away. His final instruction was to follow the five-Indic Buddhist rites for cremation. Thus it was done.
His bones were divided into two parts: one was enshrined at his own burial mound on Mount Qun, and the other was placed in a stupa at Zu Yuan in the southern city.

Those who deliberated on the matter noted that while all the patriarchs had been buried with their bodies intact, [the Master] had instead shaved the hair from his crown to manifest his resolve. Although nearly a year had passed and he had not yet gone there, a student happened to arrive;
upon opening the hair for veneration, they suddenly beheld śarīra filling their cupped hands, their radiance shimmering and brilliant. This is recorded as follows:
Lord Lu Yuan, the Provincial Commissioner, composed a eulogy for him; here, its essential points are summarized as follows:
In Hefa Flower of Mingzhou and Guangji of Song Fenhua, there was a monk named Fahuo. Born into the Jiang clan, he left the secular life in his youth and cultivated his innate nature.

He was simple and unassuming, wearing a coarse cotton robe upon his body; he possessed a dignified air reminiscent of the ancients. He constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, never ceasing from morning until evening;

for this reason, people called him by the name "Fa-hua" (Lotus). In the monastery, there was a lecturer-monk whom he could rely upon. One day, he adjusted his robes and asked about the matter of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja’s self-immolation.
The Master did not fully grasp the disciple's underlying intention, so he immediately expounded for him the purport of the true Dharma-offering.
Hewen heard these words and departed with great joy. It was the twenty-fourth night of the Shangyuan festival;

at that moment, in the northeastern corner of the central courtyard, a massive fire reached the heavens. The entire assembly rushed forward to extinguish it, but suddenly they beheld the Master sitting cross-legged within the flames with palms joined, his lips moving as he softly recited a scripture.
Before him were arranged incense, lamps, and offerings of lotus flowers and sutras, along with a verse on parting from this world.
The Vow Text. The verse says: "Rapidly fitting out a boat upon swift waters, one reaches the shore where the current no longer flows. The remaining snow has vanished with the red flames;
with body purified, I walk before the Sage. The brief summary of the vow text states: "May the Dharma-teacher burn this illusory body to become priceless incense.
First, may it be offered to the Triple Gem of the Ten Directions and the Supreme Vehicle of the Wondrous Dharma; next, may it be offered to the Eight Classes of Devas and Dragons. First...
"May the two Sages turn their divine carriages back to restore the state and the altars of Heaven and Earth.

Only then shall I vow to appear again in the world to constantly expound the Mahāyāna and broadly deliver all classes of beings. As he spoke, the flames rose high, and amidst them, five-colored lights shone vividly in the sky.
That night, the wind ceased and the sky cleared. Suddenly, there was heard a sound like a piercing crack or a thunderclap, accompanied by a rare and fragrant incense-like aroma.
The following day, when the Master’s remains were being collected outside his quarters, four faithful female devotees hurried to the site of the cremation.

They saw that the remaining ashes were surging and moving; as they brushed them aside to investigate, they happened to find more than twenty *śarīra* relics. The assembly then crowded around to witness them.

His bone-relics were piled up in large quantities. From that point on, his fame spread far and wide; those who requested them became ever more numerous, and his manifestations became increasingly frequent.

Eventually, the bones and ashes were completely exhausted. Someone obtained one of his teeth and stored it in a casket; a wealthy man, desiring it with great devotion, offered thirty thousand coins for it.
His profound reverence for others was consistently like this. At the entrance of the monastery, he established a stupa to enshrine [the relics].
A sign was posted. Consequently, the fourfold assembly came in a continuous stream to pay their respects and offer worship, gathering like swarms of bees or crawling ants.
At that time, those performing prostrations before the True Body on Mount Yujǐ were obstructed; they immediately raised a false accusation regarding the matter.
Governor Gōng Shàobǎo, whose administration was stern and resolute, had the presiding monk arrested and imprisoned him. After several days, when the case was presented for judgment, suddenly—
A fly alighted upon the tip of his writing brush; its cry was one of piteous weeping. Though he drove it away, it returned again and again.

The Master realized that the one who had cast off his body was responding through spiritual resonance, so he set down his brush to release it. This was the year of Jiayin, the fourth year of the Xiangxing era.

As there was no stele or record for the temple, Zongxiao inquired among the senior monks of the monastery, who were still living and had personally witnessed and heard the event. Thus, he was able to compile this account, hoping it might supplement future records.
According to the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha):

Mingzhou’s monk Yunzuo, who assisted in the propagation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, entered the monastic order at Haihui Monastery in Yin. He had long maintained the *Lotus Sūtra* and attained ordination through the state-sponsored examination. From that time on...
This man was a student of the Tiantai school. Although he had traveled back and forth across mountains and rivers for many years, he never abandoned his religious practice.

In his later years, he returned to Yanqing Temple, where for over forty years he remained in quiet chambers along the corridors, reciting the scriptures with a clear and resonant voice. He made it his daily routine to study the four Buddhist canons.
Even when he reached his eighties and fell ill, he did not become emaciated or distressed; instead, he simply requested hot water to bathe and changed his robes to ensure they were neat and orderly.

Regarding Mingzhi of Yue-lin Temple in Mingzhou:
the Chongning Pavilion at Zongfu Temple in Yue-lin, Fenghua, was bestowed by imperial decree as the place where the true portrait of Master Pūbagu (Buddhabhadra) was enshrined.
In the thirty-first year of the Shaoxing era, it was lost and completely destroyed; however, [the remains] were recovered from among the rubble.
This single volume of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* has not suffered the loss of even a hair’s breadth; it is truly the miraculous manifestation of the gateway to the Dharma.
At that time, the Dharma Master Huixun of Yuemang composed a poem in praise of it, saying: "Jade rollers and golden script arise from the Brahma palace;

Truly, one knows these wondrous verses are difficult to equal. Layer upon layer of pavilions follow the smoke and ink; A single volume of the Lotus Sutra emerges from the fiery red. Incense bears up auspicious light..."
*The Mirror of Divided Jewels*: "The moon holds its true color, casting light upon the cold void. Alas, in this age of the Dharma’s decline, people are arrogant;
thus, the merit of Kāśyapa Mātanga’s pioneering work is once again revealed. One version states: Formerly, at Jingyin Chan Monastery in Quanzhou, a precious pavilion was destroyed by fire.

Amidst the remaining ashes and embers, only a single copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* remained, solemn and as it had been before. Among the fourfold assembly, there were none who did not look up in awe and praise the Buddha-Dharma.
Shengong. Zeng Chaofeng composed this poem. However, the people of these two places are far apart, and there is no way to verify the facts.

Regarding the verse by Master Jian of Mingzhou:

At the end of the Shaoxing era, in the quarters of Venerable Yun, the *karmadāna* of Dongsi Temple in Cixi, Mingzhou, there was a mountain boy named Hongzhi who had entered the monastic life at the age of seven.
The Master disciplined him with measured rigor; he recited the Lotus Sūtra to completion and would often circumambulate the Samantabhadra Hall during the stillness of night.
He recited it; his voice was refined and elegant, and those who heard it marveled at it. In the temple, there was the Master Xue’an, Venerable Jian, who presented him with a poem that said:
"Stately and refined, the mountain boy’s disposition is naturally at ease; He knows not that body and world are mutually entangled. At times he stirs azure incense-seals beneath the window;
Constantly he grasps the flavor of blue lotuses upon his tongue. The lake moon flies in, the cloud-roofed hall grows cold; Pine winds blow—"
The moss-covered bed is cold; at this time, the sound of the flowing water is melancholy and plaintive. Tilting one's ear, the celestial beings fear the night will end.
During the Yuanyou era, there was one named Quan Fahua at Cifuyuan in Mingzhou who had recited the scriptures for thirty years. Because of his [recitation of] the *Baoen*...
In total, there were fifteen thousand [volumes]. In his daily life, he dwelt in a solitary room; leaning on his armrest, he sat with a prayer bead rosary in hand and sincere recitation in mind.
Though it was bustling outside his door, he remained unmoved. He did this by day and did this by night, without the slightest trace of indolence.
The Master had a disciple named Fanrong, who traveled to the Capital to study. At that time, the Head Registrar of the Left Street...
Chan Master Jingzhao Daozhen resided at Jinyin Li Temple in Shifang. Having heard of the Master’s virtue, he composed a poem to send him.

Upon seeing it, the court nobles were filled with admiration and congratulations, which filled their scrolls. Xu Yun, a Left Court Attendant and Assistant Registrar of the Court of Judicial Review, composed a preface.

It was carved into stone within the monastery; six stanzas are now recorded here to briefly transmit the Master’s virtue. The Monastic Registrar says: "How many times has [the Dharma]... (text fragment ends).
The wooden axis has snapped and the leather bindings have frayed; yet his recitation from the heart grows ever firmer with age. Hearing this account, I am doubly inspired to exert myself;
may his tongue be like a single red lotus. Thus spoke Li Zhichun, Court Consultant of the Left and Minister of the Department of Water Conservancy.
Leaving the village to become a monk, you untied the door-bolt and compiled this collection. You have maintained the wondrous Dharma with such purity that it has grown ever firmer over time.
With body and mind so pure, what could possibly compare? Like the jade-well lotus atop Mount Dahua. Lin Shao, Grand Master of the Left, Court Gentleman of the Ministry of Revenue, said:
Leaning on his armrest in serene stillness, he recites this precious compilation; as True Suchness remains unmoving, his mind is steadfast. At dawn, he reads several scrolls.
"Merely to shield my eyes; I long to face the lotuses within the community of Mount Kuanglu. Mo Junchen, the Left Chao-san-taifu, Shangshu Xingbu Langzhong, says:
'The great causal connection has been recited through seven volumes; by the incense burner, the old resolve remains firm.
May you, Master, attain realization and purity of body; I wish to emulate those of old in praising the azure lotus. Left Chaofenglang, serving as Secretary..."
The provincial governor, Huang Tingjian, wrote: "Concentrating the mind and upholding the sutras until the kalpa’s ashes are spent, A wondrous lotus blooms in every corner of the human world.
In years to come, when you have recited three thousand volumes, You shall seek out that single phrase from Caoxi. (Twenty poems are recorded on the stone inscription.)

Zhiqin, a monk from Mingzhou who was devoted to the Lotus Sutra, was born into the secular surname Xue. He was a native of Wanling in Yinqian County. Having left home to become a monk at the age of seven, he resided at Qixinsi Temple.

There he received the *Lotus Sutra* from his teacher and vowed to recite it from memory. At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, when the imperial court held an examination for the selection of monks, he passed and was ordained as a monk.

From that time on, he studied the teachings and the Vinaya extensively to awaken his fundamental mind. Subsequently, he returned to his former place of seclusion, closing his door in a single room and severing all ties to fame and profit.

He made it his rule to recite one fascicle daily. At that time, a group was gathering at the eastern part of the city to chant and study this sutra, and they requested the Master to serve as their instructor.
Reluctantly, the Master took charge of them; this community was known as the Tanhua Society (Society of Dharma Flowers), which continues to this day.
These [teachings] still survive today. In his later years, he redoubled his efforts in practice, expounding the two *Vidyādhara-piṭakas* twice daily, or sometimes even thrice.

The Master served in ten official capacities, never failing in his duties as a lecturer and upholder of the Dharma. At that time, Chan and lecture traditions were prevalent; consequently, his fame spread far and wide. His collected poems number thirty volumes, which was itself a great cultural achievement of the era.
His disciple Famo still preserves the Master’s original manuscripts; I have now extracted their essentials here, hoping they may be transmitted to posterity.
Chan Master Cangzhou Huipu first sang: "A blue lotus upon the tongue emits a wondrous fragrance; Having accomplished ten thousand scrolls, they may be extolled.
Never resting in sleep, ever diligent— This one is truly a pillar among monks.
Chan Master Luoyue said: "By the sutra-curtains all day long, facing incense in the burner; The clear sound of flowing water naturally rises and falls. If one possesses the Way, one should only..."
A monk was born in an interval between eras. It was not only during the Qi and Liang dynasties that eminent monks appeared. Master Huiyun said: "In the secret chamber, the lotus fragrance wafts afar;

the great matter of the three turnings is widely proclaimed. Beneath the thatched hut lies a pillar that supports the heavens; the great mansion and lofty hall have empty rafters and beams. Master Zhixin said:
"Having read extensively from the Indian scriptures, he is fully saturated with their fragrance; his tongue rolls forth the ocean-sound, proclaiming it everywhere."
The magpie’s cauldron harbors its intent to perfume the mundane with purity; the swallow’s mud no longer defiles the carved beams.

The monk Daochun of Huideng Monastery in Mingzhou, whose secular surname was Wang, entered the Way during the Zhenghe era and continued until the Jianyan period. He was a devoted practitioner of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

When bandits and rebels entered the borders, they slaughtered and harmed the common people beyond counting. Upon witnessing this, Master Shi felt profound compassion; he reflected that only the Buddha-dharma could deliver them to salvation.
Consequently, he resolved his great mind upon the exclusive recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*. For barely twenty years, he completed fourteen thousand fascicles;
this total does not include the volumes he had previously memorized and practiced. When he reached the age of seventy, he prepared a vegetarian feast to celebrate [his achievement].
Confession. Next, I obtained the preface composed by Chan Master Ruanshan Xun, a portion of which reads:

"Since our nation was beset by the calamity of the rising flames of war and the people suffered the misery of being submerged in the mire, I have been moved to stir my sincere heart and cultivate pure deeds with increased diligence.

I uphold the secret edicts of the One Vehicle and emulate the lingering spirit of tireless and earnest exertion. The incense smoke never ceases before the bright window, and the palm-leaf scriptures [are read]..."
A long mat is spread upon a clean desk; as spring and autumn pass before one’s eyes, how many times do leaves fall and flowers turn crimson?
Regarding all things with an empty mind, ten thousand realms are like flowing water and dispersing clouds. Beholding the Dragon Maiden attaining Buddhahood, one realizes that form is not the reality;

admiring the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja who offered his arms, one vows to sacrifice the body. Bathed thrice and perfumed thrice, one expends the white days within seven thousand two hundred [moments]. One.

He unfurled one scroll [of scripture], yet translated ninety-eight thousand scrolls of yellow paper. Having obtained such favorable conditions without difficulty, his profound gratitude was boundless.
The Master lived to the age of eighty-seven. On the full moon day of the tenth month in the twenty-seventh year of the Xiangshu era, he bathed, washed his hands, and changed into clean robes.

He addressed the assembly and passed away while seated. During the cremation, they vied with one another to collect the *śarīra* relics; their number was beyond reckoning. Thus did the Buddha’s transformation flourish.
Is this not the very person in whom that light resides?
At Gwanggyeongsa Temple in Gyeongju, there was a monk named Beopgye.

He was a lecturer on the *Śīla-sūtra* from Mingzhou. He hailed from the Guan River in Yin County and belonged to the Du clan; he left the household life through the True Cause (*zhengyin*). His religious practice...

He was truthful and had maintained a vegetarian diet throughout his life, disregarding his physical form. He once constructed a great Buddha hall and erected a Prabhūtaratna stūpa within the monastery;
he also dredged and built a vast reservoir to irrigate the southern fields, so that the multitude benefited from his bounty for more than a day.

In the twentieth year of the Shaoxing era, when the Dharma Hall was dilapidated and leaking, he resolved to rebuild it. He immediately dispatched people everywhere and drew blood to transcribe one copy of the Lotus Sūtra.

[He] accumulated offerings and profits to complete it. Next, in the process of turning over the roof-covering, he divided this scripture into three parts, wrapped them in a triple-layered cloth case, and bound the exterior with an oil-saturated cloth.
He enshrined them within the "Three-Path Fire-Beads" (*trivartma-maṇi*), intending thereby to stabilize the monastery buildings so that they might endure forever without decay.
Twenty years later, the ridgepole was damaged once again, and Śīla repaired the fire[-altar] once more.
The beads were taken down together; yet when examining the sutra, not even a single fragment was to be seen. Both monastics and laypeople deeply marveled at this marvel.
Those with discernment maintained that the Master’s sincere devotion had moved the devas and nāgas, who had welcomed the sutra away to venerate it.
Later, that monk transmitted the Tiantai teachings and resided as abbot on this mountain. Zongxiao once visited him in person and thereby obtained these details.
Nuns (totaling thirteen individuals):

At the age of twenty, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, investigating their principles and flavors with increasing diligence as he grew older. It was from him that the practice of bhikṣuṇīs reciting scriptures began.

The Venerable Nun of Sizhou, whose name was Zhixian, was of the Zhao clan and a native of Changshan. Her observance of the precepts was refined and meticulous; she was expansive in spirit and remained untainted by worldly entanglements.

At that time, Du Ba, the Governor of Sizhou, placed his faith in the teachings of Huang-Lao and harbored jealousy toward the Buddhist tradition. He issued an edict to purge and cull the monastic community, establishing regulations of such high severity.

Fajun was not someone who could be measured by ordinary standards. When tested by the standards of the worthy, he excelled; yet, when pressed to dwell alone, the worthy one understood his intent and vowed never to transgress outwardly again.
When Fu Jian ascended the throne, he held him in particular esteem and respect, commissioning the creation of a brocade *kāṣāya* for him.

She was constantly used by various birds as a place of refuge and roosted there as they followed her in her walking meditation (*cankrama*) (from the *Biographies of Nuns*).

He then made a vow, saying, "If my illness is cured, I shall immediately go forth into the monastic life. His illness was indeed cured, and he consequently underwent tonsure and became a monk.

The nun Master Huiyu of Jiangling was a native of Chang’an.

She was diligent in the practice of precepts and goodness, and her realization of the Way and its Virtue was complete. In her travels for the purpose of teaching and transforming others, she did not avoid cold or heat.

This was considered extraordinary. During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he practiced asceticism and made a vow, saying:

He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with complete mastery and was moreover able to explain its essential meaning. Whenever he sat or lay down, a canopy would suddenly appear covering him from above.
When a marriage proposal arrived, he vowed to refuse it. Upon reaching the age of twenty, his parents took him to Qiming Temple to enter the monastic order;
on that very day, the canopy vanished. Thereafter, he extensively studied the sūtras and śāstras, probing the depths of their profound principles until his later years.

She moved to Shaoming Temple in Shanyin, where she took turns lecturing on the Sutras and the Vinaya; her fame resounded through Yuxue. With the offerings she received, she commissioned the creation of statues and the transcription of scriptures.
When Yuanjian, the Prince of Heng of the Liang dynasty, arrived at the commandery, he invited her to serve as a teacher for his mother (from the *Biographies of Eminent Nuns*).
The nun Huashou of Gaoyou was a native of Gaoyou County.
Her resolve was as pure as frost and her conduct as clear as ice. She recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* day and night without ceasing.
When she had first finished reciting one fascicle, suddenly a flower grew upon the nail of her right hand; its form resembled a patterned silk ribbon. It unfolded in succession...

When she reached the fifth recitation, a flower grew upon each of her five fingernails. When she completed the sixth and seventh, two flowers grew simultaneously upon her palms, larger than those on her nails.
Consequently, word spread to the imperial palace. Emperor Wu of the Chen dynasty issued an edict for her to be brought in for inspection.
From that time on, the people of the commandery vied with one another to call her "The Nun with Flowered Hands" (*Lingrui ji*).
Regarding the nun Faxin of Hedong:

During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, there was a nun named Faxin who was thoroughly versed in the *Lotus Sūtra*. She was conscientious and devout from beginning to end and desired to produce a meticulously transcribed copy of the scripture herself.
She consequently sought out a scribe, offering him double the usual fee and setting aside a separate hall for his use to have it written. For every...
He took a single bath and changed into clean robes. He then bored a hole through the wall from the desk to the outside, like a bamboo tube.
Whenever the student exhaled, he would gently hold the bamboo tube in his mouth and breathe out through it. He transcribed seven volumes of sutras, completing them in eight years.
A vegetarian feast was prepared for the celebration and repentance, and a pure *maṇḍala* was established, where incense and flowers were offered in veneration.

In the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era, the monk Fadu of Longmen Monastery, who regularly lectured on this sutra, sent someone to request it, as he found this nun’s manuscript to be exceptionally refined and complete.
The nun declined repeatedly and would not accept it, yet she personally escorted it away. When Fadu opened it to read, he saw only yellow paper with not a single character.

Feeling ashamed and fearful, he immediately returned it. The nun, knowing that she had committed an offense, poured fragrant water over the box to purify it, then carried it on her head while circumambulating the Buddha and performing acts of merit for seven days and nights.
When she opened it to look inside, it was restored to its original state. (From *Fayuan zhulin*)
The two masters Zhulin and Faren of Dongjing were both of the Huang family of Jinling.
They had two daughters; the elder was five years old and the younger three. Once, someone happened to be reciting the Lotus Sutra in their courtyard.
The Sūtra says: "Sisters, listen to this," whereupon she said, "I understand this. From that time on, she was able to discourse upon the meaning of the True Mark (dharmatā).
Later, both became nuns at An-guo Temple in the capital; the elder was named Chih-fa, and the younger was called Hui-jen.
The two women shared the same aspiration to practice the Lotus Samādhi. Suddenly, there appeared a nun who called herself Kung-ku; her speech and appearance were most extraordinary. She...
They stayed together overnight. Every time it reached midnight, her body would emit a brilliant radiance. After three years, she departed.
When someone questioned her about this, both nuns merely smiled and did not answer. Those who understood the scriptures identified her immediately as Samantabhadra.
Consequently, her fame spread throughout the capital, such that even Master Xingxiang (Yixing) held her in deep reverence. Liang Su composed a biographical sketch for her, stating: [text follows].
The Two Sisters of Jingzhou:
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, there were two sisters who were nuns in Jingzhou. They recited the Lotus Sūtra together and were deeply weary of their physical bodies;

both desired to sacrifice their lives to seek the unsurpassed path. From then on, they gradually ceased eating grain and consumed various fragrant oils, announcing their intention in advance to the monastics and the laity.
The day was fixed for the cremation. Accordingly, two high seats were erected in the main street of the city. Their bodies were wrapped in waxed cloth, leaving only their faces exposed.
They recited the Lotus Sūtra up to the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja. First, the elder sister applied a flame to her younger sister’s crown;

then, the younger sister applied a flame to her elder sister’s crown. In the clear night, the two torches shone with equal brilliance. When the fire reached their eyes, the sound of the sūtra was still clearly audible. Upon reaching [the end],...

At dawn the following day, the entire assembly cremated the remains together; while the bones and flesh were entirely consumed, both tongues remained intact. The community erected a stupa to commemorate them for ten thousand generations.
This is recorded in the "Section on Leaving the Body" (*yishen ke*) of the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
The nun Faron of Runzhou, whose secular name was Faron, resided at Samadhiraja Temple in Danyang. Having entered the path since her youth, she cultivated meditative wisdom with diligence.

She could recite the Lotus Sutra from memory without fail day and night until she passed away at the age of seventy-four. Her final instruction was to leave her body exposed as an offering to living beings.

The disciples followed his instructions. Although insects and beasts devoured [the body] until it was exhausted, only the heart and tongue remained. The tongue was still red in color, while the heart was somewhat blackened.
The assembly immediately erected a stupa to enshrine them (from *Lingrui ji*).
Regarding the nun Tengtong of the capital:
During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, there was a nun named Zhītōng at Jiǎnjìng Temple in the capital. She was of beautiful appearance and youth, yet her faith in the Way was not firm.
Having divorced from her husband Liáng Qúnpǔ, she later bore a son who was seven years old; as the family was poor and lacked clothing, she became a nun.

At that time, there were several scrolls of sutras, including the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, all written on plain silk. He immediately washed and pounded them to make clothes. When his son wore them, he fell ill;
he became dazed and agitated, his body transformed and began to slough off and rot as if from a fire-wound. White worms emerged, consuming more than a sheng of flesh each day.
He suffered from parching pain and agonizing toxins, wailing day and night. Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air proclaim: "You have destroyed the sutras to make clothes!"
He received this severe retribution and died within ten days (*Fayuan zhulin*).
Faithful laymen (thirty-two in total):
Liu Yimin of Mount Lu.

Liu Chengzhi was styled Yimin. A descendant of Liu An, Prince Yuan of Han and Chu, he was deeply versed in the Classics and the Hundred Schools of thought, yet he took particular delight in Buddhist principles.

When the Duke and Marquis of Yizhao issued summons to appoint him to office, he declined and excused himself from both. Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu established the Lotus Society of the Eighteen Worthies and honored him as their preeminent guest.
Thereupon, he chose to reside at Xilin, where for twelve years he practiced the *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) samādhi.
One day, while he was bedridden with illness and focused his mind in meditation, he beheld the white tuft of light between the Buddha’s eyebrows.

He further saw the body of Amitābha as a mountain of purple gold, its rays of light scattering brilliant colors. Cheng requested that the Buddha stroke his head and cover him with his robe; the Buddha immediately stroked his head.
He drew his robe over himself. Again, he saw his body enter a pool of the seven treasures and drink the water of eight virtues.

Having drunk it, its sweet flavor and extraordinary fragrance issued from his pores. He then addressed the assembly, saying, "When these signs appear, my karmic conditions for the Pure Land have reached their fulfillment."
He then burned incense before the sacred image and made this vow: "By means of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed teachings, I have come to know that there is the Western Pure Land.
First, I offer this incense to Śākyamuni; next, I present it to Amitābha, praying that he will surely gather us in through his power of conversion.

Third, I reverently uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; it is because of the merit of this sutra that I shall attain rebirth. Having spoken thus, he joined his palms toward the west and passed away. Liu.
"It was entirely due to the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that he attained such [results].
Consequently, he invited the assembly of monks to recite this sutra several hundred times together to assist his practice" (*Lushan ji*, by Dharma Master Huiyuan).

Regarding the "Miraculous Tongue" of one who recited the sutras in Bingzhou during the reign of Emperor Wucheng of the Northern Qi: beside Mount Donghan in Bingzhou, someone was digging the earth when they encountered a patch of soil with alternating yellow and white hues.
Suddenly, they discovered an object shaped like two lips, within which was a tongue of a vivid crimson color.
The prefectures and counties found this extraordinary and reported the matter to the throne. When the Emperor questioned his officials, none could provide an answer.

He immediately issued an edict to the Great Master of the Śramaṇas, Fashang, who submitted a memorial stating: "This is the retribution for one who upholds the Lotus Sūtra, whereby their six sense faculties remain unimpaired."

He recited the scripture one thousand times, and the miraculous signs were as described. The Emperor then issued an edict to Gao Zhen of the Chancellery, saying: "You are a person of faith and devotion;
go there yourself, and there will surely be some spiritual manifestation. Gao Zhen received the command and went there.

He assembled the monks who upheld the Lotus Sūtra, and they held incense burners while circumambulating. As they proclaimed and recited this sūtra, he addressed them, saying: "The Bodhisattva has already entered Nirvāṇa..."
He said, "If the transmission of the sutras and images of the Dharma is to be free from error, I pray that you manifest a spiritual omen. Having spoken, he chanted aloud;
his lips and tongue moved simultaneously as if in the act of recitation. When the fourfold assembly beheld this, their hair stood on end.

Emperor Zhenhui reported this to the throne, who then issued an edict to enclose the relics in a stone casket and erect a stupa to commemorate them (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*).
Regarding Zhang Chang, the Senior Secretary:
During the Jin dynasty, there was a Zhang Chang who served as the Senior Secretary to Prince Xiao of Qiao. The Prince and Chang were imprisoned together by the Court of the Judicial Inspector.

Having long possessed correct faith, Chang immediately resolved his mind to recite the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra* one thousand times in order to seek release. As he maintained this mindfulness...

As soon as he spoke these words, his shackles and fetters were instantly broken and destroyed, and both men were able to escape. This is recorded in the *Biography of Xie Fu* regarding Guanyin, translated during the Jin dynasty, and is cited in the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sutra* (Fahua yishu) circulated separately at Tiantai.
Yu Xian, a man of integrity and virtue, was a native of Xinye during the Liang dynasty.
His courtesy name was Yanbao. From childhood, he possessed a keen intellect and devoted himself to the study of the classics and histories. By nature, he was easygoing and simple.
He was particularly fond of forests and springs; he maintained a vegetarian diet and wore tattered clothing, never engaging in business or industry. When young, he was on good terms with Emperor Wu.

When the Emperor raised his army, [Huiyuan] was appointed as the Secretariat Director of the Pacification of the West (Pingxi Fu), and later by imperial decree as Palace Attendant (Huangmen Shilang); in both instances, he declined on the grounds of illness.

In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the teachings of Śākyamuni. He established a *dharma-śālā* within his residence, where he performed prostrations and repentance during the six periods of the day and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* once every day.
One night, toward the end of the third watch, he saw a Daoist practitioner who called himself Master Yuan. His appearance and demeanor were most extraordinary;
he addressed Huixian as "Master Shangxing," bestowed upon him incense, and departed. Later, while Huixian was ill in bed, he woke up with a start and said, "Master Yuan has come again."

He could not remain for long; his complexion did not change, and he suddenly passed away. The entire household heard a voice in the air proclaiming, "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Pure Land of Amitābha.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chushi Zhenjie (Retired Scholar of Upright Integrity) to manifest his lofty and heroic virtue (*Nanshi*).
Cui Yanwu, the Prefectural Governor of Weizhou during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty—
Cui Yanwu of Boling, who served as the Prefectural Governor of Weizhou— was traveling through the provinces on official business when he arrived at a certain district.
Suddenly, she said to her attendants, "In the past, I lived in this town as the wife of a man; I now recognize my former dwelling.

Thereupon, she mounted her horse and followed the winding alleys until she reached a house. She ordered the door to be knocked, and the elderly master opened the gate to welcome her, inviting her inside.
Wei ascended the hall and sat down. The old man asked, "For what purpose has the official come here? Wei immediately replied, "I..."
"My former life was your wife. The old man asked, "What proof do you have?
Wu said, "The Lotus Sutra I recited in the past, along with five gold hairpins, were hidden on the eastern wall, six or seven feet from the floor; it is at that high spot.
The last page of the seventh fascicle of that sutra was burned by fire and its characters lost; I am now reciting this [remaining portion]."
The scripture had subsequently been lost and forgotten. He therefore ordered someone to bore through the wall at a high point. Indeed, they found the scripture;

although the paper was damaged by fire, they also recovered a gold hairpin, exactly as he had said. The host wept and said, "When my late wife was alive, she constantly recited this scripture, and the gold hairpin was also hers.
Yanwu spoke again, saying, "The catalpa tree in front of the courtyard is where I was born in the past."
He untied his hair and placed it in the air among the branches of a tree, challenging anyone to retrieve it. When people tried to reach for it, they indeed found his hair.
Upon seeing this, the host was filled with a mixture of grief and joy. Yanwu then left his belongings as a gift for him and departed (from the *Lingrui ji*).
The Scholar of Bingzhou:
To the west of the city of Bingzhou, there was a scholar who had not yet reached the age of thirty. He recited and upheld the Lotus Sutra and attained its profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
Vowing to offer his own body by cremation as an offering to the Mahayana, he gathered several hundred bundles of dry mugwort and stacked them to form a tower.
When asked the reason for this, he kept it secret and did not speak. Suddenly, in the middle of the night, he took fire and set himself ablaze.
By the time others arrived to rescue him, he had already bitten his own navel (from the *Lingrui ji*).

Jiangling’s Cen Wenben, the Grand Secretary (Zhongshuling) Cen Wenben, was a native of Jiangling. From his youth, he harbored upright faith and constantly recited the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Once, while traveling by boat along the Ruojiang River on official business, a wind arose in midstream; both man and vessel were submerged. Wénbén floated...
Upon the surface of the water, he heard a voice say, "If you merely recite the Buddha’s name and chant the sutras, you shall certainly not die.
This was said three times. From then on, he followed the waves and reached the northern shore. Later, when a vegetarian feast was held in Jiangling, the assembly of monks gathered together;
there was one monk who remained behind alone. He said to Wenben, "The world is currently in turmoil. You have fortunately escaped harm; you shall surely encounter the Great [Sage]."
"He will attain peace, prosperity, and nobility. Having said this, he departed. Suddenly, at one time, Wenben found two śarīras within his rice bowl.
He attained peace, prosperity, and nobility, exactly as the monk had foretold (*Lingrui ji*).

During the Kaihuang era, there was a man named Wang Fanxing from Linyi who was blind in both eyes from childhood. Out of compassionate concern for him, his mother orally transmitted the *Lotus Sūtra* to him;
he recited it a total of seventeen thousand times. Later, although his eyes remained blind, he traveled back and forth every day and night to weave.

He faced no obstacles regarding matters such as weaving mats or sewing clothes. People suspected he had attained some special realization, yet when questioned, he was ultimately unwilling to speak of it.

He wore plain cloth and ate simple vegetables, remaining unmarried for his entire life. At the age of seventy-one, he passed away. His final instruction was that his corpse be sent to the wilderness to be devoured by birds and beasts;
once the flesh was gone and only the bones remained, his tongue would not decay, its color like that of a lotus flower. There was [a record of this].
His younger brother, Huiyi, placed it in an ornate casket and venerated it with incense and lamps (*Lingrui ji*).
Wang Yan of Linyi was a native of Linyi in Langya.
His grandfather and father were both prominent officials; Yan himself served as a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate. He was born...
He was dull-witted, yet he devoted himself exclusively to the Mahāyāna. He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in its entirety from beginning to end. Later, he died of illness.

He had a younger brother named Gu, who was the Governor of Xin’an and also recited the Lotus Sutra. One day, Gu suddenly dreamed that his elder brother said to him: "I have been born in the Western Land within the calyx of an iron-leafed lotus flower.
It will be five hundred years before the flower opens and I can finally see the Buddha; this is because I recited the sutra with such bitter resolve."
"I have attained birth in the Western Land. Because of my dullness and lack of acuity, I still receive the retribution of a womb-birth. I inform you all to know this:
you should contemplate the retribution that awaits you, apply yourselves diligently to the scriptures, and do not be indolent. Having spoken thus, he took his leave (*Lingshui ji*).
Lu Chun of Wu Commandery.
A native of Wu Commandery, although he lived in a secular dwelling, his heart constantly yearned for the Way. He recited and maintained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* day and night.
Later, he suddenly fell ill and lay facing upward; with his eyes open, he gazed at the ceiling without blinking for even a moment. There was a monk who was a spiritual friend...

When [the messenger] came to inquire after his illness, [Lü Chun] asked, "Why are you lying on your back and gazing at the ceiling? He replied, "The Buddha has prophesied that I shall be reborn in the Yāma Heaven.
Now I see the palaces, towers, and city gates of that celestial realm, as well as the hosts of devas; for this reason, I am not weary of looking about.
Four days later he passed away. This was during the Daye era (the *Lingrui ji*).
During the Great Sui dynasty, there was Yan Gong of Danyang in Yangzhou. His entire family placed their faith in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and constantly recited it.

On one occasion, while reciting as far as the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," he paused his recitation and sighed, saying: "Within the jeweled stupa, there are two Tathāgatas who have manifested their bodies in various ways."
"The Buddhas are not few in number; why then am I unable to move them to appear before me? He sighed with deep regret for a long while.

At night, he suddenly dreamed of a Hu monk who called himself Fatao. The monk said to him, "If you recite this sutra and desire to see the various Buddhas, you should explain it, copy it, circulate it, and make offerings to it;
then this wish may be fulfilled. Respectfully following these instructions, he resolved to produce one hundred copies of the sutra.
Before he had yet completed the task, he suddenly fell gravely ill. He then made a renewed vow to produce an additional one thousand copies.

Once his illness had healed, he immediately constructed a scripture hall at his residence in the capital of Yangdu. Whether for paper or brushes, he employed a pure heart and refrained from any deception, undertaking the work as resources became available.
He maintained a constant staff of ten or more scribes, providing them with supplies according to the Dharma and personally supervising their labors with great diligence.
He never complained of weariness. Once, there was a man who came to him to borrow ten thousand coins for the sake of sutras. Zhi Gong, having no other choice, gave them to him.

When the man reached the middle of the river with the money, his boat suddenly capsized; he lost the money but survived. That day, when Zhi Gong entered the storehouse, he saw that the original coins were all damp.
He found this quite strange. Later, upon seeing the man who had borrowed the money, he learned that the man had drowned. One day, suddenly, a marvel occurred.
The monk was about eighty years old. He said of himself, "I have come from the kingdom of Kucha and am now going to Mount Luofu.

Hearing that you are producing scriptures, I wish to request a copy. He respectfully handed over a scripture and presented a bottle of gold weighing forty *liang*, saying, "I hope this will assist in the production of the scriptures.
Having spoken, he withdrew. [Kong] searched for him again, but could not discover where he had gone. Furthermore, there was Hou Zhi, who followed...
Hailing from Poyang, Zhi was traveling to Gongting when he encountered a storm; his fellow passengers were drowned, but he alone survived.

Someone led him into a temple, where he saw a divine being sitting with a sword resting on his knee. The deity asked Zhi, "Do you still recognize Jiangshan and Yan Gong, who commissioned the production of the Lotus Sutra?
I wish to entrust ten thousand coins to their merit. Having spoken, the deity vanished instantly. On the following day, Zhi arrived at Dang...

While he was applying the ointment, he suddenly saw a man who said his surname was Xu and that he had come to seek Houzhi. The man left ten thousand coins, pressing him to accept them before departing.
Zhi reflected on this and realized they were divine coins. As soon as he arrived in Jiangning, he gave the money to Gong.
His reverent resolve became even more steadfast, and he produced as many as three thousand fascicles. Furthermore, a fisherman saw at night a blazing flame floating upon the river;
when he approached it by boat, it was found to be a single case of scriptures—precisely those produced by Yan Gong. Later, he made this vow:
"There shall not be a single character that has not passed before my eyes, nor a single character for which I have not applied my mind. Thus did Yan Gong produce these scriptures.
His descendants continued to transmit his legacy for generations, and he was popularly known as "Gong the Lotus Sutra Master.
During the final years of the Sui dynasty, when bandits were rampant, they all made a pact not to enter his village upon hearing of his accumulated merit;
the villagers relied on him for protection (as recorded in the *Lingrui ji* and the *Nanshan Sanbao Ganying lu*).
Shi Heshi of Shicun Village, Fenggu Township, southwest of the capital city of Tang. From his youth, he cherished the path of goodness and maintained a spirit of pure integrity.

He constantly recited the "Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, never ceasing for a moment. With compassion and forbearance held in his heart, he vowed not to...
He rode a horse because the sutra says one should have compassion for all beings. With a mind of sincere restraint, he was known as Zhan Lingshi.

As he traveled back and forth between the capital and the provinces, his heart remained fixed on the recitation of the scripture; fearing he might encounter acquaintances, he would invariably carry a copy of the sutra with him.

On the day of his death, a rare fragrance filled his room, which his relatives and neighbors smelled together. Ten years later, when his wife died and they were buried together, he took the opportunity to open the grave and look inside.
He then beheld the tongue-mark, which was a brilliant crimson. Consequently, he moved [the relics] to another location at Xiansuo (in Zhulin).
Li Shanlong of Fengyi, a Left Gate Guard Commandant, was a native of Fengyi. During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, he died suddenly; [the practitioner] then extracted his heart.
She remained warm; her family could not bear to bury her, and on the seventh day she revived.

She recounted that she had first been pursued by an official to the presence of King Yama, where she saw thousands of prisoners. The King asked Long: "What meritorious deeds did you perform? She replied:
He was able to recite two fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The King praised him, saying, "Excellent! The King immediately ordered seats to be spread and requested that he recite it.

The Dragon began chanting the first chapter, the "Introduction," of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The King said, "Stop for now. The Dragon then descended from his seat and looked back at the various prisoners;
they all departed, traveling through the air. The King praised the merit of reciting the sutra, whereby all who heard it attained liberation.
The king immediately sent the dragon back to life and commanded his messenger to lead him on a tour of the various hells.
The dragon saw an iron city, vast and high, with a roof covering it and many small windows on its sides; men and women were all flying into it, never to emerge again.

The dragon was filled with grief and fear, and crying out "Namo Buddha," he entreated the messenger to find a way for him to escape. He then saw boiling cauldrons and other such horrors. The messenger said:
"You have now been spared; this is entirely due to the power of the *Sūtra*. When you return, you must prepare a meal for me. The dragon immediately granted his request.
Once he had revived, he saw his relatives preparing funeral equipment. He then sent someone to prepare food by the water's edge to offer as a sacrifice.
Suddenly, he saw three men who thanked him, saying, "You have not proven unfaithful to your word. Having spoken, they vanished (from the *Tàipíng guǎngjì*).

In the fifth year of the Zhenguan era, Li Yonggui of Basix County in Longzhou, who held the Buddha-dharma in deep faith, transcribed such sutras as the Lotus Sutra, the Diamond Sutra, and the Nirvana Sutra.
Fearing that errors might occur, he relied upon Master Tuhang to oversee the work; once the transcription was complete...
He immediately took them to his estate in Qizhou. One day, while he was away on a journey, the estate was consumed by an external fire and utterly destroyed.
When Yuan Gui returned, his lamentations were boundless. He then had someone sift through the ashes to retrieve the gold and copper axis-heads;
suddenly, the various scriptures were found intact, their yellow lacquer color unchanged, except for the title of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, which was scorched black. From this...

Regarding the cause of this: when it was first transcribed, there was an official skilled in calligraphy who, being in a hurry, did not take the time to ensure the manuscript was clean and wrote directly upon it.
Consequently, it was burned. That person is still living, and the auspicious scripture remains extant;
this was witnessed and recounted by Master Shencha, the abbot of Ximing Monastery in the capital (as recorded in the *Nanshan Sanbao Gantong Lu*).
Dong Xiong of Hedong.

Dong Xiong was a native of Hedong. During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he served as the Vice Director of the Court of Judicial Review. He was upright and sincere, and he devoted himself to Buddhism, maintaining a vegetarian diet for many years.
Later, due to certain circumstances, he was imprisoned along with his colleagues Li Jingxuan and Wang Xin; while in confinement, Dong Xiong focused his mind exclusively on the Dharma.
He recited the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumen pin*) of the *Lotus Sūtra* three thousand times in order to seek liberation. Suddenly, one night, his shackles fell off of their own accord.

The prison officials were struck with alarm and, in astonishment, re-secured him with heavy locks and seals before departing. Xiong continued his recitation until the fifth watch; at that time, the locks once again fell away.
Jingxuan had previously been a non-believer in Buddhism, but upon witnessing this event involving Xiong, he finally came to realize the spiritual power of the Buddha-dharma.
King Xin also recited the names of the eight honored Bodhisattvas thirty thousand times; together with Xiong and others, he was able to escape punishment (*Fayuan zhulin*).
Yuan Zhitong of Longcheng...
Yuan Zhitong was a native of Longcheng County. From his youth, he observed the fasts and precepts and recited the two sutras, the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra.

At the age of twenty, he entered the army and was dispatched to campaign against the Eight Man tribes. Traveling ten thousand *li* from home, he continued his recitations without ceasing along the way.

Upon reaching the southern border, his army was defeated; many were wounded, and they were in a state of incessant distress. Suddenly, five men appeared riding horses ahead of them, and the last of them said to Tong:
"Because you have cultivated the fruits of goodness and recited the scriptures, we, a group of virtuous beings, shall protect you;
no harm can come to you. Travel about seven *li*, and there will be a stupa where you may enter and hide. The barbarian [leader] immediately—
Upon returning to his camp, he again saw two monks who said to Tong, "Because of your power of recitation, we have just dispatched five people to protect you.
You must remain diligent; good spirits will always assist and support you. Having spoken, they ascended into the air and departed.

From that time on, he passed through three battles without being struck by even a fragment of iron. When the Mian tribes were pacified and he was able to return, he fell ill in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era and issued his final instructions.
At last, he saw the messengers pursue him to the front of King Yama’s hall. The King asked what virtuous deeds he had performed.

He replied that he constantly upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, observed the precepts, and performed rites of repentance. Upon hearing this, the King joined his palms and praised him, saying, "Excellent!

He then ordered an investigation into the truth of these matters to determine the source of his arrival. After the Heavenly Office submitted its report, the King further requested the case files and searched through them himself, saying: "This person..."
"Six more years of life remain," he said. "Have the golden bed and jade stool brought to the hall and arrange them with felt mats and cushions.

Invite Tongshangzu; have him recite two sutras, each to the full length of one scroll, and then stop. He then ordered the Keeper of the Archives to bring the merit-tablet to the inner chamber, saying:

"Zhitong shall recite the *Lotus Sutra* and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* ten thousand times each. Perform prostrations to the Buddha, observe the fast, and engage in repentance for every single instance."
While they were there, the King said, "Your virtuous deeds are profound; you should further observe the hells so that you may know that retribution for sin and merit does not fail.
Have him lead the way five li to the west. They saw a great city with watchtowers and defensive parapets, from which iron nets hung down.
At the gate stood two jailers, their bodies immense, each holding an iron fork and standing to the left and right. Copper dogs were at the entrance.
Molten copper was spat out and poured over the offenders; all eighteen hells were present therein, which Tong saw and viewed with terror.
He then went before the King, who said: "Since you have seen the hells, you ought to practice with even greater diligence.
Therefore, I now grant you long life. Tong revived and recounted the events as above (*Lingrui ji*).
During the Daye era, there was one named Murong Wencè in Qinzhou.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* day and night without ceasing.
One day, two men suddenly appeared, holding a document and showing it to him, saying: "The Great King Yama has sent us to summon you; you must [go]."
He set out at once. Wen-ce was terrified; accompanied by the messenger, he arrived at a great city with six layers of walls and gates shrouded in darkness.
Having passed through these, he beheld a palace where King Yama sat presiding, surrounded by a formidable and majestic retinue. Below were men and women of various nations with diverse appearances.
One by one, they called out their names until it reached Wen-ce. The King questioned him regarding his deeds and conduct, to which Wen-ce replied that he was able to recite the *Vajra* Dharma.

Regarding matters such as the Flower Fast (huāzhāijì), the King joined his palms and ordered his officials to consult the scriptures. They reported that he did not deserve death. The King judged him fit for release and sent him back.
As Śreṇika traveled westward, he lost his way. Suddenly, he encountered a śrāmaṇera who said, "You may follow behind me.

After passing through six successive gates, they came upon a place of pitch-black darkness. The śrāmaṇera held a bright torch in his hand, and thus they were able to emerge and return to life. Śreṇika—
From this diligent and arduous recitation (*Lingshui ji*):
At Guishan Xianquan Temple in Jiangzhou, there was the Chan Master Fazhe. While walking in the mountains, he saw a leper.
He lived in an earthen cave, begging for food from his teacher. The teacher took pity on him, led him back to the monastery, and further dug an earthen cave for him to dwell in.
He provided him with clothing and food, and instructed him to recite the Lotus Sutra. This man had never known how to read or write before, and moreover, he was coarse and vulgar.
