The Master instructed him word by word, never wearying until the end. When he had recited about half, he suddenly dreamed of a monk who gave him guidance;

from then on, he gradually became more intelligent. By the time he reached the fifth or sixth fascicle, the sores on his body began to heal, and when he mastered the entire canon, his four limbs were completely restored.
As the Buddha said, "The sutras are the excellent medicine for illness"—these words have been proven true (from the *Lingrui ji*).
Gao Wenlong of the capital during the Longshuo era; Gao Wen, the grandson of Gao Biao-ren of the capital, once read the Lotus Sūtra.
One day, while riding out through Shunyi Gate on horseback, he suddenly saw two riders pursuing and seizing him. When they questioned him, they said, "I am King Yama."
He was sent to pursue you. As Wen fled in terror, he could not escape; he was immediately dragged down from his horse, and his hair was pulled out as if being cut by a blade.

His family carried him home, and when night fell, he regained consciousness and said: "The King of Yama questioned me, asking why I had stolen the monks' fruit and why I had spoken ill of the Triple Gem.
Consequently, I was made to confess my crime according to the law, and I did not dare utter a word in defense. The King—
The judge sentenced him for the crime of theft to swallow four hundred and fifty iron pellets, which he was to receive over the course of four years.

For the crime of slandering the Dharma, he was sentenced to have his tongue plowed. Consequently, he was released and immediately revived; however, after a short while, his life-breath ceased again, and his mouth appeared as if it were swallowing something.
His entire body was covered in blisters and redness, bearing the marks of intense suffering. After another day had passed, he regained consciousness and said, "I have been in hell for four days.
I have finished swallowing all the pellets; the bitter torment is beyond description. Just as they were about to pull out my tongue to plow it, they pulled, but it would not come out."
Upon investigating the circumstances, it was said that he had once read the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and his tongue could not be drawn out; consequently, he was released and restored to life.
It is recorded that he is currently at Huadu Monastery, attending the Dharma and performing repentance under Master Yuanman (from the *Nanshan Sanbao Gantong Lu*).

In the third year of the Longshuo era, Xiao Keng and his maidservant Suyu were involved in a matter concerning the officials Yuan Shaocangbo and Cui Yiqi, husband and wife, who were profoundly skeptical of Buddhism.
Xiao Keng, the father of Cui Yiqi’s wife, did not allow meat or wine to enter his door; he specialized in reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* several thousand times.
One day, his wife passed away. During the *sāptāhika* (seven-day) rites for her, while the ritual feast was being held, she appeared through a maidservant named Suyu and said:
"In my lifetime, although I heard of the existence of hell, I did not believe it. Now I am suffering unspeakably.
It is because you have recited sutras and lit lamps on my behalf that I have been able to return for a moment. After a few days have passed, I shall come again to take Suyu to the underworld."
The execution was carried out. When the appointed time arrived, Suyu indeed died suddenly. She then saw a great city and an official government office.
The lady entered a separate courtyard, where in a short while, cauldrons of fire and iron beds all appeared. The lady underwent various forms of torment.
Suddenly she saw her father, Xiao Keng, sitting upon a lotus pedestal, who said to Suyu: "When my daughter was born, you did not follow my words; you did not believe in the good."

"Evil! You were constantly full of anger and envy; now you undergo this suffering. When you return, you may tell your children and grandchildren to perform various meritorious deeds so that they may attain liberation.
At that time, she again saw a Brahmin monk descend from the air, instructing Suyu to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vajracchedikā*, and the *Bhaiṣajyaguru* Sūtras once each.
She recited them all with a pure, melodic voice (*brahma-svara*), and Suyu understood every word.
[She] made this sound. In this manner, after three days, Suyu revived and recounted the aforementioned events in detail. At that time, General Xue heard of this and held her in high esteem;
he prepared a vegetarian feast to welcome Suyu and ordered her to test her mastery of the scriptures. When she ascended the seat and recited them, there was not a single character left out.

Within the assembly, a Brahman monk joined his palms and sighed in admiration, saying, "It is exactly as it is in the Western Regions; there is no difference in their speech. The entire multitude was struck with wonder.
Xue then submitted a memorial to the Son of Heaven, who sighed and remarked, "Among my hundred officials, there are still those who do not believe in the Buddha-dharma."
"The path of the underworld is such as this; how can one not stand in awe? May those of high rank at court all hear this and give rise to right faith" (*Xiantong lu*).
There was a lay devotee (*upāsaka*) in Fuzhou.
In Fuzhou there is Huazang Temple, located seventy paces south of the county seat. In the past, during the Tang dynasty of the Li clan, it was known as Guangdu Temple.
Temple: It is said that there was once an upāsaka who devoted himself exclusively to reciting the Lotus Sūtra at this site.

One day, he suddenly saw an old man who spoke to him, saying: "I am the Lord of Seven (Tambae Chil-langgun; the shrine of Tambae Chil-langgun is enshrined within the local sacrificial canon). I request that you cease your recitation for a short while."
He took a detour to pass by, saying, "I shall build a vihāra here. That evening, thunder, lightning, wind, and rain broke out violently.

At dawn, when the weather cleared, he suddenly saw rafters, beams, and purlins piled atop one another upon the site. Afterward, the upāsaka passed away and was interred with his entire body in a stūpa to the south of the temple.
During the Xiangfu era of our present dynasty, seven lotus flowers suddenly sprouted from within the stūpa.
The entire district marveled at this. The Prefect submitted a memorial to the throne, and the monastery was granted its current name (as recorded in the *Fuzhou Tujing*).

During the tenure of Zhang Bing as Governor of Jizhou, there were frequent instances of bandits plundering the people’s property and committing sexual assaults upon their daughters. The parents brought these matters to the authorities for redress.
The Duke was enraged. He ordered a rack to be set up and the thief to be nailed to the gate, decreeing that he be minced into paste (hǎi) within three days.

Those who discussed the matter were gratified by this. Several years later, [the Duke] was suddenly summoned to the Underworld. From beneath pearl curtains at the foot of the hall, a voice spoke in a harsh tone:
"Zhang Bing unlawfully contended for and killed a human life. He was led before the prison to face his accuser; there he immediately saw a prisoner with blood and flesh dripping down, who wept.
He said, "You have killed me unjustly; now I have no place to take rebirth. You, sir, should rather remember that I was a rebel from Jizhou.
He then reviled him, saying, "Even if I were to grind ten thousand bodies of yours to dust, it would not suffice to avenge the shame brought upon my parents. How dare you still dare to appeal?
A subordinate official standing nearby said, "The five punishments have their own established statutes; one must not harbor resentment because of such an appeal. The Duke looked at him.
He then proceeded to the office of the River Yang for one day. The official asked, "How should this be done? He replied, "It is fortunate that Your Honor’s lifespan is not yet exhausted;
it will suffice simply to dispatch him to receive rebirth. The official, distressed and terrified, asked the clerk for the method of dispatching him.

The clerk said, "In terms of the greatness of merit, nothing compares to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. The official immediately consented to recite it one hundred times, increasing the number to one thousand times.
The prisoner would not relinquish it either. The official said, "There is no need for such excess; it is simply a matter of being long-term.
How about holding one fascicle each day and never forgetting it for the rest of your life? Sengbing agreed to his words. Suddenly, the prisoner was released.
Once Sengbing had regained consciousness, he recited and held the text for the remainder of his life, never forgetting it (from the *Leshan ji*).
Li Yu of Wuweijun, in the twenty-eighth year of the Xianxing era: Li Yu, a military officer of Wuweijun, went out west of the city to welcome the new prefect.
Having traveled some ten li, he heard that [the official] was still far away and so returned home. Suddenly, he saw about a hundred people following him from the side of the road.

They all emerged looking like children of three or five years old. Shouting loudly, they advanced and surrounded him to strike him down. Li was not afraid at first and engaged them in hand-to-hand combat;
every time he swung his fist, dozens of men would fall to the ground. As soon as they fell, they rose again;

having dispersed, they closed in once more. This happened four or five times. Some leaped up, climbed onto his shoulders, seized his headcloth, and grabbed his hair. Li became increasingly desperate and could not escape.
As they struck and pressed forward, suddenly an old man appeared, wearing a coarse robe and straw sandals, his origin unknown.
He rebuked them in a stern voice, saying, "This official constantly recites the Lotus Sūtra; if you harm others, will it not bring trouble upon me?
He shouted for them to retreat, and the ghosts dispersed. The old man also vanished. When Li returned to the gate, he was unable to move, so the gatekeeper supported him back home. Upon arriving—
The family was in a state of confusion and did not realize what had happened. When the sons lifted his clothes to examine him, they found only blue bruises covering his entire body.

They immediately performed the rite of summoning the soul at that very spot and invited monks to recite the Lotus Sūtra. It was only after more than half a year that the old man was able to walk again with the aid of a staff.
The family suspected it was the local earth deity (as recorded in the *Yijian Dingzhi*).
Zuoshen of Taizhou.
A native of Linhai in Taizhou, he was humble, respectful, upright, and honest. In managing his household, he would not take even the slightest advantage through unrighteous means.
Before reaching full maturity, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from Dharma Master Shenzhao of Dongye. From that time on—

He remained steadfast. On all days of fasting, apart from his midday meal, he would not even take medicinal broth. He carved images of the Western Sage and devoted himself diligently to the incense and lamps.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* three thousand four hundred times and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* twenty thousand times.

He constructed bridges and paved roads, and provided relief to the orphaned and destitute. In the third year of the Shaosheng era, while suffering from illness, he forced himself to rise and call upon the Buddha’s name with a resolute voice.
As he was about to depart this life, he instructed his son, Sengjingyuan, to expound the great meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra* and increase the methods for receiving the precepts.
He then dreamed of three people with radiant complexions standing on a riverbank, who called out to him to board a boat; they suddenly departed toward the west.

Upon waking from the dream, he immediately requested a monk to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Before the recitation was finished, he said, "I have already seen the Buddha’s light; I shall be reborn in the Pure Land."
"It is certain. He then rose, bathed, and changed his robes. He told them not to weep, immediately invoked the Buddha, formed mudrās, and passed away with a serene expression (*Baozhu ji*).
Fan Yan of Lin’an Prefecture was a native of Renhe County.
He regularly maintained a vegetarian diet and did not involve himself in worldly affairs. His son, however, was unable to manage the household.
Yan paid him no heed, saying only, "I am merely a guest here. Thereupon, he read the *Lotus Sūtra* daily with single-minded devotion and without slackening.

He also transcribed a copy of this sūtra. During the Zhongnian era of the Daguang reign, when he was over seventy years old, he happened to call his nephew Xu Kan and said, "You must attend to my funeral arrangements;
I have but three or two days left. Kan subsequently heard Yan...

In the Buddha hall, he called out loudly for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. The voice responded several times. When he remarked that the name "Puxian" (Samantabhadra) consisted of two characters, Kan questioned him further.
He replied, "I saw Samantabhadra riding a six-tusked white elephant, its radiance shining upon me and appearing entirely golden.
I thought to myself: 'Because I have studied the Lotus Sutra and recited the name of Amitābha Buddha, I shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land; therefore, he has come.'"
He replied, "Inform him: 'Tomorrow at the hour of the morning, you should depart; I shall come together with that Buddha to welcome and guide you. I have accepted this from him.
When the time arrived, Zhiyan immediately called upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whereupon he beheld the multitude of sages extending their hands toward him.

They asked, "Who is this person named Zhiyan who has received the guidance of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? He repeatedly exclaimed, "This is truly difficult to bear! Thereupon, he took his seat and joined his palms in reverence.
He closed his eyes and departed (*Baozhu ji*).

Chao Shizhi of Mount Song was Chao Shuo-zhi, a Palace Attendant of the Central Secretariat during the reign of Emperor Huizong; his courtesy name was Yidao. He was the fourth-generation descendant of Duke Wenyuan.
He was a descendant of Sun. Wen-yuan retired from office as Grand Master for the Heir Apparent to live out his years in Qingfeng.

With a mind at ease and daily rejuvenated, he turned toward the Buddha Vehicle, composing the *Fazang Bei* (Stele of the Dharma-Treasury) and the *Jindao Yuan Ji* (Anthology of the Golden Way Garden), both of which circulated throughout the world. The subtlety of his principles was such that both Confucians and Mohists took them as their model.
The Academician had long cultivated his family learning and had extensively perused the Buddhist scriptures.
While serving as an official in Siming, he studied under Master Zhongli of Mingzhi at Yanqing Temple, thereby attaining a profound and deep understanding of the Tiantai teachings.

Zongxiao once read several essays in the collected works of Gong from Mount Song that extensively expounded upon Tiantai doctrines such as the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" (*yīniàn sānqiān jìngguān*). Judging by what he composed, [Gong] was no less than Liang Jingxiu.
His re-emergence could not have been for the sake of competing as an equal carriage. The Master’s grandson was named Zikjian. There is a record stating:
"My ancestor studied the teachings of Tiantai Master Zhizhe; he recited the Lotus Sūtra daily and was styled a Tiantai Teaching Monk.

He was also called 'Old Lotus' (Lao Fahua). Upon seeing this, one can sufficiently know that the Master enjoyed the perfectly wondrous Buddha-vehicle and that its profound essence was stored within him.
This is superficial.

Lu Langzhong of Mingzhou, whose secular name was Lu Yuan and whose style name was Jushi Sheng’an, resided at Hengxi in Mingzhou. He was a descendant of Lu Tian, the Minister of the Left for Literary Affairs.

Sun served as an official up to the rank of Duguan Langzhong of the Ministry of Punishments. He was appointed as the Provincial Commissioner of Fujian, but returned home upon the death of his mother to observe the period of mourning.

Following the advice of his successor, Zheng Xingyi, he retired from public life. Whenever guests arrived at his residence, he would invariably join his palms in reverence and say, "I have no grievance against Zheng;
this is merely a karmic debt from past kalpas. If I truly do not forget this intention, we shall surely meet again to settle our accounts."
"There will be no time of completion. I shall diligently explain it through wholesome dharmas. Thereupon, he focused his mind on upholding the Lotus Sūtra.
Every morning upon rising, he bathed and changed his robes. Entering the pure chamber, he burned incense and sat in the lotus posture with his eyes fixed without blinking.
He first chanted this verse: "Washing my hands at dawn, the palm-leaf sūtras unfold; I seek no worldly blessings, nor do I avert calamity. Worldly ties are severed—"
He remained in a secluded place, cutting off all external ties. Amidst the flames of the kalpa-ending fire, he performed a single dance.

Thereafter, he opened his scroll and read it, neither too slowly nor too quickly, with a voice like a string of pearls. He recited it once every day for thirty years; upon reaching eighty years of age, he increased the practice to three sections.
He composed a poem to express his intent, containing the line: "Three times at dawn I arrive at Mount Ling.
He then used paper to form square grids, marking out one hundred sections for each verse to constitute a single diagram. These were accumulated by the son into a massive scroll;
the total number of verses was nine thousand four hundred and eighty-five, while the calculated number of scrolls was sixty-six thousand three hundred and ninety-five. During his leisure time...

Furthermore, he perused the Great Canon of Vairocana; there was no teaching of the Tiantai school, nor any section of the Vinaya, nor the Mind School of Shaolin that he did not investigate extensively.
He also recited the name of Amitābha Buddha, directing his mind single-mindedly toward the West.

In the fifth year of the Shaoxi era, at the age of eighty-five, on the sixth day of the fourth month, he requested hot water to cleanse his body, adjusted his cap and robes, composed himself, and passed away while lying in bed. Upon his enshrinement in the coffin, a lotus fragrance was suddenly perceived.
The fragrance of the flowers was so lush and pervasive that its source remained unknown; yet when one lifted the lid and inhaled it into one’s mouth and nostrils, the scent was unmistakable.
At that time, many women could not perceive the fragrance—could this have been due to the obscuration of the five hindrances?
Your younger brother, Lu You, Academician of the Huawen Pavilion, composed the tomb inscription for the Master and recounted these events in full detail.

In Mingzhou, there was Du Xin of Xiangfeng Township in Yin County; the local name for the area was Guanjian. There lived a man named Du Xin who established the Beifushe (Society for Redoubling Repayment) and recited the Lotus Sutra.
He then cleared two rooms of his house to serve as a gathering place for the assembly. Later, at one time, a certain unprincipled sorcerer named Weichi happened upon them.
Those [who lived there] resided in it. Consequently, that place was abandoned and turned into a site for roasting, boiling, slaughter, and killing.

In the eighth year of the Qiandao era, heavy rains fell in the autumn and the floodwaters overflowed; they moved to the Xianbian Stream, where even their five-bay high pavilions were swept away and submerged.
Neither the earth nor the stones remained; the sutra he was reciting drifted with the waves for over ten li and came to rest upon the surface of the sea.
After three or four days, it emerged from beneath the water. A man surnamed Jin from Guanshan found it;
when he first opened its cloth wrapper, it was stained with muddy water, yet when he next examined the sutra itself, both its front and back were pure and clean, without a single spot of moisture.
How great! The Buddha taught that those who read this sutra cannot be swept away by water. Beholding such an auspicious marvel, it is truly worthy of faith.
How many in this degenerate age who revile the Buddha’s sutras could ever know that there exists such an indestructible state?

In Mingzhou, there was Wu Zhen of Chixian County who served the public with devotion. He dedicated his heart to the path of goodness and once transcribed a copy of the Lotus Sūtra with ink-stained hands.
He recited it without ceasing until he passed away on the twentieth day of the sixth month in the year of Renyin during the Shaoxi era. Upon his death, the people rushed to [his side].
During the Jiu Shi-lu (Jiushi) era, the texts were scattered by fire. After the conflagration, he sought the sutra and finally recovered it from a neighbor's house the following day.

Shortly thereafter, he lost the fourth fascicle; knowing it had been consumed by the flames, seven days passed. While his son, Xingzong, was clearing away rubble, this sutra was found lying upright beneath the debris.
Only the beginning of the first fascicle was slightly damaged. When the fourfold assembly witnessed this, they sighed again at its rarity.
How extraordinary! His descendants still treasure and revere this scripture. One day, when Chan Master Fozhao was summoned to court, he passed by this place and knocked on the door;
at the request of the resident, he left behind a verse. Layman Siji of Yanling was of pure and sincere lineage, and his power of aspiration was firm and unyielding.
I personally transcribed this Lotus Sutra; it remains unharmed by fire. I have composed these mountain verses as a testament:

"Seven volumes of scripture survive amidst the kalpa-fire, relying solely on a single thought to accord with the true nature. Shining upon the present and illuminating the past without change, they are all but those who were present at the assembly on Vulture Peak.
Written by Yuyang Zhu’an Deguang.
During the Shaoxi era, there was a man named Chen Shiyin at the Patrol Inspection Post outside the West Gate of Mingzhou.
One night, he dreamed of a strange person, whose crown and robes were magnificent like those of a sovereign; this figure called out to Shiyin, saying, "I have seven bright pearls to bestow upon you."
Yin said, "My family is but poor; I dare not greedily accept this. The King said, "This pearl is a priceless treasure.
Since I have bestowed it upon you, you may simply take it with you. Yin then signed the document, received it, and returned home to place it upon a table.
Suddenly, it emitted a great radiance, causing all his family members to rejoice. Upon waking, he reflected on it; though he did not know its origin, his heart was ultimately filled with [reverence].
This was an auspicious omen. At dawn, a virtuous friend suddenly arrived at my door to organize a group for the recitation of the Lotus Sūtra.
I immediately resolved to join the assembly and recorded my name on the roster. Suddenly, I recalled my dream of the seven pearls given to the King;

surely these were the seven scrolls of the Lotus Sūtra bestowed upon me by the Dharma King. Such is the power of the resonance between mind and spirit. The teacher who transmitted the sūtra to me was a youth.
I write this letter of thanks to Wenbin. Because of this single dream, the entire community was moved with one accord, and I was thus able to become a monk;
I remain so even now. At that time, many offered verses in praise of me. The Dharma Master Miaoyun of Cishi at Yanqing Temple said: "The seven pearls obtained in the dream were clear;
at dawn, I encountered someone who urged me to recite the sutras. Before my teeth had even moved, the response was already manifest—only then did I realize its wondrousness."
The Dharma is fundamentally perfected. Regarding the "Retiring from the Hall" verse for the sake of repaying kindness, Chan Master Huiying said:

"A bright pearl of seven spheres within a dream, The wondrous Dharma is fully contained, not transmitted by mind. If you can now realize the meaning therein, It is entirely present among the hundred grasses in the spring breeze."

In Ningbo Prefecture, there was a man named Wang Jing of Leifeng, Ning County. His son, named Longzhuan, made his living by the butcher trade and managed the household. Wang Jing was eighty-eight years old;
he had long possessed a virtuous heart and had joined the Lotus Society since the Qian Dao era, continuing until the second month of winter in the first year of the Qing Yuan era.
On the seventeenth day, a fire broke out. Two thatched huts were completely consumed by the flames. Among them was a copy of the Lotus Sūtra kept within the Buddha hall;
a neighbor rescued it, but only half remained, as the rest suddenly vanished amidst the smoke and fire. Seen up close, it appeared like flying white silk;
viewed from afar, it was said to be a white dragon suspended in the air. It drifted away until it reached the depths of Cixi, some ten *li* distant.
It was found by a woodcutter surnamed Zhang living in the village atop a *liàn* tree; it consisted of seven chapters of the sutra, beginning from the "Expedient Means" (*Upāyakauśalya*) chapter.
Subsequently, a mountain woman surnamed Sheng picked up the "Introduction" (*Nidāna*) chapter in a field.
She reverently invited each of them back to her home; only the "Preface to the Propagation" (*Guǎngchuán xù*) was missing. (Zongxiao) It was heard that [the preface] was not far from the hermitage.
One day, he visited Wang Jing in person and requested to examine his scriptures. It was a copy donated by the jinshi (provincial graduate) Wang Duo.
In Mingzhou, there was a man named Wang Wenfu;
on West Guangde Lake in Yinkun County, there were two brothers of the Wang family who made their living as fishermen using fine-meshed nets. The elder brother...
Wenfu possessed a slight degree of virtuous intent. In his leisure time, he read the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which he enshrined within the Buddha hall.
In the fourth month of the fifth year of the Chunxi era, a great rain fell; suddenly, a thunderclap struck and killed Wenfu’s sister-in-law, followed by a conflagration that burned the thatched hut.
Yet, three pillars alone remained, supporting four rafters and covering the Buddha hall above. The scripture lay solemnly beneath them. When Master [Shi] arrived...
The shaman performed divination by means of the milfoil stalks. People from the four distant quarters came to observe, all of whom praised him as a divine marvel.
There were fourteen women who believed [in him], including the "Horse-Lang Wife" from Shaanxi.

The Maiden of the Horse-herd: Her origins are unknown. During the flourishing era of Buddhism in the Great Tang, the local customs in the region west of the Pass favored horsemanship and archery, and the name of the Triple Gem was rarely heard.
The woman took pity on their ignorance and went to that place. People, seeing the young maiden’s graceful demeanor as she stood alone, wished to adopt her as their own;
the girl said, "I have no parents, and I too wish to find a home, yet I do not delight in the world."
Wealth. However, if there is a person who is intelligent, virtuous, and capable of reciting the Buddhist scriptures, I vow to serve them.

A crowd of men gathered to watch; she then gave the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter) to a woman. She said, "If you can master this in a single night, I shall become your follower. When the next day arrived—
There were more than twenty people who had mastered the recitation. The woman said, "I am but a single woman, and my family lineage has been one of pure integrity.
It is not right that one body should serve many people; you should each recite separately. She then taught them the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and by dawn, ten or so had memorized it.
She further gave them the seven fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and instructed them to master it within three days. When the time arrived, she rode alone on her horse.
The son of the family was able to penetrate her meaning. The girl said, "Since you are able to surpass others, you may inform your parents;

once the formal marriage rites and betrothal ceremonies are completed, we shall become husband and wife. When the Ma family came to welcome her with due ceremony, she said as she approached the gate, "I have just been attending to guests, and my health has been somewhat unwell.
I wish to request a separate room to wait until I am recovered before meeting you. Thereupon, she halted there.
In another room, while the guests were still gathered for a banquet, the woman passed away; her body soon began to decay. They then divined an auspicious day to bury her.
Before many days had passed, a monk wearing a purple *kāṣāya*, with a countenance both ancient and austere, came seeking the woman. The Ma family led him to the burial site.
The monk immediately used his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) to clear away the sand and soil. He saw that the corpse had already transformed, leaving only a skeleton bound by golden chains.

The monk took it to the river to wash it, then placed it upon his staff and said to the assembly, "This holy one, out of compassion for you who do not believe in the True Dharma, has employed skillful means to guide and transform you.
You should contemplate the causes of goodness so as to avoid falling into the sea of suffering. Suddenly, he ascended into the air and departed. The assembly...
Seeing her weeping, he gazed upon her and paid homage without ceasing. From that time forth, the entire region venerated the Buddha and recited the sutras;
this was due to the power of the woman (from the *Shishi bian xun lu*).
The Mountain Valley Recluse’s eulogy on Avalokiteśvara says: "If you wish to see Avalokiteśvara in truth, look for her at the sands of Jinsha as the horse-herding maiden.
Furthermore, Chan Master Ti of Wanshou in Pingjiang composed a verse: "With such exquisite beauty, whose daughter could she be?
With a hundredfold intelligence, she was the horse-herding youth. One must laugh at their tryst by the banks of Jinsha; from beginning to end, this union never became a pair."
Huainiṅ had two sisters-in-law.
Near the city on the northern bank of the Yellow River was Huatai Temple. Originally, it belonged to a prominent family whose daughter could recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Her elder brother took a wife, and she too delighted in [the Dharma]. Before long, both the sister-in-law and the wife were able [to recite the sutra].
They neglected it. Whenever the watches of the night had passed and the moon was bright and the breeze clear, the two would recite together in unison;
even the clashing of jade and the ringing of metal in this world could not match their resonance. At one time, they both fell ill, and the sister-in-law and her brother-in-law died together.
Later, a single red lotus suddenly sprang up from the sister-in-law’s grave, blooming with exquisite beauty. Everyone marveled at it, and upon opening the ground to examine it, they beheld it.
The lotus root extended from the mouth of the sister-in-law directly to the tomb of her mother-in-law;
furthermore, when the mother-in-law’s tomb was opened, its root was found to emerge from the base of the mother-in-law’s tongue. This clearly demonstrates the causal connection between the two.

Upon learning of this, the provincial and prefectural authorities submitted a memorial to the throne, whereupon an imperial plaque for Huatai Temple was granted so that it might be established (*Lingrui ji*).

According to Wang Huicheng of the Southern Song, in the fourteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Liu Song dynasty, the family of Sun Yanzeng had long been devoted to Buddhism. They had a concubine named Wang Huicheng who, from her youth, had placed her faith in the teachings;
by adulthood, she was reciting the Lotus Sūtra. One day, she suddenly beheld a light of variegated colors in the river estuary and sent someone to dig there.
He dug three feet deep and discovered a golden Buddha image, complete with its halo and pedestal, standing two feet one inch high. On the pedestal was an inscription which read:
"In the first year of Jianwu, the year being Gengzi, made by the Daoist practitioner Faxin and others of Waguan Monastery.
He immediately polished it to a lustrous finish and enshrined it for veneration (from the *Sanbao gantong zhuan*).

The daughter of Su, the Regional Inspector, was married to Tang Changshou, the Director of Waterways during the Wude era of the Tang dynasty. He was subsequently appointed as the Regional Inspector of Bazhou.

Accompanied by his family, he traveled to his post and, while crossing the Jialing River, a wind arose in midstream. The ship’s sails were driven down, and more than sixty men and women were swept away all at once.

She perished. Her only female servant was constantly reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. When the ship drifted into the waves, the woman placed the scripture case upon her head and vowed to drown with it.
Thereupon, the woman did not sink; she floated along with the current and reached the shore in an instant.
She carried the case ashore and opened it to examine the scripture, finding it entirely free from moisture. This woman later married in Yangzhou, where her devotion [remained steadfast].
Through faith, recitation, and study, she recovered better than before (*Fayuan zhulin*).
Liu Gongxin of the Chen family in Chang’an’s Tonggui Ward had his wife, the mother of Lady Chen, pass away due to illness. Suddenly, Lady Chen...
She died suddenly. She saw a man lead her into hell, where she witnessed all manner of sinful retributions.

Later, she saw a stone gate to a hell suddenly open; her mother was inside, undergoing extreme suffering. The mother saw her daughter and said, "You should transcribe one copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for me, so that I may be delivered from this place.
Having spoken, the gate closed. Lady Chen revived once more and recounted these events, which Chen Xìn believed.
He then relied upon his nephew, Zhao Shizi, to transcribe this sutra. Suddenly, a professional scribe arrived with a newly transcribed copy of the *Lotus Sutra* to pawn for money.

Zhao said, "Fortunately, I have this very sutra; you may redeem it with this one. There is no need to transcribe another. Liu followed his advice, and after the preparations were complete, he handed it over to Lady Chen.
One day, while Lady Chen was preparing food for her mother, she dreamed that her mother said to her: "I previously..."
"I am having you transcribe a copy of a scripture; why do you not do so? The daughter replied, "I have already finished redeeming one copy.

The mother said, "Because of this scripture, I shall incur even heavier retribution. The hell-wardens beat my back until it was shattered because I improperly took Fan’s copy of the scripture as my own.

The daughter awoke from her dream and urgently requested someone to transcribe it. When the scripture was completed, she dreamed again that her mother informed her: [The remainder of the narrative follows.]
"By the power of the sutra I have received, I have already been liberated from the underworld and am dwelling in peace in a good realm. I have now come to inform you;

you should maintain faith and dwell well in this world. Furthermore, upon inquiring about the aforementioned sutra, it was indeed written by a person surnamed Fan during the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty (from *Fayuan zhulin*).
In Ningzhou lived Fei Xi, the wife of Luo Yu of the Song dynasty. She was a native of Ningzhou; her father’s name was Yue, who served as the governor of Ningzhou.

Fei had deep faith and reverence for the Triple Gem and recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. For several years she practiced with diligent perseverance without slackening. Suddenly, she contracted an illness characterized by heart pain, which gradually...
The situation reached its peak, and the entire family was filled with terror. Fei made this vow: "I have recited the sutras with diligent hardship;

surely there must be some auspicious protection. I shall certainly not meet my death because of this. Shortly thereafter, while lying down to sleep, he dreamed that the Buddha extended his hand through the window to stroke his heart.
Both inside and out, they all beheld golden light filling the room, and they also smelled a wondrous fragrance that permeated everyone. From that time on...
The illness was cured. Those who saw this could not help but give rise to faith (*Taiping Guangji*).

Regarding the daughter of Ren Zhengjun of Taizhou at Yongquan Temple in Linhai County, Taizhou: Previously, during the Tang dynasty, there was a Master Ren who cultivated his conduct with purity and integrity.
His resolve was steadfast and lofty, and he possessed deep faith in the Buddha-way, cultivating many fruits of merit.
There was a woman who devoted herself to the recitation of the Lotus Sutra; at one time, seven blue lotuses grew within her sutra chamber—an event deemed most rare by the world.

Upon seeing this, the Retired Scholar’s virtuous mind was stirred within him, and he immediately desired to donate his residence to establish a temple. While these matters were still unfolding in secret, there was at that time the Chan Master Gaoyu.

The Master was residing at Zhuo’an on Mount Loushi, not far from where he was. While the Master was in a state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he flew there with his mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*).

He landed directly in the courtyard of the Retired Scholar Zheng Qian. The scholar exerted all his strength to pull him out, but the staff sank three feet into the ground, causing spring water to gush forth three feet high.

Consequently, he converted his residence into a temple and invited the Zen Master to be the founding patriarch, preach the Dharma, and serve as its abbot. It was for this reason that [the temple was established].
The temple’s name plaque reads "Yongquan Yuan" (Surge-Spring Monastery), and a record of this exists. I obtained this from the lecturer Jingming Shibao of Fenghua.
Bao once personally visited this temple and saw an inscription on a stele which stated:

The elder sister-in-law of Yu Zhi, the Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and Governor of Gaoyang, was a widow at the age of nineteen. She vowed to eat but one meal a day and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* for the rest of her life, never marrying again.
While Yu governed Gaoyang, his sister-in-law was already over seventy years old; her face and eyes were radiant and lustrous.

His deportment was light and agile. In the sixth month of summer in the sixth year of the Zhenghe era, he suddenly gathered his sutra cases, arranged his clothing and ornaments, and entrusted them to his handmaidens.
When asked the reason for this, he smiled and said, "I shall die in three days.
When the time arrived, he passed away peacefully and without illness (from *Hong Juefan’s Zhizheng zhuan*).
Regarding the courtesan Lu Meier of Yingzhou:

during the time when the Duke Wenzhong of Ou-yang governed Yingzhou, there was an official slave girl named Lu Meier. She was of elegant and beautiful appearance and skilled in conversation and laughter;
a lotus fragrance constantly emanated from her mouth, pervading the entire assembly, which everyone marveled at, yet none could fathom its origin.
The reason for this was as follows: shortly thereafter, a monk arrived from Shu who was quite capable of knowing the affairs of people's previous lives.
The official spoke with him, and the monk said, "This girl’s previous life was once that of a nun. She recited the *Lotus Sūtra* for thirty years;
it was due to a single moment of negligence that she has come to this. The official did not believe him at first. Later, seeing the slave, he asked her, "Did you ever read the *Lotus Sūtra*?"
The slave said, "I have lost my person here; I have no leisure for such things. The Master ordered that this scripture be brought and shown to him.
Upon a single glance, he recited it as if he had long been familiar with it. When another scripture was substituted, however, he was unable to do so.

A monk remarked on his error in the *Xianlan* (Leisurely Glimpses) of the *Lunqi* (Dun Qi). Alas! Having spent thirty years as a nun reading and reciting, she too was among those who were diligent and persevering.
Because a single moment’s lapse leads immediately to losing one's way, should not the thoughts of worldly people be rectified?
Those who today serve as courtesans take bodies that are most noble among humans and subject them to base and impure acts.

If they could turn their light back upon themselves and reflect, becoming weary of such deeds, and instead devotedly recite the Mahāyāna sūtras, then in a single instant they would become like the Dragon Girl.

At that moment, one will achieve the seed of awakening; every person has this share. If you do not awaken to this, evil realms will manifest before you, and there will be no place of escape from the three miserable paths of hell.
Regarding the courtesan Yang Yun of Huzhou:

there was a courtesan in Huzhou named Yang Yun who transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* by hand. Whenever she took up the brush, she would first observe a vegetarian fast, bathe, and change her clothes.
Later, on the night she died of illness, her mother suddenly dreamed that Yun came to bid her farewell, saying: "Because I transcribed the sutra..."
By the power of that [merit], she has now been reborn as a daughter in the household of Cai, an official at the Yucheng County Hall.
At that time, Cai’s wife, Fangniang, dreamed one night of a palanquin arriving at her door; when she went out to welcome them, it was Yang Yun, who said she had come to stay for the night.
Upon waking, she gave birth to a girl. Several days later, her mother went to visit her; the girl broke into a silent, enigmatic smile (the *chēzhì* gesture).
This was the Gao Dao-ren of Lin’an Prefecture.
The female practitioner from the Guo family, whose Dharma name was Miaoyuan, was a native of Renhe County. In her youth, she married into the Wen family of Anxi;

however, as her husband was fond of pleasure and neglected his household duties, she left him. She donned monastic robes and plain white garments, vowing to abstain from meat for the rest of her life.
She recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and performed the *Lotus Repentance*, while chanting the name of Amitābha. She constantly faced westward, gazing intently at the setting sun.
One day, a voice from the sky proclaimed: "Guo Miaoyuan, because of your practice, you shall certainly be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

From then on, she redoubled her diligence, never allowing her mind to rest for even a moment. When the time of her passing arrived, she bathed, changed her clothes, invited monks to recite the Buddha’s name, and passed away while sitting upright.
This was the year of Yichou in the Shaoxing era (1145 CE). (From the *Baizhu ji*)

In the early years of the Shaoxing era, there was a woman surnamed Shen of the Shen clan in Mingzhou. Her mother-in-law was of the Wu clan of Shi'e; she was a native of Jiangnan in Dinghai and possessed a nature of integrity and purity.

She cultivated herself through virtuous deeds. Every morning her mother-in-law would recite the Lotus Sutra, and the daughter-in-law served her with meticulous care. Whenever [the ritual] was performed...
Whenever the scrolls were brought out for her to listen to and receive, she would study one or two chapters, or even an entire volume, never growing weary over time. Suddenly, she fell ill;

immediately, she said to her mother-in-law, "While you, my mother-in-law, recite the sutras, I, your daughter-in-law, have been able to hear them. Now that worldly ties must come to an end, I shall not be able to serve you further.
I pray that we may meet again in the assemblies of the Buddhas in future lives. Please transmit this single verse I have composed at random. She was truly joyful throughout her life.
Alive, he was indeed elegant in death. With his final move, he entrusted [his remains] to the firewood. Having said this, he straightened his body, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away.

His sister, seeing his transcendent liberation, went to report it to the Chan Master Hongzhi of Tiandong. Upon hearing this, the Master praised him with joy and subsequently gave him his own funerary niche.
When the cremation was completed, among the remaining bones, what were known as the "solid seeds" (śarīra) were brilliantly lustrous.

It was beyond measure. When the fourfold assembly saw and heard this, they marveled at its rarity and offered praise. This temple on the heart of the lake was personally witnessed and heard by the Dharma Master Fazheng, through whom it was transmitted to later generations.
Zhao of Mingzhou served as its patron.
At the end of the Shaoxing era, there was a man surnamed Zhao in Fenghua County. His mother, a noble lady, revered the Buddha, observed the precepts, and recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.
She had a female servant who would often listen in secret. After some time, the servant suddenly remembered four lines:

"The fragrance of blue lotuses, the fragrance of white lotuses, the fragrance of flowering trees, and the fragrance of fruit trees. From then on, whether moving or at rest, in whatever she did, [she was filled with these fragrances].
She constantly chanted and recited without ceasing; when others heard her, they took it for mere idle chatter, unaware that this woman also possessed a place of deep devotion.
One day, she acted contrary to the master’s wishes and was subjected to a slow execution until death. Consequently, he secretly buried her corpse in the back garden.
Later, suddenly, a single stalk of blue lotus sprouted from atop it, its fragrance and color most lovely. Others—
The cause of this was unknown; only Lady An knew it in silence. Such was the response of the four-line sutra she recited.
Lady An did not conceal her virtue, but privately spoke of it to the Dharma Master Xutang Benkong.
Benkong frequently cited these accounts to transform others. Zongxiao once personally heard these words and has recorded them here for your reference.
Zhu Ruyi of Mingzhou: Zhu’s personal name was Ruyi.
She was the wife of Xue Jun of Siming. Her lineage descended from Empress Qincheng;
she was the granddaughter of two generations from the palace of Emperor Shanyuan. Since returning to the Xue family, she has regarded worldly flavors as mere dust and mud. At the age of twenty—
Her sister then informed her husband. She dwelt in purity, wearing the simple robes of a religious practitioner and maintaining a state of ritual cleanliness.
She once commissioned a scribe to copy seven scrolls of the Lotus Sutra on yellow silk; she then embroidered them by hand with green woolen thread.

The paths of the lines and the needle-holes were so dense and precise that they appeared as fresh as if they had just been read from ink. It took ten years to complete. She further embroidered images of Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara, which were no different [in quality].
He produced paintings and, beginning from the title of the scripture, paid homage eighty-four thousand times. For every phrase and every character, he performed three prostrations.
He was able to recite the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* from memory after three months. Furthermore, he exhorted two hundred thousand people to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha;

he carved woodblocks to create illustrations for this purpose, and once the count reached one hundred thousand recitations, he ceased. He then used the proceeds to purchase bridal trousseaus and established a three-day assembly.

He gathered ten thousand monastics and laypeople. He provided meals for a thousand *bhikṣus* and commissioned precious banners (*ratnadhvaja*) containing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the names of those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
These were escorted back to Yanqing Temple. Suddenly, he was afflicted with a slight illness; when the time came for him to close his eyes, he rose and sat in the full lotus posture.
His attendant, Bi, said, "In my family, there is no such custom. Please go to bed. Thereupon, he passed away lying on his right side at the age of thirty-seven. (From the *Jǔ*)
Chan Master Baotan’s Eulogy states:
*The Record of Manifested Responses of the Lotus Sūtra*, Scroll Lower (End).
Preface to the Carved Edition of the *Record of Manifested Responses of the Lotus Sūtra*.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the king of all sūtras and the ultimate, most profound teaching.

Consequently, its recitation and chanting have been most prevalent, and those who have obtained spiritual efficacy through it are beyond counting. However, these accounts are scattered throughout various records and cannot be easily found;
even when some have been compiled, they are often incomplete. The regrets here are indeed many. The Song dynasty monk Shi-zhi Xiao... [text continues]

The *Xianying lu* (Records of Manifested Responses) in two fascicles collects instances of spiritual resonance from both ancient and modern times that have already been recorded in various texts, as well as those clearly and prominently manifest, including what the author himself has personally heard and witnessed.
This compilation constitutes a great achievement, truly sufficient to verify the accounts of past ages and provide exhortation for the future.
Although it was once transmitted to our country, it had long remained hidden in a remote place. I happened to seek it out, obtain it, and read it; I now wish to have it carved into printing blocks.

It was carved for wide distribution, yet the conditions for its dissemination had not yet been met. Recently, several senior practitioners from a Pure Land society in the mountains saw it and said to me:
"The five kinds of wondrous practices are the supreme causes for rebirth in the Pure Land. Now that this book is being circulated, would you not rejoice in this?"

He then exhorted his fellow members of the society to contribute funds for the incense to collectively assist in this undertaking. I was delighted and once again collated and proofread the text, so that it might be carved upon woodblocks.
Written on the first ten days of the middle month of autumn in the year of Dingwei during the Kyōhō era. Respectfully recorded by the monk Tōei (Ryōten).
